items.title: The Birth of Venus
items.creator: Sandro Botticelli
facts: Tempera on canvas, about 172 by 278 centimetres, in the Uffizi; canvas was an unusual support in fifteenth-century Florence, where panel was the rule.
First recorded by Vasari in 1550 at the Medici villa at Castello, together with the Primavera; who commissioned it is not documented, though Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici is the usual guess.
Venus stands in the pose of an ancient Venus pudica, blown ashore by Zephyr while a figure usually identified as one of the Horae holds out a flowered cloak.
The subject is usually traced to Poliziano's Stanze per la giostra, a poem of the 1470s for Giuliano de' Medici that describes the birth of Venus.
items.remark: Nobody knows who ordered it: it turns up first in 1550, when Vasari saw it at the Medici villa at Castello beside the Primavera, and everything said about Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco commissioning it is inference.
items.gaffe: Looking for it in the Accademia. That is where the David is; the Venus is in the Uffizi, in the same room as the Primavera, and it is on canvas, not fresco.
sources: Uffizi Galleries, catalogue entry 'The Birth of Venus'
Ronald Lightbown, Sandro Botticelli: Life and Work (1989)
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists (1550/1568), Life of Botticelli

items.title: Primavera
items.creator: Sandro Botticelli
facts: Tempera on panel, about 203 by 314 centimetres; listed in a 1499 inventory of the Florentine town house of Lorenzo and Giovanni di Pierfrancesco de' Medici, and seen by Vasari at the villa at Castello in 1550.

Read from right to left: Zephyr seizes the nymph Chloris, who turns into Flora, the figure scattering roses, as told in Ovid's Fasti; Venus stands in the middle with a blindfolded Cupid above her, then the three Graces, then Mercury.
The title is not Botticelli's: Vasari described the picture as Venus adorned by the Graces with flowers, 'denoting spring', and Primavera stuck.
Botanists have identified well over a hundred species of plants in the meadow, most of them flowering in spring.
items.remark: Read it from right to left: the blue Zephyr grabs the nymph Chloris, flowers spill from her mouth, and she becomes Flora next to her; the story is from Ovid's Fasti, and the title is Vasari's, not Botticelli's.
items.gaffe: Confusing it with the Birth of Venus. Venus is in both, but here she is clothed and standing in an orange grove, there is no shell, and it is on panel rather than canvas.
sources: Uffizi Galleries, catalogue entry 'Spring (Primavera)'
Ronald Lightbown, Sandro Botticelli: Life and Work (1989)
Ovid, Fasti, Book V

items.title: David
items.creator: Michelangelo
facts: Carved between 1501 and 1504 from a block of Carrara marble that Agostino di Duccio had roughed out in the 1460s and abandoned; it had lain in the cathedral workshop for decades before Michelangelo, aged twenty-six, was given it.
Meant for a buttress of the cathedral, it went instead to the front of the Palazzo della Signoria in 1504, after a committee that included Leonardo and Botticelli discussed where to put it.
Over five metres tall, it shows David before the fight, sling over his left shoulder; Donatello and Verrocchio had shown him afterwards, with Goliath's head at his feet.
Moved indoors to the Galleria dell'Accademia in 1873; the copy in the Piazza della Signoria dates from 1910.
items.remark: It is the David before the fight, sling over the shoulder and no head at his feet, which is how you tell it from Donatello's; the republic put it outside the town hall in 1504, which was the point.
items.gaffe: Admiring the marble in the Piazza della Signoria. That is a copy of 1910; the original went indoors to the Accademia in 1873, where it has a rotunda to itself.
sources: Galleria dell'Accademia, Florence, catalogue entry 'David'
Charles Seymour, Michelangelo's David: A Search for Identity (1967)
Grove Art Online, 'Michelangelo'

items.title: The Gates of Paradise
items.creator: Lorenzo Ghiberti
facts: Ghiberti's second pair of doors for the Baptistery, commissioned in 1425 and installed on the east side, facing the cathedral, in 1452; his first pair, won in the competition of 1401 against Brunelleschi, took from 1403 to 1424.
Ten square gilded-bronze panels of Old Testament scenes, from Adam and Eve to Solomon and Sheba, in place of the twenty-eight small quatrefoils of the earlier doors.
Vasari reports Michelangelo saying they were beautiful enough to be the gates of Paradise, which is where the name comes from.

The gilded originals, damaged in the flood of 1966, were restored over more than twenty years and have been shown since 2012 in the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo; the doors on the Baptistery are copies installed in 1990.
Ghiberti put his own portrait in the frame, a bald head looking out from among the prophets.
items.remark: What you are looking at on the Baptistery is a copy from 1990; the gilded originals were battered by the 1966 flood and now live across the piazza in the Museo dell'Opera, and the name is Vasari's report of a remark by Michelangelo.
items.gaffe: Saying Ghiberti won the 1401 competition with these. That contest, against Brunelleschi, was for the north doors; the Gates of Paradise are his second set, begun in 1425 and finished twenty-seven years later.
sources: Museo dell'Opera del Duomo, Florence, 'Porta del Paradiso'
Richard Krautheimer, Lorenzo Ghiberti (1956)
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists, Life of Lorenzo Ghiberti

items.title: The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden
items.creator: Masaccio
facts: A fresco of about 1425 on the entrance pier of the Brancacci Chapel in Santa Maria del Carmine, facing Masolino's Temptation of Adam and Eve on the opposite pier.
Masaccio, born Tommaso di ser Giovanni in 1401, died in Rome in 1428 aged twenty-six; Filippino Lippi finished the chapel's frescoes in the 1480s.
The fig leaves that covered Adam and Eve for three centuries, added in the late seventeenth century under the Medici grand dukes, were removed in the restoration completed in 1990.
Michelangelo's Expulsion on the Sistine ceiling is plainly indebted to it; Vasari says the chapel was where the later Florentine painters went to learn.
items.remark: For three hundred years they wore fig leaves put on under the Medici grand dukes; the restoration finished in 1990 took them off, and what is left is Masaccio, dead at twenty-six, painting grief as body weight, Eve howling and Adam hiding his face.
items.gaffe: Treating Masaccio and Masolino as one painter, or as father and son. Two men, unrelated: Masolino painted the graceful Temptation across the arch, Masaccio the Expulsion, and the contrast is the point of the chapel.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Masaccio'
Umberto Baldini and Ornella Casazza, The Brancacci Chapel Frescoes (1992)
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists, Life of Masaccio

items.title: David (bronze)
items.creator: Donatello
facts: Bronze, about 158 centimetres tall, in the Bargello; its date is not documented and estimates run from the 1430s to the 1450s.

Usually called the first free-standing nude statue since antiquity; David wears a laurelled hat and boots, nothing else, and stands on Goliath's severed head with a wing of Goliath's helmet running up the inside of his thigh.

First recorded in 1469, in the courtyard of the Medici palace, at the wedding of Lorenzo the Magnificent; after the Medici were expelled in 1494 it was moved to the courtyard of the Palazzo della Signoria.
Donatello had carved a marble David thirty years earlier, in 1408 to 1409, also now in the Bargello.
items.remark: Hat, boots and nothing else, standing on Goliath's head: it is the first free-standing nude cast since antiquity, and it stood in the Medici courtyard, so this is what the inside of a fifteenth-century bank looked like.
items.gaffe: Assuming 'the David' means Michelangelo's. In the Bargello it means this one, about sixty years older, bronze, life-size, and after the fight rather than before it.
sources: Museo Nazionale del Bargello, Florence, catalogue entry 'David'
H. W. Janson, The Sculpture of Donatello (1957)
Grove Art Online, 'Donatello'

items.title: The Annunciation (San Marco)
items.creator: Fra Angelico
facts: A fresco at the top of the stairs to the friars' dormitory in the convent of San Marco, which Cosimo de' Medici had rebuilt by Michelozzo from the late 1430s; Fra Angelico frescoed the cells and corridors over the following decade.
The loggia in which Gabriel and Mary meet is modelled on Michelozzo's own architecture in the cloister below: slender columns, plain capitals, whitewashed walls.
An inscription beneath tells the passer-by, on coming before the image of the intact Virgin, not to forget to say an Ave.

Fra Angelico, born Guido di Pietro, was a Dominican friar; he was beatified in 1982 and named patron of artists by John Paul II in 1984. He painted the Annunciation several times, including the panel now in the Prado and a second fresco inside cell 3 at San Marco.
items.remark: It is painted where the friars met it every night on the way up to bed, at the head of the dormitory stairs, and the line underneath tells you to say an Ave Maria as you pass; it was made to be used, not visited.
items.gaffe: Assuming there is one Fra Angelico Annunciation. He painted the subject at least four times, including a panel in the Prado and a second fresco inside a cell a few yards away; this is the one at the top of the stairs, with Michelozzo's loggia in it.
sources: Museo di San Marco, Florence, catalogue entry 'Annunciazione' (north corridor)
John Pope-Hennessy, Fra Angelico (2nd ed., 1974)
William Hood, Fra Angelico at San Marco (1993)

items.title: The Doni Tondo
items.creator: Michelangelo
facts: A round panel, about 120 centimetres across, of the Holy Family with the infant Baptist, painted for the Florentine merchant Agnolo Doni, probably around his marriage to Maddalena Strozzi in 1504; it is still in its original carved frame.
The only finished panel painting universally accepted as Michelangelo's; the two panels in the National Gallery, London, are unfinished and their attribution has been argued over.
Raphael painted the portraits of Agnolo and Maddalena Doni at about the same time; long in the Palazzo Pitti, they were moved to the Uffizi in 2018 and now hang in the same room as the tondo.
Vasari tells a story that Doni tried to pay less than the agreed price and Michelangelo responded by doubling it.
The nude young men on the wall behind the Holy Family have never been satisfactorily explained; the usual reading makes them the pagan world before the coming of grace.
items.remark: It is the only panel painting everyone agrees Michelangelo finished, and it looks like sculpture; the Virgin twists like a figure on the Sistine ceiling, which he began the year after.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Raphael because Raphael painted the Donis. Raphael did the husband and wife, which since 2018 hang beside it in the Uffizi; Michelangelo did their tondo, and the naked youths at the back are the giveaway.
sources: Uffizi Galleries, catalogue entry 'Doni Tondo'
Grove Art Online, 'Michelangelo'
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists, Life of Michelangelo

items.title: Giotto
facts: Born near Florence about 1267 and died in Florence in January 1337; Dante, his contemporary, wrote in the Purgatorio that Cimabue had thought to hold the field in painting, 'and now Giotto has the cry'.
His Ognissanti Madonna of about 1310 hangs in the first room of the Uffizi beside Cimabue's Santa Trinita Maestà and Duccio's Rucellai Madonna, so the change he made can be seen in one glance.
The Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, frescoed about 1305, is his masterpiece; in Florence he frescoed the Bardi and Peruzzi chapels in Santa Croce.
Appointed master of works for Florence cathedral in 1334, he designed the bell tower that still carries his name.

The stories that Cimabue found him as a shepherd boy drawing a sheep on a rock, and that he drew a perfect circle freehand for the Pope's messenger, are told by Ghiberti and Vasari a century and more later.
items.remark: Dante put him in the Purgatorio while he was still alive, saying Cimabue had held the field in painting and now Giotto had the cry, and the Uffizi hangs his Ognissanti Madonna beside Cimabue's so you can check.
items.gaffe: Placing the Scrovegni Chapel in Florence. It is in Padua; Florence has the Ognissanti Madonna in the Uffizi, the Bardi and Peruzzi chapels in Santa Croce and the Campanile.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Giotto'
Dante, Purgatorio XI, 94–96
Uffizi Galleries, catalogue entry 'Ognissanti Madonna'

items.title: Filippo Brunelleschi
facts: Trained as a goldsmith; lost the 1401 competition for the Baptistery doors to Ghiberti, and both trial panels of the Sacrifice of Isaac are in the Bargello.

Entered the 1418 competition for a model of the cathedral dome, which had stood open since Arnolfo di Cambio began the church in 1296, and built it from 1420 to 1436 as an inner and an outer shell with herringbone brickwork, without wooden centring across the void.
The dome, about 45 metres across, is still the largest brick dome ever built; the lantern on top is his design but was finished after his death.

His demonstration of linear perspective with painted panels of the Baptistery and the Piazza della Signoria, described by his biographer Manetti, is the foundation of Renaissance picture space; Alberti wrote the method up in De pictura in 1435.
Also built the Ospedale degli Innocenti, San Lorenzo, Santo Spirito and the Pazzi Chapel; he is buried in the cathedral.
items.remark: The dome went up without a wooden frame across the void, an inner and an outer shell with the bricks laid in a herringbone, and the man who worked it out had lost the Baptistery doors competition to Ghiberti twenty years earlier; both trial panels are in the Bargello.
items.gaffe: Crediting him with the cathedral. Arnolfo di Cambio began it in 1296; Brunelleschi's job, from 1420 to 1436, was the hole in the roof that nobody for a century had known how to cover.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Brunelleschi, Filippo'
Antonio Manetti, The Life of Brunelleschi (ed. Howard Saalman, 1970)
Howard Saalman, Filippo Brunelleschi: The Cupola of Santa Maria del Fiore (1980)

items.title: The Renaissance
facts: The idea is Vasari's: in the Lives of 1550 he described a rinascita, a rebirth of the arts in Tuscany after the Middle Ages; the French word and the notion of a whole period came with Michelet in 1855 and Burckhardt's Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy in 1860.
The usual starting line in Florence is the 1401 competition for the Baptistery doors; the founding generation is Brunelleschi in architecture, Donatello in sculpture and Masaccio in painting.

Linear perspective, demonstrated by Brunelleschi and written up by Alberti in De pictura in 1435, is the technical signature; the money was Medici, from Cosimo il Vecchio's return in 1434 to Lorenzo the Magnificent's death in 1492.

Art historians divide it into Early (the fifteenth century), High (Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael, roughly 1495 to 1520) and then Mannerism; the Sack of Rome in 1527 is the conventional end of the High Renaissance.
items.remark: The word is Vasari's, more or less: he wrote in 1550 of a rinascita of the arts, and he meant Florence; it took a Frenchman and a Swiss, Michelet and Burckhardt, to turn it into a period three centuries later.
items.gaffe: Using 'Renaissance' for anything old and Italian. Giotto is before it, Botticelli is Early, Leonardo and Michelangelo are High, and by the 1530s you are in Mannerism; the whole Florentine run is little more than a century.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Renaissance'
Jacob Burckhardt, The Civilization of the Renaissance in Italy (1860)
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists (1550/1568), preface

items.title: Fresco
facts: Cennino Cennini's Il libro dell'arte, written around 1400, describes the method; the seams between one day's plaster and the next can still be seen and counted on Masaccio's Brancacci frescoes.
The Sistine ceiling, the Brancacci Chapel and Fra Angelico's cells at San Marco are true fresco; Leonardo's Last Supper in Milan is not, and began to deteriorate within twenty years.
Pigments have to survive the lime, so the range is limited: blues were often added afterwards a secco, which is why so much fresco sky has flaked off.
items.remark: Fresco means fresh: the colour goes onto wet plaster and becomes part of the wall, which is why you can count the day-joins on a Masaccio, and why Leonardo's Last Supper, which was not one, started coming off within twenty years.
items.gaffe: Calling every painting on a wall a fresco. The Last Supper is the great exception, painted on a dry wall in a mixture of Leonardo's own devising, and its condition is the price.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Fresco'
Cennino Cennini, Il libro dell'arte (trans. Daniel V. Thompson, 1933)

term: Painting in pigment bound with egg yolk on a gessoed wooden panel, the standard method before oil.
A round painting or relief, popular in Florentine houses in the fifteenth century.
A full-scale preparatory drawing, pricked or incised to transfer the design to the wall.

items.definition: Painting on fresh, still-wet lime plaster, so that the pigment, mixed only with water, binds into the wall as it dries (buon fresco). The painter works in giornate, a day's patch of plaster at a time; painting on dry plaster is fresco secco, and it flakes.

items.title: Contrapposto
facts: Polykleitos's Doryphoros of about 440 BC is the textbook ancient example; the Greeks worked the pose out in the fifth century BC, and medieval sculpture lost it.
Donatello's marble Saint Mark for Orsanmichele, of about 1411 to 1413, is usually cited as the first full Renaissance revival; Michelangelo's David is the most famous.
The word in Italian also means 'antithesis' in rhetoric; art historians borrowed it for the pose.
items.remark: Weight on one leg, hip up on that side, shoulder down on the same side: it is what makes a statue look as if it could take a step, and Donatello's Saint Mark at Orsanmichele is where Florence got it back from the Greeks.
items.gaffe: Using it for any twisting pose. A figure spiralling on its own axis is a figura serpentinata, which is Mannerist and later; contrapposto is standing still with the weight on one foot.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Contrapposto'
Grove Art Online, 'Donatello'

term: The smoky blending of tones so that outlines dissolve, as in Leonardo's faces.
Strong contrast of light and shadow used to model form, as in Caravaggio.
Relief carved so shallow that the figures barely rise from the ground, a Donatello speciality.

items.definition: Italian for 'counterpoise': a standing figure with its weight on one leg, so that the hips tilt one way and the shoulders the other and the body settles into a gentle S. The Greek invention that makes a statue look able to move, revived in Florence by Donatello and made colossal in Michelangelo's David.

items.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
items.creator: Jan van Eyck
facts: Hangs in the National Gallery, London, which bought it in 1842.
The Latin inscription above the mirror reads 'Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434': Jan van Eyck was here.
The convex mirror reflects two figures in the doorway, one of whom may be the painter.
items.remark: Look at the mirror: two people are standing where you are standing, and the signature above it says the painter was here. It is a witness statement as much as a portrait.
items.gaffe: Announcing that it depicts a wedding. Panofsky argued that in 1934, and art historians have been arguing about it ever since.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG186
Erwin Panofsky, 'Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait', Burlington Magazine (1934)

items.title: J. M. W. Turner
facts: Born in Covent Garden in 1775; entered the Royal Academy Schools at fourteen.
Rain, Steam and Speed (1844) is in the National Gallery; the bulk of the Turner Bequest is at Tate Britain.
items.remark: Turner left the nation the contents of his studio on condition it be kept together; that is why so much of him is in one building at Tate Britain.
items.gaffe: Confusing him with Constable. Constable painted Suffolk skies and hay wains; Turner painted light dissolving everything.
sources: Tate, 'Joseph Mallord William Turner 1775–1851' artist biography

items.title: The Ambassadors
items.creator: Hans Holbein the Younger
facts: Painted in London and signed and dated 1533; the sitters are Jean de Dinteville, French ambassador to Henry VIII, aged twenty-nine, and his friend Georges de Selve, bishop of Lavaur, aged twenty-five.
The distorted grey shape across the floor is an anamorphic skull, which comes into focus only when the picture is viewed from the right-hand side at a steep angle.
The shelves between the men hold a celestial globe, a terrestrial globe, sundials, a Lutheran hymnbook and a lute with a broken string.
Bought by the National Gallery in 1890 from the Earl of Radnor's collection at Longford Castle; it is NG1314.
items.remark: The smear across the floor is a skull, but only from the right-hand edge; stand there and the two ambassadors flatten out while the death's head snaps into focus.
items.gaffe: Calling them Henry VIII's ambassadors. They are French, Dinteville and de Selve, at Henry's court in the year of the Boleyn marriage, and the broken lute string is not an accident.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG1314
Susan Foister, Ashok Roy and Martin Wyld, Making and Meaning: Holbein's Ambassadors (National Gallery, 1997)

items.title: The Toilet of Venus (The Rokeby Venus)
items.creator: Diego Velázquez
facts: Painted in about 1647 to 1651, and the only female nude by Velázquez to survive; nudes were rare in Spain under the Inquisition.
Venus lies with her back to us while Cupid holds a mirror; the reflected face is blurred and, at that angle, could not really show her face at all.
Named after Rokeby Park in Yorkshire, where it hung in the nineteenth century; bought for the nation in 1906 by the National Art Collections Fund, its first major purchase.
On 10 March 1914 the suffragette Mary Richardson attacked it with a meat cleaver in protest at the treatment of Emmeline Pankhurst; the cuts were repaired.
items.remark: It is the only Velázquez nude that survives, and a suffragette went at it with a meat cleaver in 1914; the restoration is good enough that you have to know where the cuts were.
items.gaffe: Asking which Italian painted it. It is Spanish, from Philip IV's court, and the name is a Yorkshire country house, not a place in Italy.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG2057
Jonathan Brown, Velázquez: Painter and Courtier (1986)

items.title: The Fighting Temeraire
items.creator: J. M. W. Turner
facts: Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1839 with the full title 'The Fighting Temeraire tugged to her last berth to be broken up, 1838'.
The Temeraire, a 98-gun ship, fought at Trafalgar in 1805 next in line behind Victory; in September 1838 she was towed from Sheerness up the Thames to a breaker's yard at Rotherhithe.
Turner refused to sell it, called it his darling, and left it to the nation in the Turner Bequest; it is NG524.
Voted the greatest painting in Britain in a BBC Radio 4 poll in 2005, and printed on the Bank of England twenty-pound note issued in 2020.
items.remark: By the time she was towed the masts and rigging had already been stripped out; Turner put them back, because a bare hull would not have made an elegy.
items.gaffe: Calling it a picture of Trafalgar. Trafalgar was 1805; this is 1838, an old ship being pulled to the breakers by a steam tug, and the tug is the villain.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG524
Judy Egerton, Turner: The Fighting Temeraire (National Gallery, 1995)

items.title: The Hay Wain
items.creator: John Constable
facts: Exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1821 as 'Landscape: Noon' and left unsold; painted in Constable's London studio from sketches made on the Stour.
The house on the left is Willy Lott's cottage at Flatford, Suffolk, beside the mill that Constable's father owned; the cart is crossing the millpond, not stuck in it.
Bought by the Paris dealer John Arrowsmith and shown at the Salon of 1824, where Charles X awarded Constable a gold medal.
Presented to the National Gallery by Henry Vaughan in 1886; the full-size oil sketch for it is in the Victoria and Albert Museum.
items.remark: Nobody bought it at the Academy in 1821; a French dealer took it to the Salon of 1824, where Charles X gave it a gold medal and the French painters took notes.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Turner. Turner painted light dissolving ships; Constable painted the Suffolk he grew up in, and the view from Flatford is still there to check.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG1207
Graham Reynolds, The Later Paintings and Drawings of John Constable (1984)

items.title: Mr and Mrs Andrews
items.creator: Thomas Gainsborough
facts: Painted in about 1750: Robert Andrews and Frances Carter, married in 1748, on their estate, the Auberies, near Sudbury in Suffolk, Gainsborough's home town.
Half the canvas is given to the couple's land, with the wheat in neat drilled rows; the patch on Mrs Andrews's lap was left unfinished and nobody knows what was meant to go there.
Stayed with the family's descendants until the National Gallery bought it in 1960; it is NG6301.
John Berger's Ways of Seeing (1972) made it the textbook example of a portrait of property as much as of people.
items.remark: Half the picture is a field, and that is the point: they are showing you the acres as much as themselves, and the blank on her lap was never painted in.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Reynolds. Reynolds painted his sitters as Roman senators and goddesses; Gainsborough put his under an oak tree with their own wheat behind them.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG6301
John Berger, Ways of Seeing (1972)

items.title: Whistlejacket
items.creator: George Stubbs
facts: Painted in about 1762 for Charles Watson-Wentworth, 2nd Marquess of Rockingham, later twice prime minister, who owned the horse; it hung at Wentworth Woodhouse in Yorkshire.
A rearing Arabian stallion at life size, nearly three metres tall, against a plain bare ground: no rider, no landscape, no sky.
Stubbs had spent about eighteen months dissecting horses in a farmhouse at Horkstow in Lincolnshire, and published The Anatomy of the Horse from those drawings in 1766.
Bought by the National Gallery in 1997 with help from the Heritage Lottery Fund; it is NG6569.
items.remark: There is no rider, no landscape, nothing but a life-size Arabian on bare canvas, painted by a man who had spent eighteen months dissecting horses in a Lincolnshire barn.
items.gaffe: Dismissing Stubbs as a horse painter. He was an anatomist who published The Anatomy of the Horse from his own dissections, and the Academy's snobbery about animal pictures is the reason he is undervalued.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG6569

items.title: Sunflowers
items.creator: Vincent van Gogh
facts: Painted in Arles in August 1888 to decorate the room in the Yellow House that Gauguin was coming to occupy; fifteen sunflowers in a vase on a yellow ground.
One of seven vase pictures: four painted in August 1888 and three repetitions in January 1889; the Amsterdam canvas is Van Gogh's own copy of the London one.
Signed 'Vincent' on the vase, as he always signed; bought by the National Gallery in 1924 through the Courtauld Fund, and it is NG3863.
items.remark: He painted them in August 1888 for the bedroom Gauguin was about to move into; the London canvas is one of the originals, and Amsterdam's is his own copy of it.
items.gaffe: Saying 'the Sunflowers' as if there were one. There are seven of the vase pictures in Arles alone, and the National Gallery's is the one he copied for the Amsterdam version.
sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG3863

items.title: Ophelia
items.creator: John Everett Millais
facts: Painted in 1851 and 1852 and exhibited at the Royal Academy in 1852; the subject is Gertrude's speech in Hamlet, Act IV, describing a drowning that happens offstage.

The riverbank was painted from life on the Hogsmill at Ewell in Surrey over about five months, from July into November 1851; Elizabeth Siddal then posed for the figure in a bath of water in Millais's London studio, warmed by lamps underneath.
The lamps went out, Siddal caught a bad cold, and her father threatened Millais with an action for the doctor's bills.
Presented to the nation by Sir Henry Tate in 1894; it hangs at Tate Britain.
items.remark: The drowning happens offstage in Hamlet; Millais painted Gertrude's speech, and did the river first, at Ewell, for about five months before the girl went into a bath in London.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Rossetti or Waterhouse. Rossetti drew Siddal endlessly but not this, and Waterhouse's drowning girls came forty years later.
sources: Tate, catalogue entry N01506, 'Ophelia'

items.title: William Hogarth
facts: Born in Smithfield, London, in 1697, the son of a schoolmaster who was imprisoned for debt; apprenticed to a silver engraver before turning to painting.

Invented what he called 'modern moral subjects', stories told in a series of pictures and sold as engravings: A Harlot's Progress (1732), A Rake's Progress (1732 to 1734, engraved 1735, Sir John Soane's Museum) and Marriage A-la-Mode (about 1743, National Gallery).
The Engravers' Copyright Act of 1735, still called Hogarth's Act, was passed after pirates copied A Harlot's Progress; it was the first copyright protection for artists in Britain.
Painted himself with his pug, Trump, in 1745 (Tate Britain); the six Marriage A-la-Mode canvases came to the National Gallery with the Angerstein collection at its foundation in 1824.
items.remark: The paintings were almost a sideline; he told the stories in six or eight scenes, sold the engravings by subscription, and got Parliament to pass a copyright act in 1735 so nobody else could.
items.gaffe: Treating Marriage A-la-Mode as six separate pictures. It is one story in order, from the marriage settlement to the countess's suicide, and the point is the sequence.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Hogarth, William'
Ronald Paulson, Hogarth (3 vols, 1991 to 1993)

items.title: James McNeill Whistler
facts: Born in Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1834; left America for Paris in 1855 and never went back; settled in London in 1859 and lived mostly in Chelsea until his death in 1903.
Gave his pictures musical titles, Symphony, Arrangement, Harmony, Nocturne; the portrait of his mother is Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 (1871, Musée d'Orsay).

Sued Ruskin for libel in 1877, after Ruskin wrote that he was 'flinging a pot of paint in the public's face' with Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket; at the trial in November 1878 he won a farthing in damages, and the costs bankrupted him in 1879.
Tate Britain holds the Thames Nocturnes, including Nocturne: Blue and Gold, Old Battersea Bridge and Nocturne: Blue and Silver, Chelsea.
items.remark: Ruskin accused him of flinging a pot of paint in the public's face; Whistler sued, won a farthing, and the costs bankrupted him, which makes it the most expensive farthing in English art.
items.gaffe: Calling him English. He was American, from Lowell, Massachusetts, left for Paris at twenty-one and never went home; London and Paris were his cities.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Whistler, James Abbott McNeill'
Linda Merrill, A Pot of Paint: Aesthetics on Trial in Whistler v. Ruskin (1992)
Tate, 'James Abbott McNeill Whistler 1834–1903' artist biography

items.title: The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood
facts: Founded in London in September 1848 by seven young men, none older than twenty-three: Dante Gabriel Rossetti, John Everett Millais and William Holman Hunt, with Thomas Woolner, James Collinson, Frederic George Stephens and William Michael Rossetti.

They signed early pictures with the secret initials PRB and rejected the conventions the Academy taught from Raphael, preferring the sharp detail and bright colour of art before him; Reynolds they nicknamed 'Sir Sloshua'.

Dickens attacked Millais's Christ in the House of His Parents in Household Words in 1850, calling the boy Jesus 'wry-necked, blubbering, red-headed'; Ruskin defended the group in letters to The Times in 1851.
The Brotherhood had dispersed by 1853, but Burne-Jones and William Morris carried a second Pre-Raphaelite wave into the 1860s and beyond; the Tate holds the core collection.
items.remark: The name means before Raphael: they thought painting went wrong with him and that Reynolds, whom they called Sir Sloshua, finished the job; Dickens loathed them and Ruskin saved them.
items.gaffe: Assuming they painted like Raphael. The whole point was to paint as if he had never happened, in hard-edged detail from nature, and on a white ground so the colour glowed.
sources: Tate, art term 'Pre-Raphaelite'
Elizabeth Prettejohn, The Art of the Pre-Raphaelites (2000)
Malcolm Warner et al., The Pre-Raphaelites (Tate Gallery exhibition catalogue, 1984)

items.title: Conversation piece
facts: The term was in use in England by the 1720s; Hogarth, Arthur Devis, Johann Zoffany and the young Gainsborough were its chief practitioners.
Gainsborough's Mr and Mrs Andrews in the National Gallery is the example everyone knows; Zoffany painted the royal family and the Academicians in the same idiom.
The scale is that of a cabinet picture: full-length figures a foot or so high, which is what separates it from the life-size portrait of the Grand Manner.
items.remark: A conversation piece is a small group portrait of people doing something, tea or cards or a walk over their acres, and the joke of the name is that nobody in one is ever talking.
items.gaffe: Using it to mean an object that starts a conversation. In a gallery it is a genre, Hogarth and Devis and Zoffany, small full-length figures at home.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Conversation piece'
Mario Praz, Conversation Pieces: A Survey of the Informal Group Portrait in Europe and America (1971)

term: A portrait in which the sitter is shown in the costume and pose of a classical hero or goddess.
A painting of a crowded public entertainment such as a fair, a masquerade or a race meeting.
A pair of portraits of husband and wife painted to hang facing each other.

items.definition: An informal group portrait, usually small in scale, showing a family or friends at some shared occupation, taking tea, making music, walking their land, in a domestic or landscape setting; a British speciality of the eighteenth century.

items.title: The Grand Manner
facts: Reynolds delivered fifteen Discourses to the Royal Academy between 1769 and 1790 as its first President; the Academy was founded in 1768 and he was knighted the following year.
In practice it meant painting a sitter in the pose of an antique statue or as a figure from mythology, and treating portraiture as a branch of history painting.
Reynolds's Discourse XIV, delivered after Gainsborough's death in 1788, praised him generously while noting that he had never attempted the grand style.
The Pre-Raphaelites' nickname for Reynolds, 'Sir Sloshua', was aimed at exactly this manner.
items.remark: The Grand Manner is Reynolds's term for painting a general as a Roman and a lady as a goddess; he laid it down in fifteen Discourses to the Academy, and it is what the Pre-Raphaelites meant by Sir Sloshua.
items.gaffe: Calling Gainsborough's portraits Grand Manner. Gainsborough is the counter-example, and Reynolds's own Discourse XIV credits him with everything except the grand style.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Grand Manner'
Joshua Reynolds, Discourses on Art, ed. Robert R. Wark (1975)

term: A loose, rapid way of painting in which the brushstrokes remain visible on the surface.
The British fashion for small informal group portraits of families at their leisure.
A landscape style of ruined temples and golden evening light modelled on Claude.

items.definition: The elevated style of history painting and portraiture, drawn from the Italian High Renaissance and the antique, that Joshua Reynolds set out in his Discourses to the Royal Academy: idealised figures, classical poses and general truths in place of particular detail.

items.title: Mona Lisa
items.creator: Leonardo da Vinci
facts: Oil on poplar panel, 77 by 53 centimetres, Louvre Inv. 779; Leonardo took it with him to France in his last years, and it has been in the French royal and then national collection since Francis I.

Vasari's Lives (1550) says Leonardo painted the wife of Francesco del Giocondo, hence La Gioconda and La Joconde; a marginal note by Agostino Vespucci dated October 1503, found at Heidelberg in 2005, confirms he was at work on the portrait of Lisa del Giocondo then.
There are no drawn outlines: the face is modelled by thin glazes shading into shadow, the technique known as sfumato, and there are no eyebrows or lashes.

Stolen on 21 August 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian house painter who had worked on glazing pictures at the Louvre; recovered in Florence in December 1913 when he tried to sell it to the Uffizi through a dealer.
Hangs behind glass on its own wall in the Salle des États, the largest room in the Louvre, facing Veronese's Wedding at Cana.
items.remark: Until August 1911 it was an admired Leonardo and no more; then Vincenzo Peruggia, who had fitted glass at the Louvre, walked out with it under his smock, and two years on a missing wall did more for its fame than four centuries on a full one.
items.gaffe: Asking who she was as if nobody knew. Vasari named her in 1550, Lisa Gherardini, wife of the Florentine cloth merchant Francesco del Giocondo, and a note found at Heidelberg in 2005 has Leonardo at work on her in October 1503.
sources: Musée du Louvre, catalogue entry Inv. 779 (Portrait de Lisa Gherardini, épouse de Francesco del Giocondo, dite Monna Lisa, la Gioconda ou la Joconde)
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists (1550/1568), Life of Leonardo da Vinci
Martin Kemp and Giuseppe Pallanti, Mona Lisa: The People and the Painting (2017)

items.title: The Raft of the Medusa
items.creator: Théodore Géricault
facts: Oil on canvas, 491 by 716 centimetres, Louvre Inv. 4884; shown at the Salon of 1819 under the neutral title Scène de naufrage, and bought for the Louvre after Géricault's death in 1824.

The frigate Méduse ran aground on the Arguin bank off the West African coast on 2 July 1816, bound for Senegal; the officers took the boats, about 147 people were put on a raft that was cut loose from its tow, and thirteen days later the Argus found fifteen of them alive.

The captain, Hugues Duroy de Chaumareys, was a returned émigré given the ship by the restored Bourbon government; two survivors, the surgeon Savigny and the engineer Corréard, published an account in 1817 that became a scandal against the regime.

Géricault interviewed the survivors, had a model of the raft built, and painted severed limbs and heads borrowed from the Beaujon hospital; Delacroix, then twenty, is said to have posed for the corpse lying face down in the foreground.
Shown in London at Bullock's Egyptian Hall in Piccadilly in 1820, where it drew tens of thousands of paying visitors; Géricault died in January 1824, aged thirty-two.
items.remark: It went to the Salon of 1819 as 'Scene of a Shipwreck', because naming the Medusa would have named the Bourbon ministry that gave a frigate to an émigré captain chosen for his loyalty rather than his seamanship.
items.gaffe: Calling it a Delacroix. Delacroix is the twenty-year-old friend who is said to have posed for the corpse in the foreground; Géricault painted it, and was dead at thirty-two five years later.
sources: Musée du Louvre, catalogue entry Inv. 4884 (Le Radeau de la Méduse)
Lorenz Eitner, Géricault's Raft of the Medusa (1972)
Jonathan Miles, Medusa: The Shipwreck, the Scandal, the Masterpiece (2007)

items.title: Liberty Leading the People
items.creator: Eugène Delacroix
facts: Oil on canvas, 260 by 325 centimetres, Louvre RF 129; painted in the autumn of 1830 and shown at the Salon of 1831 as 'Le 28 juillet: La Liberté guidant le peuple'.

The subject is the July Revolution of 1830, the three days of 27 to 29 July that ended the reign of Charles X and put Louis-Philippe on the throne; the towers of Notre-Dame stand at the right with a tricolour flying from one of them.
Delacroix wrote to his brother in October 1830 that he had taken on a modern subject, a barricade, and that if he had not fought for his country he would at least paint for her.
The state bought it in 1831 for 3,000 francs, hung it briefly, then kept it out of sight as too inflammatory; it came back on view after 1848 and entered the Louvre in 1874.

The man in the top hat with the musket has often been taken for Delacroix himself, an identification most scholars now reject; the boy with two pistols is usually said to have suggested Gavroche in Hugo's Les Misérables (1862), and the picture was on the 100-franc note from 1978 to 1995.
items.remark: It is not 1789: it is the three days of July 1830 that got rid of Charles X, and Delacroix, who had watched rather than fought, told his brother that if he had not won for his country he would at least paint for her.
items.gaffe: Placing it in 1789, or on the barricades of Les Misérables. It is July 1830; Hugo's barricade is June 1832, though the boy with the pistols is generally taken to have suggested Gavroche.
sources: Musée du Louvre, catalogue entry RF 129 (Le 28 juillet 1830. La Liberté guidant le peuple)

items.title: The Oath of the Horatii
items.creator: Jacques-Louis David
facts: Oil on canvas, 330 by 425 centimetres, Louvre Inv. 3692; commissioned by the Crown through the comte d'Angiviller, painted in Rome in 1784 and shown there in David's studio before it reached the Paris Salon of 1785.

The story is from Livy: three brothers of the Horatii fight three Curiatii of Alba Longa to settle a war between the two cities, and Corneille made a tragedy of it, Horace, in 1640. The oath sworn on the swords is in neither Livy nor Corneille.

The women at the right are Sabina, a Curiatius sister married to a Horatius, and Camilla, a Horatius sister betrothed to a Curiatius; in Livy the surviving brother kills Camilla for mourning her lover.

Three arches, three groups, straight lines for the men and curves for the women: it became the model for Neoclassical history painting, and later, against its own date, an image of Revolutionary virtue.

David went on to sit in the Convention, vote for the death of Louis XVI, sketch Marie Antoinette on the cart to the scaffold in October 1793, paint the Death of Marat and the Coronation of Napoleon, and die in exile in Brussels in 1825.
items.remark: It was a royal commission, painted in Rome for Louis XVI's Bâtiments du Roi five years before the Bastille, and the oath itself is in neither Livy nor Corneille: David invented the one moment the picture is about.
items.gaffe: Reading it as a Revolutionary manifesto. It is 1784 and paid for by the Crown; David's politics came later, and by January 1793 he was voting for the king's death.
sources: Musée du Louvre, catalogue entry Inv. 3692 (Le Serment des Horaces)

items.title: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe
items.creator: Édouard Manet
facts: Oil on canvas, 208 by 264.5 centimetres, Musée d'Orsay RF 1668; rejected by the Salon jury of 1863 and shown at the Salon des Refusés, which opened on 15 May 1863, under the title Le Bain.

The group is lifted from Marcantonio Raimondi's engraving after Raphael's Judgement of Paris, and the idea of naked women beside dressed men from Titian's Pastoral Concert in the Louvre; the nude is Victorine Meurent, who posed for Olympia the same year.

The men are one of Manet's brothers and his future brother-in-law, the sculptor Ferdinand Leenhoff; the still life of clothes and fruit at the lower left is painted with more care than the landscape behind.
Given to the state by Étienne Moreau-Nélaton in 1906; it hung in the Louvre from 1934 and moved to the Orsay when that museum opened in 1986.
Manet never exhibited with the Impressionists, though the younger painters treated him as their leader; he kept submitting to the Salon until his death in 1883.
items.remark: Its scandal was not the nude but her company: Titian's Pastoral Concert in the Louvre has naked women beside clothed men too, but Manet's men wear the frock coats of 1863, and the woman looks straight at you.
items.gaffe: Calling it an Impressionist painting shown at the Salon. The jury threw it out; it hung at the Salon des Refusés of 1863 as Le Bain, eleven years before the first Impressionist exhibition, which Manet declined to join, as he declined all eight.
sources: Musée d'Orsay, catalogue entry RF 1668 (Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe)

items.title: Impression, Sunrise
items.creator: Claude Monet
facts: Oil on canvas, 48 by 63 centimetres, in the Musée Marmottan Monet in Paris, given in 1940 by Victorine Donop de Monchy, daughter of Monet's doctor and collector Georges de Bellio.
The view is the port of Le Havre from a hotel window, signed and dated '72'; the museum's work with astronomers in 2014 put the sunrise on a November morning in 1872.

Shown in April 1874 at the first exhibition of the Société anonyme of painters, sculptors and engravers at 35 boulevard des Capucines, the photographer Nadar's former studio; Louis Leroy's review in Le Charivari on 25 April was headed 'Exhibition of the Impressionists', and the name stuck.
Monet told the journalist Maurice Guillemot in 1897 that, asked for a catalogue title, he had said it could hardly pass for a view of Le Havre, so they should put 'Impression'.
Stolen from the Marmottan on 27 October 1985 with eight other pictures and recovered in Corsica in December 1990.
items.remark: The name of the whole movement is a joke that stuck: Louis Leroy, reviewing this in Le Charivari in April 1874, headed his piece 'Exhibition of the Impressionists', and the painters adopted the insult.
items.gaffe: Looking for it in the Musée d'Orsay. It is in the Marmottan, out in the sixteenth arrondissement, where it was stolen in 1985 and came back from Corsica five years later.
sources: Musée Marmottan Monet, collection entry 'Impression, soleil levant'
Marianne Mathieu and Dominique Lobstein (eds), Monet's Impression, Sunrise: The Biography of a Painting (Musée Marmottan Monet, 2014)

items.title: Bal du moulin de la Galette
items.creator: Pierre-Auguste Renoir
facts: Oil on canvas, 131 by 175 centimetres, Musée d'Orsay RF 2739; shown at the third Impressionist exhibition in 1877 and left to the state by Gustave Caillebotte in 1894.

The Moulin de la Galette was a dance garden beside two old windmills at the top of Montmartre, open on Sunday afternoons; Renoir took a studio nearby in the rue Cortot in 1875 and had the canvas carried down to paint on the spot.
The sitters are friends: the journalist Georges Rivière at the table, the painters Franc-Lamy and Norbert Gœneutte, and the models Estelle and Jeanne in the foreground.
The dappled patches on the dancers' clothes and the ground are sunlight through acacia leaves.
A smaller version sold at Sotheby's in New York on 17 May 1990 for 78.1 million dollars to the Japanese businessman Ryoei Saito, two days after he bought Van Gogh's Portrait of Dr Gachet.
items.remark: The patches on the dancers' clothes are sunlight through acacia leaves, painted on the spot on a Montmartre Sunday afternoon; the Moulin was a real windmill with a dance floor, and the Moulin Rouge did not exist for another thirteen years.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Monet, or confusing the Galette with the Moulin Rouge. The Galette was a windmill with a dance garden at the top of Montmartre; the Moulin Rouge opened at the foot of the hill in 1889 and its sails never turned for flour.

items.title: Edgar Degas
facts: Born in Paris in 1834 into a banking family that spelled the name De Gas, and died in Paris in 1917; trained under Louis Lamothe, a pupil of Ingres, and told Paul Valéry that Ingres himself had advised him in 1855 to draw lines, many lines.

Showed at seven of the eight Impressionist exhibitions, all but 1882, and disliked the name; he preferred Independents, worked in the studio from drawings and memory, and had no use for painting outdoors.

Dancers make up something like half his output, mostly at class and rehearsal at the Paris Opéra rather than on stage; the Little Dancer Aged Fourteen, a wax figure dressed in a real tutu and shown in 1881, was the only sculpture he exhibited in his life, and the bronzes were cast after his death.
The Musée d'Orsay holds The Dance Class and L'Absinthe; his eyesight failed from the 1870s, and the late pastels are large, coarse and mostly of women bathing.
An anti-Dreyfusard who broke with Jewish friends, including the Halévy family, during the affair.
items.remark: He showed with the Impressionists at seven of their eight exhibitions and hated the word: no sunsets, no painting outdoors, everything worked up indoors from drawings and memory, which is why his dancers look caught rather than posed.
items.gaffe: Calling him a painter of pretty ballerinas. They are working girls of the Opéra at class and rehearsal, scratching and yawning, and the Little Dancer of 1881, wax in a real tutu, so repelled the critics that he never showed another sculpture.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Degas, (Hilaire-Germain-)Edgar'
Jean Sutherland Boggs et al., Degas (exhibition catalogue, Grand Palais, National Gallery of Canada and Metropolitan Museum of Art, 1988)
Paul Valéry, Degas Danse Dessin (1936)

items.title: Paul Cézanne
facts: Born in Aix-en-Provence in 1839, a banker's son, and died there in 1906; at school in Aix his closest friend was Émile Zola, and the friendship faded after Zola's novel L'Œuvre (1886), whose failed painter was widely read as a portrait of him.

Showed at the first and third Impressionist exhibitions, 1874 and 1877, after working beside Pissarro at Pontoise and Auvers; the Salon jury refused him year after year and accepted him once, in 1882, as the 'pupil' of a friend who sat on the jury.

His first one-man show was at Ambroise Vollard's gallery in the rue Laffitte in 1895, when he was fifty-six; the retrospective at the Salon d'Automne of 1907, the year after his death, was studied by Braque and Picasso.
He wrote to Émile Bernard on 15 April 1904 that nature should be treated by the cylinder, the sphere and the cone; he painted Mont Sainte-Victoire, outside Aix, dozens of times.

The Musée d'Orsay holds one of the five versions of The Card Players; another was bought for Qatar in 2011 at a price reported at over 250 million dollars. He died of pneumonia a week after being caught in a storm while painting outdoors.
items.remark: He told Émile Bernard in 1904 to treat nature by the cylinder, the sphere and the cone, and the retrospective the year after his death was the exhibition Braque and Picasso were looking at when Cubism began.
items.gaffe: Filing him under Impressionism. He showed with them twice, in 1874 and 1877, then went back to Aix and spent thirty years painting one mountain until it was structure rather than weather.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Cézanne, Paul'
Paul Cézanne, Letters, ed. John Rewald (rev. ed., 1976)
Alex Danchev, Cézanne: A Life (2012)

items.title: Auguste Rodin
facts: Born in Paris in 1840, refused three times by the École des Beaux-Arts, and died at Meudon in 1917; his first exhibited figure, The Age of Bronze (1877), was so lifelike that he was accused of casting it from the model.

In 1880 the state commissioned a bronze door, The Gates of Hell, for a museum of decorative arts that was never built; he worked on it until his death without finishing it, and The Thinker, The Kiss and dozens of other figures began there.

The Thinker was the poet, Dante, above the doors; enlarged in 1902 to 1904, the first monumental cast was set up in front of the Panthéon in 1906 by public subscription and moved to the garden of the Musée Rodin in 1922.

The Kiss is Paolo and Francesca from Dante's Inferno; the marble commissioned by the state in 1888 was shown at the Salon of 1898 beside the Balzac, which the Société des Gens de Lettres had commissioned and then refused.

Went to Italy in 1875 to 1876 to see Michelangelo; Camille Claudel worked in his studio from 1884 and became his lover; in 1916 he gave his work and the Hôtel Biron to the state, and the Musée Rodin opened there in 1919.
items.remark: The Thinker was never meant to sit alone: he is Dante above the Gates of Hell, a door commissioned in 1880 for a museum that was never built, and Rodin worked on it for thirty-seven years without finishing.
items.gaffe: Asking whether the Thinker in front of you is 'the original'. Rodin's bronzes are casts, more than twenty full-size Thinkers exist, and the Musée Rodin went on casting after his death under the terms of his gift.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Rodin, Auguste'
Musée Rodin, collection entries 'The Thinker', 'The Gates of Hell' and 'The Kiss'
Ruth Butler, Rodin: The Shape of Genius (1993)

items.title: Impressionism
facts: The first exhibition opened on 15 April 1874 at 35 boulevard des Capucines, the photographer Nadar's former studio, organised by a Société anonyme of painters, sculptors and engravers with about thirty exhibitors; Monet, Renoir, Pissarro, Sisley, Degas, Morisot and Cézanne were among them.
The name came from Louis Leroy's mocking review of Monet's Impression, Sunrise in Le Charivari; there were eight exhibitions between 1874 and 1886, and Pissarro was the only painter at all of them.

Paint in metal tubes, patented by John Goffe Rand in 1841, made painting outdoors, en plein air, practical; broken brushwork, colours laid side by side rather than blended, and subjects from modern life were the shared habits, though Degas worked indoors.
Manet was the elder the group looked to and never exhibited with them; the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel, who met Monet and Pissarro in London in 1871, kept them going through decades of poor sales.

Gustave Caillebotte's bequest of 1894 brought the movement into the national collections over official reluctance; the state's Impressionists are now in the Musée d'Orsay, opened in 1986, with Monet's Water Lilies at the Orangerie since 1927.
items.remark: Pissarro is the only one who showed at all eight exhibitions, from Nadar's old studio in 1874 to the last in 1886; Monet, whose picture named the group, missed three of them.
items.gaffe: Calling Manet an Impressionist. He was their elder and their cause, and he declined to show with them every single time; the Salon was where he wanted to win.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Impressionism'
John Rewald, The History of Impressionism (4th ed., 1973)
Charles S. Moffett (ed.), The New Painting: Impressionism 1874–1886 (exhibition catalogue, 1986)

items.title: The Salon
facts: First held in 1667 by the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture; in the Salon Carré of the Louvre from 1725, which gave it the name; opened to all artists in 1791, when the Revolution ended the Academy's monopoly.
Diderot's reviews of the Salons from 1759 to 1781 are the beginning of art criticism; to be 'skyed', hung near the ceiling, was a verdict, and the eye-level line was the prize.

In 1863 the jury rejected about three thousand of some five thousand submissions; Napoleon III ordered the rejects shown in rooms next door in the Palais de l'Industrie, and the Salon des Refusés opened on 15 May with Manet's Déjeuner sur l'herbe and Whistler's White Girl in it.

In 1881 the state handed the Salon to the Société des Artistes Français; the Salon des Indépendants (1884, no jury, no prizes) and the Salon d'Automne (1903) became the venues for new painting, and the Fauves were named at the Salon d'Automne of 1905.
items.remark: The rejections of 1863 were so wholesale that Napoleon III ordered the rejects shown next door, and the Salon des Refusés, with Manet's Déjeuner in it, is the exhibition anybody now remembers from that year.
items.gaffe: Confusing the Salon with a salon. Madame Geoffrin's drawing room was a salon; the Salon, capital S, is the state exhibition named after a room in the Louvre, and being skyed there, hung up by the ceiling, was a judgement.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Salon'
Patricia Mainardi, The End of the Salon: Art and the State in the Early Third Republic (1993)
Thomas Crow, Painters and Public Life in Eighteenth-Century Paris (1985)

term: An exhibiting society founded in 1884 that admitted any artist who paid the fee, with no jury and no prizes.
The drawing-room gathering of writers, philosophes and patrons over which a hostess presided in eighteenth-century Paris.
The state school of art whose annual prize sent the winner to Rome for several years at the Crown's expense.

items.definition: The official exhibition of living artists in Paris, held by the Académie royale from 1667 and named after the Salon Carré of the Louvre, where it hung from 1725. In the nineteenth century it was the event that made or broke a painter: a jury chose the works, hung them frame to frame up to the ceiling, and rejection could mean ruin. 'Salon painting' means the polished, academic kind it rewarded.

items.title: Japonisme
facts: Philippe Burty coined the word in articles in La Renaissance littéraire et artistique in 1872; the Japanese pavilion at the Paris Exposition Universelle of 1867 had been the first large public showing, and the dealer Siegfried Bing published the magazine Le Japon artistique from 1888 to 1891 and mounted an exhibition of prints at the École des Beaux-Arts in 1890.

Monet collected some 230 Japanese prints, still on the walls at Giverny, and painted his wife in a red kimono in La Japonaise (1876); Manet's Portrait of Émile Zola (1868, Musée d'Orsay) has a sumo print and a Japanese screen behind the sitter.

Van Gogh copied Hiroshige's Plum Orchard and Bridge in the Rain in oils in 1887 and painted Père Tanguy against a wall of prints; Mary Cassatt made her colour prints of 1891 after seeing Bing's exhibition.
Degas's cropped figures and high viewpoints, Toulouse-Lautrec's flat poster colour and Whistler's Peacock Room all owe something to it.
items.remark: Monet owned about two hundred and thirty Japanese prints and they are still on the walls at Giverny; the cut-off figures and high viewpoints in Degas come from Hiroshige as much as from photography.
items.gaffe: Saying 'Japanism' and meaning kimonos. The kimono pictures are the least of it; the point is what the prints did to composition, which is why Van Gogh copied Hiroshige in oils in 1887.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Japonisme'
Siegfried Wichmann, Japonisme: The Japanese Influence on Western Art since 1858 (1981)
Geneviève Lacambre et al., Le Japonisme (exhibition catalogue, Grand Palais and National Museum of Western Art, Tokyo, 1988)

term: The eighteenth-century taste for Chinese and pseudo-Chinese decoration: pagodas, lacquer and blue-and-white porcelain.
Painting outdoors, in front of the subject, rather than working up a landscape in the studio.
The North African and Near Eastern subjects painted by Delacroix, Gérôme and Ingres in the decades after the conquest of Algeria.

items.definition: The French craze for Japanese art after Japan's ports opened in the 1850s, and what painters took from the woodblock prints that came with it: flat areas of colour, high viewpoints, figures cut off by the frame, asymmetry and empty space. The word was coined by the critic Philippe Burty in 1872.

items.title: The Kiss
items.creator: Gustav Klimt
facts: Oil and gold leaf on a square canvas, 180 centimetres each way, painted in 1907 and 1908 during what is called his golden period.
Shown, still unfinished, at the Kunstschau of 1908 in Vienna, where the Austrian state bought it for the Modern Gallery; it hangs in the Upper Belvedere.
Klimt's father was a gold engraver, and the gold is leaf, not paint.
items.remark: The state bought it off the wall of the 1908 Kunstschau before Klimt had quite finished it, and the gold is leaf rather than paint; his father was a gold engraver.
items.gaffe: Asking to see it at the Secession. It hangs in the Upper Belvedere; the Secession has the Beethoven Frieze, and the two buildings are a tram ride apart.
sources: Belvedere, Vienna, collection entry 'The Kiss (Lovers)'
Tobias G. Natter (ed.), Gustav Klimt: The Complete Paintings (2012)

items.title: Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I
items.creator: Gustav Klimt
facts: Oil, silver and gold on canvas, completed in 1907 after studies going back to 1903, the year Klimt saw the Byzantine mosaics at Ravenna.

Seized after the Anschluss and shown for decades in the Belvedere as 'Woman in Gold', a title that kept the Jewish sitter's name off the label; an Austrian arbitration panel restituted it to her niece Maria Altmann in 2006.
Ronald Lauder bought it that year for the Neue Galerie in New York for a reported 135 million dollars.
items.remark: It has not been in Vienna since 2006; the Belvedere hung it for decades as 'Woman in Gold', which conveniently kept the name Bloch-Bauer off the label, and it now lives on Fifth Avenue at the Neue Galerie.
items.gaffe: Looking for it at the Belvedere, or calling the sitter 'the woman in gold' as though nobody knew who she was; she was Adele Bloch-Bauer, wife of a sugar industrialist, and Klimt painted her twice.
sources: Neue Galerie New York, collection entry 'Adele Bloch-Bauer I'
Anne-Marie O'Connor, The Lady in Gold (2012)
Republic of Austria v. Altmann, 541 U.S. 677 (2004)

items.title: Hunters in the Snow
items.creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
facts: Signed and dated 1565; one of a series of the seasons painted for the Antwerp merchant Niclaes Jongelinck, of which five survive: three in Vienna, one in Prague and The Harvesters in New York.
The Kunsthistorisches Museum owns twelve Bruegel panels, the largest holding anywhere.
Bruegel dropped the h from Brueghel in his signature in 1559; his sons kept it.
items.remark: It is one of a set of the seasons painted in a single year, 1565, for an Antwerp merchant; Vienna kept three, Prague has the haymaking, and the harvest got away to the Metropolitan in New York.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Pieter Brueghel the Younger, who spent his career copying his father, or spelling the father with an h; he dropped it in 1559.
sources: Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie, inv. GG 1838
Manfred Sellink, Bruegel: The Complete Paintings, Drawings and Prints (2007)

items.title: The Tower of Babel
items.creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
facts: Signed and dated 1563; the arcades are modelled on the Colosseum, which Bruegel had seen on his Italian journey a decade earlier.
King Nimrod inspects the works at the bottom left while stonemasons kneel to him; the harbour at the right is full of Antwerp shipping.
A second, smaller Tower of Babel by Bruegel is in the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam.
items.remark: There are two by him, the big one here and the little one in Rotterdam, and in both the tower is really the Colosseum, which Bruegel had walked round in Rome ten years before.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Bosch because it is busy and strange, or dismissing the Rotterdam picture as a copy; both towers are by Bruegel himself.
sources: Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie, inv. GG 1026
Manfred Sellink, Bruegel: The Complete Paintings, Drawings and Prints (2007)

items.title: The Art of Painting
items.creator: Johannes Vermeer
facts: Painted about 1666 to 1668 and never sold in Vermeer's lifetime; after his death in 1675 his widow Catharina made it over to her mother to keep it from his creditors.
The model with laurel wreath, trumpet and book is Clio, the muse of history, as Ripa's Iconologia prescribes; the map behind her shows the Seventeen Provinces.
Bought for Hitler from the Czernin family in 1940 for the museum he planned at Linz; it passed to the Austrian state after the war, and a Czernin restitution claim was rejected in 2011.
items.remark: The painter has his back to us and the girl is Clio, the muse of history, so it is an allegory rather than a studio scene; it is the one Vermeer he would not sell, and his widow fought his creditors for it.
items.gaffe: Calling it 'The Artist's Studio' and assuming the man at the easel is Vermeer. He is seen only from behind, in fancy dress a century out of date.
sources: Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie, inv. GG 9128
Walter Liedtke, Vermeer: The Complete Paintings (2008)

items.title: Young Hare
items.creator: Albrecht Dürer
facts: Watercolour and bodycolour on paper, monogrammed and dated 1502; the Albertina holds it with the largest collection of Dürer drawings and watercolours anywhere.
It is so sensitive to light that the Albertina shows the original only for limited periods and a facsimile the rest of the time.
Praying Hands (1508), a brush drawing on blue paper made as a study for the Heller Altarpiece, is in the same collection.
items.remark: It is a watercolour, not a painting, and there is a window reflected in the eye; most of the year the Albertina shows a facsimile, because light would ruin the original.
items.gaffe: Calling it a rabbit, or expecting to see the original on an ordinary visit; it is a hare, and it comes out of the dark only for special showings.
sources: Albertina, Vienna, collection entry 'Hare' (inv. 3073)
Jane Campbell Hutchison, Albrecht Dürer: A Biography (1990)

items.title: Self-Portrait with Physalis
items.creator: Egon Schiele
facts: Oil and gouache on wood, barely 32 by 40 centimetres, in the Leopold Museum, whose founder Rudolf Leopold assembled the largest Schiele collection in the world.

Its pendant, the Portrait of Wally Neuzil, was seized in New York in 1998 while on loan and returned to the Leopold in 2010 after a settlement of nineteen million dollars with the heirs of the dealer Lea Bondi Jaray.
Painted in 1912, the year Schiele spent twenty-four days in custody at Neulengbach over his drawings.
items.remark: It is hardly bigger than a sheet of paper, and its pair, the portrait of Wally, spent twelve years impounded in New York before the Leopold paid the heirs nineteen million dollars to bring it home.
items.gaffe: Calling it a Klimt. Klimt was his mentor, but Klimt never drew a contour like that; the taut outline and the blotched skin are Schiele.
sources: Leopold Museum, Vienna, collection entry 'Self-Portrait with Chinese Lantern Plant'
Jane Kallir, Egon Schiele: The Complete Works (1990)

items.title: Gustav Klimt
facts: Born in 1862 at Baumgarten outside Vienna, the son of a gold engraver; trained at the School of Applied Arts rather than the Academy.
With his brother Ernst and Franz Matsch he painted the Burgtheater ceilings and the spandrels of the Kunsthistorisches Museum staircase before founding the Secession in 1897 as its first president.
His three ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna caused a scandal and were burned at Schloss Immendorf in 1945 as the SS retreated.
Died in February 1918 after a stroke, months before Schiele.
items.remark: Before he was the Secession's rebel he was an imperial decorator, painting the spandrels on the Kunsthistorisches Museum staircase; look up when you go in.
items.gaffe: Calling him an Expressionist. He was the Secession's founding president and a decorator by training; Schiele and Kokoschka are the Expressionists, and both were a generation younger.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Klimt, Gustav'
Tobias G. Natter (ed.), Gustav Klimt: The Complete Paintings (2012)

image.source: Photograph by Josef Anton Trčka, 1914, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (photographer died 1940); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Egon Schiele
facts: Born in 1890 at Tulln on the Danube, a stationmaster's son; admitted to the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts at sixteen, and left it in 1909 to found the Neukunstgruppe.
Klimt took him up in 1907, bought and swapped drawings with him and introduced him to patrons.
Held for twenty-four days in 1912 at Neulengbach, where the judge burned one of his drawings in court.
Died of Spanish influenza on 31 October 1918, three days after his pregnant wife Edith, aged twenty-eight.
items.remark: He died at twenty-eight in the influenza of 1918, three days after his wife, having already left well over two thousand drawings and watercolours; the Leopold Museum has more of him than anywhere else.
items.gaffe: Saying 'Sheel'. It is two syllables, SHEE-luh; and he was Klimt's protégé, not his rival.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Schiele, Egon'
Jane Kallir, Egon Schiele: The Complete Works (1990)

image.license: Public domain (pre-1929 photograph); verify the file's tag and photographer when fetching

items.title: The Vienna Secession
facts: Founded in April 1897 by Klimt, Koloman Moser, Josef Hoffmann and Joseph Maria Olbrich among others, in a walk-out from the conservative Künstlerhaus; Klimt was its first president.

Olbrich's exhibition hall opened in 1898 under a dome of gilded laurel leaves that the Viennese call the golden cabbage; the motto over the door, 'To every age its art, to art its freedom', was coined by the critic Ludwig Hevesi.

Klimt painted the Beethoven Frieze for the fourteenth exhibition in 1902, around Max Klinger's statue of Beethoven; it was meant to be temporary and has been shown in a purpose-built basement room since 1986.
Its journal was Ver Sacrum (1898 to 1903); Klimt and his group walked out in 1905, and the association still holds exhibitions in the building.
items.remark: The motto over the door, to every age its art and to art its freedom, was written by a critic rather than an artist, and the Beethoven Frieze in the basement was painted for a single exhibition in 1902 and meant to be scraped off afterwards.
items.gaffe: Calling the building the Secession Museum, or assuming Klimt stayed; he and his friends walked out in 1905, and the association still runs its own exhibitions there.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Secession'
Carl E. Schorske, Fin-de-siècle Vienna: Politics and Culture (1980)
Secession, Vienna, 'The Beethoven Frieze'

items.title: Kunsthistorisches Museum
facts: Opened by Franz Joseph in 1891 in a building by Gottfried Semper and Carl von Hasenauer on the Ringstrasse; its twin across the square is the Natural History Museum.

The picture gallery is the Habsburg collection: twelve Bruegels, Vermeer's Art of Painting, Raphael's Madonna of the Meadow, Arcimboldo's composite heads and Velázquez's portraits of the Infanta Margarita Teresa, sent from Madrid to her uncle and future husband Leopold I.
The Kunstkammer holds Cellini's gold salt cellar, the Saliera, stolen from the museum in 2003 and dug up in a forest near Zwettl in 2006.
Klimt, his brother Ernst and Franz Matsch painted the spandrels of the main staircase in 1890 and 1891.
items.remark: The Velázquez infantas are here because Madrid posted them to Vienna as progress reports: Leopold I was Margarita Teresa's uncle and her fiancé, and he watched her grow up by portrait before he married her.
items.gaffe: Going there for Klimt, or calling it the Belvedere. The collection stops around 1800; Klimt is at the Belvedere, though he did paint the staircase here.
sources: Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, 'History of the Museum'
Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie
Carl E. Schorske, Fin-de-siècle Vienna: Politics and Culture (1980)

items.title: Jugendstil
facts: Named after Jugend ('Youth'), an illustrated weekly founded in Munich in 1896.
The Viennese version, under Josef Hoffmann and Koloman Moser, preferred squares and grids to whiplash curves; the Wiener Werkstätte, founded in 1903, put it on furniture, silver and tableware.
Otto Wagner's Karlsplatz Stadtbahn pavilions and his Majolikahaus on the Linke Wienzeile, both of 1898 and 1899, are the examples on the street.
items.remark: Jugendstil is Art Nouveau with a German name taken from a Munich magazine; the Viennese version went square under Hoffmann and Moser, so if it has a grid it is Vienna and if it whiplashes it is Paris or Brussels.
items.gaffe: Calling the Secession 'Art Nouveau' to a Viennese as though it were a French import, or pronouncing the J as in English; it is YOO-gent-shteel.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Jugendstil'

term: The stripped, ornament-free manner of the Bauhaus in the 1920s.
The Gothic revival in nineteenth-century German architecture that completed Cologne Cathedral.
A school of German history painting of the 1840s that took its subjects from folk tales and the Nibelungenlied.

items.definition: The German-speaking world's Art Nouveau: the decorative style of about 1895 to 1910, named after the Munich magazine Jugend, built on flowing line, flat pattern and stylised plant forms; in Vienna it turned geometric in the hands of the Secession and the Wiener Werkstätte.

items.title: Biedermeier
facts: The name comes from 'Gottlieb Biedermaier', a fictional philistine schoolmaster whose spoof verses appeared in the Munich comic paper Fliegende Blätter from 1855; it was a joke before it was a style.
Ferdinand Georg Waldmüller is the Viennese painter of the period, and Schubert's evenings among friends, the Schubertiades, belong to the same world.
Its plain cherry and walnut furniture was admired by Josef Hoffmann and the Wiener Werkstätte as a native ancestor of modern design.
items.remark: Biedermeier was an insult before it was a style, a spoof schoolmaster-poet in a Munich comic paper, and the name stuck to the whole Metternich era of quiet parlours and Schubert evenings.
items.gaffe: Using it for anything grand. Biedermeier is the bourgeois parlour, cherrywood and Waldmüller; the gilt and sphinxes of the years just before it are Empire.
sources: Grove Art Online, 'Biedermeier'

term: The gilded imperial style of the Napoleonic court, all sphinxes, eagles and mahogany.
The Viennese Baroque of Fischer von Erlach and Hildebrandt in the decades after the Turkish siege.
The Austrian painting of the interwar years that turned away from Expressionism toward sober realism.

items.definition: The middle-class domestic culture of the German-speaking lands between the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and the revolutions of 1848: plain, well-made furniture in pale veneers, small genre pictures and landscapes such as Waldmüller's, and a general retreat from politics into the parlour.

items.title: Dante, the factions and exile
facts: Florence was Guelph, the papal party, against the Ghibellines of the emperor; in the 1290s the Guelphs split into Whites and Blacks, and Dante, born in Florence in 1265, was a White. He served as one of the city's six priors from June to August 1300.

After Charles of Valois entered the city in November 1301 and the Blacks took power, Dante was condemned in January 1302 to a fine and exile, and on 10 March 1302 to be burned alive if he ever returned. He never did.

He wrote the whole Commedia in exile, setting it in Holy Week 1300 so that Boniface VIII, still alive, could be foretold a place among the simoniacs of Inferno XIX; he died in Ravenna in September 1321 and is buried there. Santa Croce's tomb for him, of 1829, is empty.

Boccaccio gave the first public lectures on the Commedia in Florence from October 1373, paid by the commune; the adjective 'divina' was his, and the title Divina Commedia first appears on a Venetian edition of 1555.
items.remark: Dante was one of the six priors of Florence for two months in 1300, and two years later the city sentenced him to be burned alive if he came back; he wrote the whole Commedia in exile and is buried in Ravenna, which has never given him up.
items.gaffe: Calling it the Divine Comedy as if Dante had named it. He called it the Commedia; the 'divine' was Boccaccio's compliment, and no title page carried it until 1555.
sources: Marco Santagata, Dante: The Story of His Life (trans. Richard Dixon, 2016)
John M. Najemy, A History of Florence 1200–1575 (2006)
Dante, Inferno XIX; Purgatorio XI

items.title: The Black Death and the Decameron
facts: The plague reached Florence in the spring of 1348 and, by most estimates, killed something like half the city, perhaps more; the chronicler Giovanni Villani died of it, and his brother Matteo took up the chronicle where it stopped.

Boccaccio's Decameron, written in the years after 1348, opens with the plague in Florence: seven young women and three young men meet in Santa Maria Novella and withdraw to a villa in the hills, where they tell ten stories a day for ten days and end each evening with a ballata.
Petrarch recorded in his copy of Virgil that Laura died at Avignon on 6 April 1348, in the same epidemic.

Millard Meiss's Painting in Florence and Siena after the Black Death (1951) argued that the plague pushed Florentine painting back toward stiff, otherworldly forms; the thesis is much disputed but still sets the terms of the debate.
items.remark: The Decameron is a plague book only for its first thirty pages: ten Florentines meet in Santa Maria Novella in 1348, go up to a villa, and tell a hundred stories while the city dies, closing each evening with a ballata of the kind Landini was writing.
items.gaffe: Calling the narrators ten young men, or the book a chronicle. Seven of the ten are women, the villa is fiction, and the plague is the frame, not the subject.
sources: Giovanni Boccaccio, Decameron, Introduction to the First Day
John M. Najemy, A History of Florence 1200–1575 (2006)
Millard Meiss, Painting in Florence and Siena after the Black Death (1951)

items.title: The Council of Florence and the Greeks
facts: The council to reunite the Latin and Greek churches opened at Ferrara in 1438 and moved to Florence in January 1439, with Cosimo de' Medici's money behind the move; the Byzantine emperor John VIII Palaiologos came with the patriarch and some seven hundred Greeks.

The decree of union, Laetentur caeli, was read in the cathedral on 6 July 1439, in Latin by Cardinal Cesarini and in Greek by Bessarion; Constantinople rejected it, and the city fell to Mehmed II on 29 May 1453.

Patriarch Joseph II died in Florence in June 1439 and is buried in Santa Maria Novella. Pisanello's medal of John VIII, made for the council, is usually called the first portrait medal of the Renaissance.

Gemistos Plethon lectured on Plato while in Florence; Marsilio Ficino wrote in 1492 that Cosimo's idea of reviving Plato came from hearing him. Manuel Chrysoloras had already taught Greek in Florence from 1397 to 1400.

Gentile Bellini went from Venice to Constantinople in 1479 and painted Mehmed II; the portrait, dated 25 November 1480 and much restored, is in the National Gallery, London, which catalogues it as attributed to him.
items.remark: The union of the churches was proclaimed in the Duomo on 6 July 1439 and repudiated in Constantinople within a few years; what stayed in Florence was Plato, because Ficino said Cosimo caught the idea from hearing Plethon lecture that summer.
items.gaffe: Saying Greek learning reached Florence in 1453 with refugees from the fall of Constantinople. The Greeks came in 1439, for the council, fourteen years before the city fell, and Chrysoloras had been teaching Greek in Florence since 1397.
sources: Joseph Gill, The Council of Florence (1959)
James Hankins, Plato in the Italian Renaissance (1990)
National Gallery, London, catalogue entry 'The Sultan Mehmet II', Gentile Bellini
