items.title: The Pazzi conspiracy
facts: On Sunday 26 April 1478, at High Mass in the cathedral, Giuliano de' Medici was stabbed to death and his brother Lorenzo, wounded, escaped into the sacristy. The Pazzi, bankers and rivals of the Medici, and Francesco Salviati, Archbishop of Pisa, were behind it, with the knowledge of Pope Sixtus IV.

The hired soldier Montesecco refused to commit murder in a church, so two priests took his place and bungled the attack on Lorenzo; by nightfall the archbishop and Francesco de' Pazzi had been hanged from the windows of the Palazzo della Signoria.

Bernardo Bandini Baroncelli fled to Constantinople, was sent back in chains by the sultan and hanged in December 1479; Leonardo da Vinci drew the body and noted the colours of its clothes. Botticelli was paid to paint the hanged conspirators on a wall of the Palazzo della Signoria.

Sixtus IV excommunicated Lorenzo and made war on Florence with Naples; in December 1479 Lorenzo sailed to Naples and negotiated peace with King Ferrante in person. Giuliano's illegitimate son Giulio, born a month after the murder, became Pope Clement VII.
items.remark: They chose High Mass in the Duomo on a Sunday in April 1478, killed Giuliano and missed Lorenzo, and by nightfall the Archbishop of Pisa was hanging from a window of the Palazzo della Signoria; Giuliano's posthumous son grew up to be Pope Clement VII.
items.gaffe: Assuming the Pazzi won. They killed the wrong brother: Lorenzo ruled for another fourteen years, the Pazzi name was banned and their arms were scraped off the city's walls.
sources: Lauro Martines, April Blood: Florence and the Plot against the Medici (2003)
Angelo Poliziano, Coniurationis commentarium (1478)
Ronald Lightbown, Sandro Botticelli: Life and Work (1989)

items.title: Savonarola and the Bonfire of the Vanities
facts: Girolamo Savonarola, a Dominican from Ferrara, was prior of San Marco from 1491; after Piero de' Medici fled before the French army in November 1494 the friar's sermons in the Duomo set the tone of the republic, and his followers were nicknamed piagnoni, the weepers.

On Shrove Tuesday, 7 February 1497, his boys collected mirrors, cosmetics, wigs, playing cards, dice, secular books and pictures and burned them on a pyre in the Piazza della Signoria; the bonfire was repeated at Carnival 1498.

Vasari says Botticelli became a follower and gave up work, and that Baccio della Porta, the future Fra Bartolomeo, threw his drawings of nudes into the fire; Fra Bartolomeo's profile portrait of the friar, of about 1498, is in San Marco.

Excommunicated by Alexander VI in May 1497, Savonarola was arrested after a trial by fire fizzled out in April 1498, and on 23 May 1498 he was hanged and burned with two companions on the spot where the vanities had gone up; a plaque marks it. Machiavelli's Prince cites him as the unarmed prophet who was destroyed.
items.remark: It was Shrove Tuesday 1497, in the Piazza della Signoria: mirrors, wigs, dice, cards and pictures went up on one pyre, and fifteen months later the friar was hanged and burned on the same spot; the plaque is still set in the paving.
items.gaffe: Treating Savonarola as a Florentine. He was from Ferrara, the Florentines who followed him were the piagnoni, the weepers, and the city that burned its vanities for him burned him too.
sources: Donald Weinstein, Savonarola: The Rise and Fall of a Renaissance Prophet (2011)
Lauro Martines, Scourge and Fire: Savonarola and Renaissance Italy (2006)
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists, Lives of Botticelli and of Fra Bartolomeo
Niccolò Machiavelli, The Prince, chapter 6

items.title: Machiavelli writes The Prince
facts: The Medici returned to Florence in September 1512 and Machiavelli lost his post in the chancery; in February 1513 he was implicated in a plot, tortured with the strappado, and released in March under the amnesty for Leo X's election. He withdrew to the family farm at Sant'Andrea in Percussina.

His letter to Francesco Vettori of 10 December 1513 describes the evening ritual of putting on court clothes to read the ancients, and says he has written a little work De principatibus; the dedication went first to Giuliano de' Medici and, after Giuliano's death, to Lorenzo, Duke of Urbino.

Cesare Borgia is the model of chapter 7, including the morning at Cesena in December 1502 when his lieutenant Remirro de Orco was found cut in two in the piazza; Machiavelli was there on embassy and reported it.
The book circulated in manuscript and was printed only in 1532, five years after Machiavelli's death; it went on the Index in 1559.
items.remark: He wrote it in 1513 on a farm outside Florence, sacked and tortured after the Medici came back, and told Vettori that December that he dressed in court clothes each evening to read the ancients; it was not printed until 1532, five years after he died.
items.gaffe: Quoting 'the end justifies the means'. The phrase is not in the book; the nearest thing, in chapter 18, is that in the actions of princes one looks to the outcome. And the book is dedicated to a Medici, which anyone calling it a republican satire has to explain.
sources: Niccolò Machiavelli, letter to Francesco Vettori, 10 December 1513
Quentin Skinner, Machiavelli: A Very Short Introduction (2000)
Roberto Ridolfi, The Life of Niccolò Machiavelli (trans. Cecil Grayson, 1963)
cast: Lorenzo de' Medici Duke of Urbino

items.title: The Medici popes: Leo X and Clement VII
facts: Giovanni de' Medici, Lorenzo the Magnificent's second son, was made a cardinal at thirteen and elected Pope Leo X in March 1513, aged thirty-seven; Raphael painted him around 1518 with his cousin Cardinal Giulio de' Medici and Luigi de' Rossi, and the picture is in the Uffizi.
Leo X excommunicated Luther in January 1521 and died that December; Giulio, the posthumous son of the Giuliano murdered by the Pazzi, was elected Clement VII in November 1523.

Clement sat out the Sack of Rome in the Castel Sant'Angelo in May 1527, refused Henry VIII the annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, crowned Charles V at Bologna in 1530, and after a siege the same year put the Medici back into Florence; Alessandro de' Medici became duke in 1532.

Between them the two popes gave Michelangelo the New Sacristy and the Laurentian Library at San Lorenzo. Clement also arranged his young kinswoman Catherine's marriage to the future Henri II of France and presided at it in Marseille in 1533.
items.remark: Lorenzo the Magnificent's son became Leo X in 1513 and Lorenzo's nephew Clement VII ten years later; between them they got Raphael's best portrait, Luther, the Sack of Rome and Henry VIII's divorce, and still found time to order Michelangelo's Medici Chapel.
items.gaffe: Calling Clement VII Leo's son, or either of them a grand duke. Leo was Lorenzo's son, Clement the illegitimate son of the murdered Giuliano, and the grand dukes come later, with Cosimo I in 1569.
sources: Uffizi Galleries, catalogue entry 'Portrait of Leo X with Cardinals Giulio de' Medici and Luigi de' Rossi'
J. R. Hale, Florence and the Medici (1977)
Kenneth Gouwens and Sheryl E. Reiss (eds), The Pontificate of Clement VII: History, Politics, Culture (2005)

items.title: Galileo's trial
facts: Galileo, born in Pisa in 1564, published the moons of Jupiter in the Sidereus Nuncius of 1610, named them the Medicean Stars after Cosimo II, and was rewarded with the post of Philosopher and Chief Mathematician to the Grand Duke; he moved from Padua to Florence that year.

Warned in 1616 not to hold or defend Copernicus, he published the Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems in Florence in 1632; summoned to Rome, he was examined under threat of torture, sentenced on 22 June 1633 and abjured on his knees at Santa Maria sopra Minerva.

The prison sentence was commuted to house arrest, first with the Archbishop of Siena and from December 1633 at his villa at Arcetri, above Florence, where he wrote the Two New Sciences, printed at Leiden in 1638; Milton visited him there in 1638 and mentions it in Areopagitica. He died at Arcetri in January 1642.

Grand Duke Ferdinando II, who had Frescobaldi on the court payroll from 1628 to 1634, did not shield his mathematician. Galileo's father Vincenzo Galilei had been the theorist of the Florentine Camerata.
Buried in Santa Croce; when the body was moved to its monumental tomb in 1737, three fingers and a tooth were taken, and the middle finger of his right hand is displayed in the Museo Galileo.
items.remark: He was tried in Rome but he was Florence's man: Chief Mathematician to the Grand Duke since 1610, with Jupiter's moons named the Medicean Stars in the family's honour, and he served his sentence at home in Arcetri, where Milton called on him in 1638.
items.gaffe: Saying he was tortured, thrown in a dungeon or burned. He was threatened with torture, abjured on his knees, and spent eight and a half more years under house arrest outside Florence writing his best book; Bruno was the one burned, in 1600.
sources: Maurice A. Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair: A Documentary History (1989)
J. L. Heilbron, Galileo (2010)
Museo Galileo, Florence, 'Galileo's middle finger'

image.source: Joseph-Nicolas Robert-Fleury, Galileo before the Holy Office (1847), Louvre, Paris, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Cosimo de' Medici
facts: Born in 1389, son of Giovanni di Bicci, who founded the Medici bank in 1397; exiled to Venice by the Albizzi faction in 1433 and recalled in 1434, after which he led Florence for thirty years without any office that said so.

He paid for Michelozzo's rebuilding of San Marco from 1437, where Fra Angelico frescoed the cells, and installed Niccolò Niccoli's books there in 1444 as the first public library in Florence; his own palace on the Via Larga, also by Michelozzo, was begun in 1444.
He brought the church council to Florence in 1439, and in the early 1460s gave Marsilio Ficino a villa at Careggi and Greek manuscripts to translate; Ficino's Latin Plato was printed in 1484.

He died at Careggi on 1 August 1464 and is buried in San Lorenzo; the commune's decree gave him the title Pater Patriae, which is cut on the tomb. Pontormo's portrait, painted about 1518, is posthumous.
items.remark: He never held an office he did not have to, was exiled in 1433, came back in 1434 and ran the city for thirty years from a bank; the Signoria had Pater Patriae cut on his tomb in San Lorenzo, which had been Cicero's title.
items.gaffe: Confusing him with Cosimo I, the first Grand Duke. Cosimo il Vecchio was a banker who died in 1464 and never held a title; Cosimo I was a soldier's son who took a ducal crown a century later and built the Uffizi.
sources: Dale Kent, Cosimo de' Medici and the Florentine Renaissance (2000)
Vespasiano da Bisticci, Lives of Illustrious Men of the XVth Century, 'Cosimo de' Medici'
Grove Art Online, 'Medici'

items.role: Banker and de facto ruler of Florence

items.title: Lorenzo the Magnificent
facts: Born 1 January 1449, grandson of Cosimo il Vecchio; took over the family's leadership of Florence at twenty when his father Piero died in December 1469. Donatello's bronze David stood in the courtyard of the Medici palace at his wedding to Clarice Orsini that year.
Survived the Pazzi attack in the cathedral in April 1478, in which his brother Giuliano was killed; in December 1479 he sailed to Naples and negotiated peace with King Ferrante in person.

Kept Poliziano, Ficino and Pico della Mirandola around him, took the teenage Michelangelo into his household around 1490, and had his own name, LAV.R.MED, cut into the antique gems and vases he collected; his own poems include the Canzona di Bacco.

Died at Careggi on 8 April 1492, aged forty-three; Savonarola came to the deathbed, and what passed between them is told differently by Poliziano and by the friar's followers. His son Giovanni, a cardinal at thirteen, became Leo X; Piero, his heir, was driven out of Florence in November 1494.
items.remark: His own carnival song says it: how fine is youth, which flees all the same, so let whoever wants to be happy be so, for there is no certainty of tomorrow. He died at forty-three in 1492, and his son was driven out of Florence two and a half years later.
items.gaffe: Crediting him with Botticelli's Venus and Primavera. So far as the documents go both belonged to his cousin Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco's branch; the Magnificent's own money went on manuscripts, gems and villas.
sources: Lorenzo de' Medici, Canzona di Bacco (Trionfo di Bacco e Arianna)
Miles J. Unger, Magnifico: The Brilliant Life and Violent Times of Lorenzo de' Medici (2008)
Grove Art Online, 'Medici'
Ronald Lightbown, Sandro Botticelli: Life and Work (1989)

items.role: De facto ruler of Florence, poet and patron

items.title: Niccolò Machiavelli
facts: Born in Florence on 3 May 1469; from 1498 to 1512 he was Second Chancellor of the republic and secretary to the Ten of War, and rode on missions to Cesare Borgia, Louis XII, the Emperor Maximilian and Julius II.
He argued for a citizen militia instead of mercenaries and raised one in 1506; it helped retake Pisa in 1509 and broke at Prato in 1512, after which the Medici returned and he lost his post.

Besides The Prince he wrote the Discourses on Livy, the comedy La Mandragola, The Art of War, the only one of his political works printed in his lifetime, and the Florentine Histories, commissioned by Cardinal Giulio de' Medici; he died on 21 June 1527, weeks after the Medici had been expelled again.

He is buried in Santa Croce, where the monument of 1787 reads 'Tanto nomini nullum par elogium', no praise is equal to such a name. The portrait by Santi di Tito in the Palazzo Vecchio was painted decades after his death; none from life is known.
items.remark: He spent fourteen years as a civil servant of the republic, riding to Cesare Borgia and the French court on Florence's business, and everything he is famous for he wrote after being sacked; his tomb in Santa Croce says no epitaph could equal his name.
items.gaffe: Using 'Machiavellian' for anyone cunning and assuming the man was a courtier. He was a republican official whom the Medici tortured; The Prince was a bid for employment, and the Discourses on Livy are the longer book.
sources: Roberto Ridolfi, The Life of Niccolò Machiavelli (trans. Cecil Grayson, 1963)
Quentin Skinner, Machiavelli: A Very Short Introduction (2000)
Grove Art Online, 'Santi di Tito'

items.role: Second Chancellor of the Florentine republic, political writer

items.title: Catherine de' Medici
facts: Born in Florence on 13 April 1519, daughter of Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino, the man to whom The Prince is dedicated; both parents were dead within a month of her birth.

Married Henri, second son of Francis I, at Marseille on 28 October 1533, aged fourteen, with her kinsman Clement VII presiding; Henri became Henri II in 1547, kept Diane de Poitiers as his mistress throughout, and died in 1559 of a jousting wound.

Three of her sons were kings of France, François II, Charles IX and Henri III; she was regent for Charles IX from 1560 and the power behind the throne through the Wars of Religion, and the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 24 August 1572 has been laid at her door ever since, on evidence historians dispute.

She began the Tuileries in 1564, and the festivals of her court, staged with Italian dancing masters, are where the French ballet de cour began. She died at Blois on 5 January 1589; her granddaughter Christine of Lorraine, whom she had raised, married Grand Duke Ferdinando I of Tuscany that spring, the wedding for which the 1589 intermedi were performed.
items.remark: Her father was the Medici to whom The Prince is dedicated, her wedding was fixed by a Medici pope, three of her sons were kings of France, and the granddaughter she raised married back into Florence in 1589, which is what the intermedi were for.
items.gaffe: Crediting her with bringing forks, ice cream and French cuisine from Florence in 1533. She was fourteen, nobody at the time remarked on it, and food historians have found no contemporary evidence.
sources: R. J. Knecht, Catherine de' Medici (1998)
Nina Treadwell, Music and Wonder at the Medici Court: The 1589 Interludes for La pellegrina (2008)
Barbara Ketcham Wheaton, Savoring the Past: The French Kitchen and Table from 1300 to 1789 (1983)

items.title: "Eppur si muove"
facts: Giuseppe Baretti, an Italian man of letters living in London and a friend of Samuel Johnson, printed the anecdote in The Italian Library in 1757; nothing earlier is known.
The sentence of 22 June 1633 and Galileo's written abjuration survive in the Vatican archives; neither records any remark, and Galileo had just been examined under formal threat of torture.
The story attaches to a real fact: Galileo went on believing the earth moved, and said so privately, while serving his sentence at Arcetri.
items.remark: The line turns up first in 1757, in a book Giuseppe Baretti published in London, and Baretti was Johnson's friend, not Galileo's; nobody in 1633 heard it, and a man just threatened with torture is unlikely to have said it aloud.
items.gaffe: Quoting it as Galileo's parting shot to the Inquisition. It is in no trial record and no letter; say it with a smile and date it to the eighteenth century.
sources: Giuseppe Baretti, The Italian Library (London, 1757)
Stillman Drake, Galileo at Work: His Scientific Biography (1978)
Maurice A. Finocchiaro, Retrying Galileo, 1633–1992 (2005)
items.claim: Rising from his knees after abjuring Copernicanism before the Inquisition in June 1633, Galileo muttered 'Eppur si muove', and yet it moves.
items.truth: No contemporary source has it: not the trial record, not Galileo's letters, not the accounts of his friends. The line first appears in print in 1757, in Giuseppe Baretti's The Italian Library, published in London a hundred and twenty-four years after the trial. A painting that surfaced in 1911, once claimed to date from the 1640s, shows the words scratched on a cell wall; that early date has never been established and is widely doubted.

items.title: The Norman Conquest and the Bayeux Tapestry
facts: Edward the Confessor died on 5 January 1066 and Harold Godwinson was crowned the next day; William, Duke of Normandy, defeated and killed him at Hastings on 14 October and was crowned in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day.

The Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry but an embroidery, wool on linen, about seventy metres long, made in the 1070s, probably in England, for William's half-brother Odo, bishop of Bayeux; its final scenes are lost.
Domesday Book, the survey of who held what, was compiled in 1086; the Conquest replaced the English landholding class almost entirely with Normans, which is where the peerage begins.

Of the five ranks of the peerage only earl is older than the Conquest, from the Old English eorl; baron came with the Normans, the first dukedom was Cornwall in 1337 for the Black Prince, the first marquess was created in 1385 and the first viscount in 1440.

Knights and baronets are not peers: a baronetcy is a hereditary dignity ranking above a knight and below a baron, invented by James I in 1611 and sold to pay for the plantation of Ulster, and it carries no seat in the House of Lords.
items.remark: Every rank of the peerage is French except earl, which is Saxon, and even the earl's wife is a countess, because English never came up with a word for her.
items.gaffe: Calling a baronet a peer, or the Bayeux Tapestry a tapestry. 'Sir Somebody, Bart.' holds a hereditary dignity, not a peerage, and has no seat in the Lords; and the Tapestry is embroidery, wool stitched on linen, not woven.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'William I'
David Bates, William the Conqueror (Yale English Monarchs, 2016)
David M. Wilson, The Bayeux Tapestry (1985)
Debrett's Peerage and Baronetage, introductory notes on the ranks of the peerage and the baronetage

image.source: The Bayeux Tapestry, scene 57, 'Harold rex interfectus est' (1070s), Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Henry VIII, the six wives and the break with Rome
facts: Cranmer annulled the marriage to Catherine of Aragon in May 1533 so that Anne Boleyn, already pregnant with Elizabeth, could be crowned; the Act of Supremacy of November 1534 made Henry Supreme Head of the Church of England, and Thomas More was beheaded in July 1535 for refusing to acknowledge it.

The six wives in order: Catherine of Aragon (annulled), Anne Boleyn (beheaded 1536), Jane Seymour (died 1537 after giving birth to Edward), Anne of Cleves (annulled 1540), Catherine Howard (beheaded 1542), Catherine Parr (survived him).
Between 1536 and 1540 Thomas Cromwell dissolved more than eight hundred religious houses and the Crown sold or granted their land; Longleat, Lacock and Syon all stand on monastic sites.
Holbein was the court's painter: the Whitehall mural of 1537, source of the legs-apart pose everyone knows, burned with the palace in 1698, and only the cartoon and the copies survive.
items.remark: It began as a divorce case and became the largest transfer of land since the Conquest: the Act of Supremacy is 1534, the dissolution ran from 1536 to 1540, and Longleat, Lacock and Syon all stand on monastic ground.
items.gaffe: Saying Henry divorced anyone. The marriages to Catherine of Aragon and Anne of Cleves were annulled, declared never to have existed; 'divorced, beheaded, died' is a mnemonic, not a legal history.
sources: J. J. Scarisbrick, Henry VIII (Yale English Monarchs, 1968)
G. W. Bernard, The King's Reformation: Henry VIII and the Remaking of the English Church (2005)
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Henry VIII'

items.title: Elizabeth I, Mary Queen of Scots and the Armada
facts: Elizabeth came to the throne on 17 November 1558, aged twenty-five; Mary, Queen of Scots, her Catholic cousin and heir, fled to England in 1568 and spent nineteen years in custody before being beheaded at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587 for her part in the Babington Plot.
Elizabeth signed Mary's death warrant and then insisted it had been sent without her final order; her secretary William Davison was fined and put in the Tower for dispatching it.

Philip II's Armada of about 130 ships was scattered by fireships off Calais and beaten at Gravelines on 8 August 1588, then driven north round Scotland and Ireland, where the weather did most of the sinking; a medal struck that year reads 'He blew and they were scattered'.

The Tilbury speech, with 'the heart and stomach of a king', survives in a version written down by Leonel Sharp decades later; the tale of Drake finishing his game of bowls is not recorded until the following century.
Elizabeth died on 24 March 1603 and the crown passed to James VI of Scotland, the son of the woman she had executed.
items.remark: She had Mary Queen of Scots beheaded in 1587 and left the throne to Mary's son in 1603; the union of the crowns was the executed woman's revenge.
items.gaffe: Saying the English navy sank the Armada. Gravelines broke its formation; the weather wrecked it on the long way home round Scotland and Ireland, which is why the medal gave the credit to God rather than to Drake.
sources: Garrett Mattingly, The Defeat of the Spanish Armada (1959)
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Elizabeth I'
John Guy, My Heart Is My Own: The Life of Mary Queen of Scots (2004)

image.source: Philip James de Loutherbourg, Defeat of the Spanish Armada, 8 August 1588 (1796), National Maritime Museum, Greenwich, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (artist died 1812); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Charles I, the Civil War and the Restoration
facts: Charles ruled without Parliament from 1629 to 1640, raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642, lost the war, and was tried by a court of his own subjects; he was beheaded on 30 January 1649 on a scaffold outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall, walking to it beneath the Rubens ceiling he had commissioned.
Parliament closed the theatres in 1642; Cromwell refused the crown in 1657 and ruled as Lord Protector until his death in 1658, and his body was dug up and hanged at Tyburn in January 1661.
The Commonwealth sold the king's pictures from 1649; Philip IV of Spain and Cardinal Mazarin were among the buyers, which is why Charles I's collection is now partly in the Prado and the Louvre.

Charles II entered London on 29 May 1660, his thirtieth birthday; the theatres reopened with women on the stage for the first time, Pepys had begun his diary that January, and the orange-seller Nell Gwyn became an actress and then the king's mistress.
items.remark: He walked to the scaffold through the Banqueting House, under the Rubens ceiling he had paid for glorifying his father, and the Commonwealth then sold his pictures, which is why so much of Charles I's collection now hangs in the Prado and the Louvre.
items.gaffe: Calling Cromwell a king, or the Commonwealth a lasting republic. He refused the crown in 1657 and took 'Lord Protector' instead, and the whole arrangement outlived him by less than two years.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Charles I'
Blair Worden, The English Civil Wars 1640–1660 (2009)
Jerry Brotton, The Sale of the Late King's Goods: Charles I and His Art Collection (2006)

items.title: The Glorious Revolution and the Whig houses
facts: Seven men, the 'Immortal Seven', signed an invitation to William of Orange in June 1688; he landed at Torbay on 5 November with a Dutch army, James II fled to France, and William and Mary were offered the crown in February 1689 on the terms of the Declaration of Right, enacted that December as the Bill of Rights.

The Act of Settlement of 1701 passed the crown over more than fifty Catholics with better blood claims to the Protestant House of Hanover, which is why a German prince became George I in 1714 and found Handel, his former Kapellmeister, already in London.

William Cavendish, Earl of Devonshire, one of the seven, was made a duke in 1694 and rebuilt Chatsworth; Blenheim was the nation's gift to Marlborough for the victory of 1704, designed by Vanbrugh from 1705, and the Duchess quarrelled with him so badly that in 1725 he was refused entry to see it finished.

Robert Walpole, First Lord of the Treasury from 1721 to 1742 and the first man to be called prime minister, built Houghton in Norfolk while in office; George II offered him 10 Downing Street in 1732, he accepted it for the office rather than for himself, and moved in in 1735.
The Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745 were the attempts to reverse 1688; the theatre audiences who took up 'God Save the King' in September 1745 were singing against the Young Pretender.
items.remark: The great English houses are mostly Whig monuments: Devonshire got his dukedom in 1694 for inviting William over, Blenheim was Parliament's thank-you to Marlborough, and Walpole built Houghton on twenty years in office.
items.gaffe: Saying William conquered England. He was invited, by seven signatures in June 1688, and it was bloodless in England, which is what 'Glorious' meant; in Ireland, at the Boyne in 1690, it was not.
sources: Steve Pincus, 1688: The First Modern Revolution (2009)
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'William III and II'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Vanbrugh, Sir John'
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978)

items.title: The South Sea Bubble
facts: The South Sea Company, founded in 1711 and holding from 1713 the asiento, the contract to ship enslaved Africans to Spanish America, offered in 1720 to take over the national debt in exchange for its shares; the price went from about £128 in January to about £1,000 by the summer and was under £200 again by December.

Parliament passed the Bubble Act in June 1720, near the top; Isaac Newton was among the losers, and Handel's opera company, the Royal Academy of Music, had been floated as a joint-stock venture in the same speculative season of 1719.
Walpole came to power in the wreckage as First Lord of the Treasury in 1721 and shielded the guilty so thoroughly that the prints called him the Screen-Master General.
The Mississippi Bubble burst in Paris the same year: John Law, a Scottish gambler who had become Controller-General of France's finances, fled the country in December 1720.

The Dutch tulip mania of 1636 to 1637 is the oldest of the three; Anne Goldgar's study of the Haarlem archives found very few actual bankruptcies, and most of the ruin is in the moralising written afterwards.
Hogarth's first satirical print, The South Sea Scheme of 1721, shows the public riding a merry-go-round while Honesty is broken on the wheel and Honour flogged.
items.remark: The shares went from about £130 in January 1720 to about £1,000 by the summer and were back where they started by Christmas; Walpole came to power by shielding the guilty, and the prints called him the Screen-Master General.
items.gaffe: Saying tulips ruined Holland. Goldgar went through the Haarlem records and found almost no bankruptcies; the South Sea, which really did ruin people, is the bubble to cite.
sources: John Carswell, The South Sea Bubble (rev. ed., 1993)
Anne Goldgar, Tulipmania: Money, Honor, and Knowledge in the Dutch Golden Age (2007)
Ronald Paulson, Hogarth's Graphic Works (3rd ed., 1989)
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Law, John'

items.title: The Regency: Brummell, Almack's and Brighton
facts: The Regency Act of February 1811 made the Prince of Wales regent for his father, George III, whose madness had become permanent; it ended when the old king died on 29 January 1820 and the Regent became George IV.

George 'Beau' Brummell, the son of Lord North's private secretary and holder of no title at all, dictated how the Prince and his friends dressed: dark coat, plain linen, a starched cravat and no scent; he quarrelled with the Prince, fled his creditors to Calais in May 1816 and died in an asylum at Caen in 1840.

Almack's Assembly Rooms in King Street, St James's, held a ball every Wednesday of the Season; the lady patronesses, Lady Jersey chief among them, issued the vouchers, and to be refused one was social death. The waltz was danced there from about 1814.
John Nash laid out Regent Street from 1813 and rebuilt the Prince's seaside house at Brighton as the Royal Pavilion between 1815 and 1822, Indian outside and Chinese within.

Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815; Jane Austen's six novels were all published between 1811 and 1818, and Emma of 1815 was dedicated, at his librarian's suggestion and to her private distaste, to the Prince Regent.
items.remark: The Regency is nine years, from George III's final madness in February 1811 to his death in January 1820, and it holds Regent Street, the Brighton Pavilion, the waltz at Almack's and Brummell, who taught the Prince how to dress and then fled to Calais owing everyone.
items.gaffe: Using 'Regency' for anything vaguely Georgian, or for Victoria's reign. It is 1811 to 1820, and Jane Austen's novels all came out inside it, which is the easiest way to keep the dates.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'George IV'
Ian Kelly, Beau Brummell: The Ultimate Dandy (2005)
Venetia Murray, High Society: A Social History of the Regency Period, 1788–1830 (1998)
Captain Gronow, Reminiscences (1862)

items.title: Victoria, Albert and the Great Exhibition
facts: The Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations opened in Hyde Park on 1 May 1851, Albert's project, in Joseph Paxton's iron-and-glass Crystal Palace, about 560 metres long and raised in under a year; six million people came before it closed in October.

The profit of about £186,000 bought 87 acres in South Kensington, on which the South Kensington Museum (now the V&A), the Natural History Museum, the Science Museum, Imperial College and the Royal Albert Hall were built; the district was nicknamed Albertopolis.
The Crystal Palace was moved to Sydenham in 1854 and burned down on 30 November 1936; the name survives in the football club and the transmitter.
Victoria reigned from 20 June 1837 to 22 January 1901; she married Albert in February 1840, he died in December 1861, and she wore black for the remaining forty years.
items.remark: The Crystal Palace paid for South Kensington: the Exhibition's profit of about £186,000 bought the land where the V&A, the Natural History Museum and the Albert Hall now stand, which is why the district was called Albertopolis.
items.gaffe: Looking for the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park, or assuming it still stands. Paxton's building went to Sydenham in 1854 and burned in November 1936; the football club and the transmitter mark the site.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Albert [Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha]'
Michael Leapman, The World for a Shilling: How the Great Exhibition of 1851 Shaped a Nation (2001)
Royal Commission for the Exhibition of 1851, 'History' (account of the surplus and the South Kensington estate)

items.title: Henry VIII
facts: Born at Greenwich on 28 June 1491, the second son of Henry VII; his elder brother Arthur died in 1502, and Henry came to the throne in April 1509 aged seventeen, marrying Arthur's widow, Catherine of Aragon, within two months.
Leo X gave him the title Defender of the Faith in October 1521 for a book against Luther; he broke with Rome in 1534 and kept the title, and F.D. is still on the coins.

Holbein painted him in 1537 for the Whitehall mural, which burned in 1698; the small panel in the Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid is the only surviving painted portrait of the king generally accepted as Holbein's own work.
'Pastime with Good Company' is his, in the manuscript songbook of about 1518; 'Greensleeves' is not, being first registered in 1580, thirty-three years after his death.
Died at Whitehall on 28 January 1547, leaving three children who reigned in turn: Edward VI, Mary I and Elizabeth I.
items.remark: He got 'Defender of the Faith' from the Pope in 1521 for a book against Luther, broke with the Pope thirteen years later, and kept the title; F.D. is still on the coins.
items.gaffe: Crediting him with Greensleeves. It is first recorded in 1580, thirty-three years after his death; the tune that is actually his is 'Pastime with Good Company'.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Henry VIII'
J. J. Scarisbrick, Henry VIII (Yale English Monarchs, 1968)
Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza, Madrid, catalogue entry for Hans Holbein the Younger, Portrait of Henry VIII of England (1537)
Grove Music Online, 'Henry VIII, King of England'

items.title: Elizabeth I
facts: Born at Greenwich on 7 September 1533, the daughter of Anne Boleyn; declared illegitimate after her mother's execution in 1536, imprisoned in the Tower by her half-sister Mary in 1554, and queen on 17 November 1558.

Never married, though the suitors included Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, and a French prince more than twenty years her junior; the childlessness made the succession the running anxiety of the reign.

The Armada Portrait of about 1588 exists in three versions, at Woburn Abbey, the National Portrait Gallery and Greenwich; the painter is unknown, the old attribution to George Gower having been dropped.

Her hand rests on a globe over the Americas; the fleet sails in one window and wrecks in the other, and a mermaid is carved on the chair. Royal Museums Greenwich bought its version in 2016 for an agreed £10 million from the Tyrwhitt-Drake family, after a public appeal that raised £10.3 million.
In 1575 she granted Tallis and Byrd the monopoly on printing music in England, and kept Byrd, a Catholic, on the books of her Chapel Royal for the rest of her reign.
items.remark: The Armada Portrait is propaganda with a globe in it: her hand rests on the Americas, the Spanish fleet burns in one window and wrecks in the other, and there are three versions because it was made to be copied.
items.gaffe: Calling it 'the Gower'. The attribution to George Gower was dropped long ago; the painter is unknown, and the version Greenwich bought in 2016 had come down in Drake's family.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Elizabeth I'
Royal Museums Greenwich, 'The Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I' (collection entry)
Roy Strong, Gloriana: The Portraits of Queen Elizabeth I (1987)

image.source: Unknown English artist, the Armada Portrait of Elizabeth I (c. 1588), Woburn Abbey version, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (anonymous sixteenth-century work); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Charles I
facts: Born at Dunfermline on 19 November 1600, the second son of James VI of Scotland; became heir when his brother Henry died in 1612, king in March 1625, and married Henrietta Maria of France the same year.

The greatest collector ever to sit on the English throne: he bought the Gonzaga collection from Mantua in 1627 to 1628, including Mantegna's Triumphs of Caesar, and had acquired the Raphael cartoons in 1623 while still Prince of Wales.

Van Dyck came to London in 1632, was knighted and made Principal Painter, and gave the king his image: the equestrian portraits, the hunting picture now in the Louvre, and the triple portrait sent to Rome so that Bernini could carve a bust; the bust burned in the Whitehall fire of 1698, but the painting survives in the Royal Collection.
He was short, about five foot four by the usual reckoning, and Van Dyck's answer was to paint him on horseback or from below.
Tried by a High Court of Justice his subjects had invented for the purpose and beheaded at Whitehall on 30 January 1649; he wore two shirts so as not to be seen to shiver.
items.remark: He was about five foot four and Van Dyck's answer was the horse: two equestrian portraits, and the hunting picture in the Louvre where the king has dismounted and still manages to look down at you.
items.gaffe: Mixing him up with his son. Charles II is the one with the spaniels and the mistresses; Charles I is the pointed beard in Van Dyck, and the only English king tried and executed by his own subjects.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Charles I'
Desmond Shawe-Taylor and Per Rumberg (eds), Charles I: King and Collector (Royal Academy exhibition catalogue, 2018)
Musée du Louvre, catalogue entry INV 1236, Anthony van Dyck, Charles I at the Hunt
Jerry Brotton, The Sale of the Late King's Goods (2006)

items.role: King of England, Scotland and Ireland

items.title: "The Battle of Waterloo was won on the playing fields of Eton"
facts: Wellington was at Eton from 1781 to 1784, was taken away early because the family could not afford it, and was not fond of the place; the cult of organised games at Eton is Victorian, after his time.
The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations traces the words to Montalembert (1856) and the 'playing fields' to the 1880s; no contemporary of the Duke's reports him saying either.
Waterloo was fought on 18 June 1815; Turner exhibited The Field of Waterloo at the Royal Academy in 1818, and Byron had put the battle into Childe Harold in 1816.
items.remark: It is French and posthumous: Montalembert printed 'C'est ici qu'a été gagnée la bataille de Waterloo' in 1856, four years after the Duke died, and the playing fields were added by English writers in the 1880s.
items.gaffe: Quoting it to an Etonian as the Duke's own words. He was taken away from the school early, disliked it, and the cult of games at Eton is Victorian, after his day.
sources: Oxford Dictionary of Quotations (8th ed., 2014), 'Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington'
Elizabeth Longford, Wellington: The Years of the Sword (1969)
Charles de Montalembert, De l'avenir politique de l'Angleterre (1856)
items.claim: Revisiting Eton in old age, the Duke of Wellington said that the Battle of Waterloo had been won on its playing fields.
items.truth: Nothing of the kind is recorded in Wellington's lifetime. The earliest version is in French, in Montalembert's De l'avenir politique de l'Angleterre (1856), four years after the Duke's death: 'C'est ici qu'a été gagnée la bataille de Waterloo', with no playing fields in it. The 'playing fields' form belongs to the 1880s; Sir William Fraser's Words on Wellington (1889) is the version the Oxford Dictionary of Quotations cites.

items.title: Raleigh's cloak in the puddle
facts: Raleigh, born about 1554 in Devon, rose at court from about 1581, was knighted in 1585, and was beheaded in Old Palace Yard, Westminster, on 29 October 1618 under a treason sentence passed fifteen years earlier.

Fuller's Worthies of England (1662) is the first place the cloak appears: 'meeting with a plashy place, she seemed to scruple going thereon; presently Raleigh cast and spread his new plush cloak on the ground'.
He spelled his own name Ralegh, and the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography lists him that way.
items.remark: The cloak comes from Fuller's Worthies of 1662, the same book that gives us the couplet scratched on the window, and Fuller was collecting Devon anecdotes eighty years after the fact; Scott's Kenilworth did the rest.
items.gaffe: Telling the cloak story as a fact about Elizabeth's court. The only thing it reliably records is what the 1660s liked to believe about the 1580s.
sources: Thomas Fuller, The History of the Worthies of England (1662), 'Devonshire'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Ralegh, Sir Walter'
Mark Nicholls and Penry Williams, Sir Walter Raleigh: In Life and Legend (2011)
items.claim: Meeting the Queen at a muddy place, the young Walter Raleigh spread his new plush cloak over the puddle so that she could cross dry-shod, and his fortune at court was made.
items.truth: No one who knew Raleigh or Elizabeth mentions it. The story first appears in Thomas Fuller's Worthies of England, published in 1662, some eighty years after the supposed event and forty-four after Raleigh's execution; Fuller is also the earliest source for the couplet scratched on a window pane. Scott's Kenilworth (1821) made it universal.

items.title: The French Revolution
facts: The Bastille fell on 14 July 1789; Louis XVI was executed on 21 January 1793 and Marie Antoinette on 16 October 1793.
The Terror of 1793 to 1794 ended with Robespierre's own execution in July 1794.
Jacques-Louis David sat in the Convention, voted for the king's death, and painted the Revolution's images.
items.remark: David voted to execute the king, painted Marat dead in his bath, and then painted Napoleon's coronation; the Revolution's official artist survived every regime.
items.gaffe: Placing the storming of the Bastille in 1793. It was 1789; 1793 is the year of the guillotine.
sources: William Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (2nd ed., 2002)

items.title: Marie Antoinette
facts: Born in Vienna on 2 November 1755, the fifteenth child of the Empress Maria Theresa.
Married the future Louis XVI in 1770, aged fourteen; guillotined on 16 October 1793.
Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun painted her some thirty times.
items.remark: She was a Habsburg first: an Austrian archduchess sent to France at fourteen, and 'l'Autrichienne' was the insult that followed her to the scaffold.
items.gaffe: Attributing 'let them eat cake' to her as fact.
sources: Antonia Fraser, Marie Antoinette: The Journey (2001)

image.source: Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Marie Antoinette with a Rose (1783), via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (artist died 1842); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: "Let them eat cake"
facts: Rousseau's Confessions, Book VI, has the anecdote; the passage was written around 1765, when Marie Antoinette was about ten.
The French is 'qu'ils mangent de la brioche', and brioche is not cake.
items.remark: Rousseau wrote that line down when she was about ten and living in Vienna; nobody pinned it on her until well after her death.
items.gaffe: Quoting it as fact at a table where anyone has read a biography.
sources: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Confessions, Book VI
Antonia Fraser, Marie Antoinette: The Journey (2001)
items.claim: Told that the poor had no bread, Marie Antoinette said: let them eat cake.
items.truth: The line appears in Rousseau's Confessions, attributed to 'a great princess', and was written when Marie Antoinette was a child in Vienna. No contemporary source connects it to her.

items.title: The Siege of Vienna and the Turkish craze
facts: The Ottoman army under the Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa reached Vienna on 14 July 1683; Leopold I had already left for Passau, and Count Starhemberg held the walls for two months until the relief army under John III Sobieski of Poland and Charles of Lorraine came down from the Kahlenberg on 12 September and broke the siege in a day.

Kara Mustafa was strangled with a silk cord at Belgrade on 25 December 1683 on the Sultan's order; the war ran on to Prince Eugene's victory at Zenta in 1697 and the Peace of Karlowitz in 1699, which gave the Habsburgs Hungary and Transylvania.

It was the second siege: Suleiman the Magnificent had sat before the city in the autumn of 1529 and withdrawn. Lepanto, on 7 October 1571, was the earlier encounter, when the Holy League fleet under Don John of Austria beat the Ottomans at sea; Cervantes lost the use of his left hand there, and Veronese painted the victory as a votive picture now in the Accademia in Venice.
Prince Eugene, who finished the Turkish wars, built the Belvedere on the proceeds: the Upper Belvedere by Hildebrandt was completed in 1723, and it is where Klimt's The Kiss now hangs.

A century on, the Turk had become a style: Mozart's Die Entführung aus dem Serail (1782) and the Rondo alla Turca of the A major sonata K. 331, Haydn's 'Military' Symphony of 1794 and the march in the finale of Beethoven's Ninth all borrow the Janissary band of bass drum, cymbals and triangle.

The first licensed coffee house in Vienna was opened in 1685 by an Armenian, Johannes Diodato; the tale of the spy Kolschitzky brewing the abandoned Turkish sacks is later embroidery, and the croissant story has no source before the twentieth century.
items.remark: The Belvedere, where The Kiss hangs, was built by Prince Eugene on the Turkish wars, the ones that began with Sobieski coming down from the Kahlenberg on 12 September 1683; Vienna's baroque is that victory paid out in stone.
items.gaffe: Saying the croissant commemorates the siege. The story has no source before the twentieth century, and the Kolschitzky coffee-house legend is not much better; the first licensed café was an Armenian's, in 1685.
sources: John Stoye, The Siege of Vienna (1964; rev. ed., 2006)
Andrew Wheatcroft, The Enemy at the Gate: Habsburgs, Ottomans and the Battle for Europe (2008)
Grove Music Online, 'Janissary music'
Alan Davidson, The Oxford Companion to Food (1999), 'croissant'

image.source: Frans Geffels, The Battle of Vienna, 12 September 1683 (late seventeenth century), Wien Museum, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (artist died 1699); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Joseph II and Mozart
facts: Maria Theresa died on 29 November 1780 and Joseph, co-regent since 1765, ruled alone for ten years: the Patent of Toleration for Protestants and Orthodox in October 1781, the abolition of serfdom in the Austrian and Bohemian lands that November, the closing of hundreds of contemplative monasteries from 1782; he had already opened the Prater to the public in 1766 and the Augarten in 1775.

Mozart arrived in Vienna in March 1781 in the retinue of the Archbishop of Salzburg and was dismissed in June; by his own account Count Arco saw him out of the room with a kick, and he stayed in Vienna as a freelance for the rest of his life.

Joseph had founded a National Singspiel company at the Burgtheater in 1778 to promote opera in German, and Die Entführung aus dem Serail (16 July 1782) was written for it; 'too beautiful for our ears, and an enormous number of notes, dear Mozart' is what Niemetschek's biography of 1798 has the Emperor say of it, with Mozart answering that there were exactly as many as were needed.

Beaumarchais's play Le Mariage de Figaro was forbidden on the Vienna stage in 1785; Da Ponte, the Emperor's Italian theatre poet since 1783, cut Figaro's speeches, and the opera opened at the Burgtheater on 1 May 1786. After the third night Joseph ordered that only solo numbers might be encored, to keep the evenings to a length.

Joseph went to war with the Turks in 1788 and the nobility followed him to the front or left town; Mozart's subscription concerts dried up and the begging letters to Michael Puchberg begin that June. The Emperor died on 20 February 1790, a month after Così fan tutte opened, and the court mourning closed it.
items.remark: Joseph banned the play and passed the opera: Beaumarchais's Figaro was forbidden on the Vienna stage in 1785, and a year later the same emperor let Da Ponte's version through at the Burgtheater, minus the speeches.
items.gaffe: Quoting 'too many notes' as verbatim history. It comes from Niemetschek's biography of 1798, seven years after Mozart's death, and was said, if at all, about Die Entführung in 1782; Shaffer's Amadeus made it the Emperor's whole character.
sources: Derek Beales, Joseph II, vol. 2: Against the World, 1780–1790 (2009)
Otto Erich Deutsch, Mozart: A Documentary Biography (1965)
Franz Xaver Niemetschek, Leben des K.K. Kapellmeisters Wolfgang Gottlieb Mozart (1798)
Grove Music Online, 'Mozart, Wolfgang Amadeus'

items.title: The Congress of Vienna
facts: The powers that had beaten Napoleon met in Vienna from September 1814 to redraw the map of Europe; Metternich hosted for Austria, Talleyrand came for defeated France and talked his way to the table, Castlereagh and then Wellington spoke for Britain, and Tsar Alexander I attended in person.
Napoleon left Elba on 26 February 1815 and was in Paris by 20 March; the Congress went on regardless, and its Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before Waterloo.
The Prince de Ligne, the old field marshal and wit, is credited with 'Le congrès ne marche pas, il danse'; he died in Vienna on 13 December 1814, in the middle of it.

Beethoven made the most of the crowd: on 29 November 1814 the Seventh Symphony, Wellington's Victory and the cantata Der glorreiche Augenblick were played to the assembled sovereigns in the Redoutensaal, and the final version of Fidelio, first given that May, was in the repertory for the visitors. Schubert, aged seventeen, wrote Gretchen am Spinnrade on 19 October 1814 while the delegates danced.

Austria took Lombardy and Venetia and the presidency of the new German Confederation; the settlement, with Metternich policing it, held the peace of the great powers for nearly forty years, and the quiet, censored decades that followed are what the Viennese call Biedermeier.
items.remark: The Prince de Ligne said the Congress did not walk, it danced, and he died in the middle of it, in December 1814; the Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before Waterloo, while Napoleon was already back in Paris.
items.gaffe: Calling it a peace treaty, or dating it after Waterloo. The Final Act came nine days before the battle; the Congress was nine months of balls with a settlement attached, and the battle only confirmed it.
sources: Adam Zamoyski, Rites of Peace: The Fall of Napoleon and the Congress of Vienna (2007)
Harold Nicolson, The Congress of Vienna: A Study in Allied Unity, 1812–1822 (1946)
Grove Music Online, 'Beethoven, Ludwig van'

image.source: Jean Godefroy after Jean-Baptiste Isabey, The Congress of Vienna, engraving (1819) after the drawing of 1815, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (Isabey died 1855, Godefroy 1839); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: 1848 and the accession of Franz Joseph
facts: On 13 March 1848 a crowd stormed the Lower Austrian Landhaus in the Herrengasse, troops fired, and by evening Metternich had resigned after thirty-nine years in office; he reached London in April and stayed in England for three years.

Windischgrätz bombarded and retook Vienna at the end of October 1848 and had the Frankfurt deputy Robert Blum shot on 9 November; on 2 December, at Olomouc, the simple-minded Ferdinand I abdicated in favour of his eighteen-year-old nephew Franz Joseph, whose father had renounced his own claim.
Hungary under Kossuth fought on until Russian troops helped end it at Világos in August 1849; thirteen Hungarian generals were executed at Arad on 6 October 1849, a date Hungary still marks.

Johann Strauss the elder wrote the Radetzky March in August 1848 for a fête celebrating the field marshal's victory over the Piedmontese at Custoza, while his son sided with the revolution, wrote a Revolutions-Marsch and played the Marseillaise; the court held it against the younger Strauss for years.

Wagner manned the Dresden barricades in the rising of May 1849 alongside Bakunin and Gottfried Semper; a warrant was issued for his arrest and he fled through Weimar to Zurich, not to be fully amnestied until 1862. Semper fled too, and thirty years later designed Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum.
items.remark: The Radetzky March is the counter-revolution's own tune: Strauss the elder wrote it in August 1848 for the field marshal who had just beaten the Italians at Custoza, while his son was playing the Marseillaise for the other side.
items.gaffe: Saying Franz Joseph overthrew his uncle, or that Metternich fell at the Congress. Ferdinand abdicated at Olomouc in December 1848 and lived on in Prague until 1875; Metternich lasted thirty-three years past the Congress and fell to the barricades of 13 March.
sources: Mike Rapport, 1848: Year of Revolution (2008)
Alan Sked, Metternich and Austria: An Evaluation (2008)
Grove Music Online, 'Strauss, Johann (i)' and 'Strauss, Johann (ii)'
Grove Music Online, 'Wagner, Richard'

items.title: Mayerling and the death of Sisi
facts: On the morning of 30 January 1889 Crown Prince Rudolf, the only son of Franz Joseph and Elisabeth, was found dead at his hunting lodge at Mayerling in the Vienna Woods with the seventeen-year-old Baroness Mary Vetsera; he had shot her and then himself. The court announced heart failure, then admitted suicide 'in a state of mental derangement' so that he could be buried in the Kapuzinergruft; Mary Vetsera was buried quietly at Heiligenkreuz.

Franz Joseph turned the lodge into a Carmelite convent. The succession passed to his brother Karl Ludwig and then to Karl Ludwig's son Franz Ferdinand, whose assassination at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 started the war.

The Empress wore black from Mayerling onward and kept moving: Corfu, Hungary, spas. On 10 September 1898, walking to a lake steamer on the quay at Geneva, she was stabbed through the heart with a sharpened file by the Italian anarchist Luigi Lucheni and died within the hour.
The story became Anatole Litvak's film Mayerling of 1936, with Charles Boyer and Danielle Darrieux, and Kenneth MacMillan's ballet of 1978 for the Royal Ballet, to Liszt arranged by John Lanchbery.
items.remark: Mayerling was a succession crisis before it was a tragedy: Rudolf's death in January 1889 moved the crown toward Franz Ferdinand, and it was Franz Ferdinand's death at Sarajevo that finished the empire.
items.gaffe: Calling Mayerling a palace, or Sisi's death an accident. It was a hunting lodge, now a Carmelite convent, and the Empress was stabbed with a file by an anarchist on the quay at Geneva in September 1898.
sources: Brigitte Hamann, The Reluctant Empress: A Biography of Empress Elisabeth of Austria (1986)
Greg King and Penny Wilson, Twilight of Empire: The Tragedy at Mayerling and the End of the Habsburgs (2017)
Brigitte Hamann, Rudolf: Kronprinz und Rebell (1978)

items.title: Vienna 1900
facts: The spring of 1897 is the hinge: Klimt and his friends walked out of the Künstlerhaus and constituted the Secession on 3 April, the day Brahms died in the city; Franz Joseph, having refused to confirm him for two years, accepted the antisemitic Christian Social Karl Lueger as mayor on 16 April; and Mahler, baptised a Catholic that February to be eligible, took over the Court Opera in October.
Freud's Die Traumdeutung was published in November 1899 with 1900 printed on the title page; he saw patients at Berggasse 19 from 1891 until he left for London in 1938.

Klimt's ceiling paintings for the University, Philosophy, Medicine and Jurisprudence, were attacked by eighty-seven professors when the first was shown in 1900; Klimt gave the fee back in 1905 and took the pictures away, and they burned at Schloss Immendorf in 1945.

Café Griensteidl, the writers' café, was demolished in 1897 and Karl Kraus wrote its obituary as 'Die demolirte Literatur'; the Café Central inherited its clientele. Adolf Loos built the plain-fronted Looshaus opposite the Hofburg in 1910 and lectured the same year on 'Ornament and Crime'.

Schoenberg's Second String Quartet was hissed at its premiere in December 1908, and the Skandalkonzert of 31 March 1913, with Berg and Webern on the programme, ended in a brawl and a court case. Lueger's admirers included a young Adolf Hitler, who lived in the city from 1908 to 1913.
items.remark: Mahler had to be baptised to get the Opera in 1897, the same spring Klimt walked out of the Künstlerhaus and the Emperor gave in and accepted Lueger as mayor; Freud's Interpretation of Dreams followed in November 1899 with 1900 on the title page.
items.gaffe: Calling it a golden age without the politics. Lueger's Christian Socials ran the city from 1897, Mahler needed a baptism certificate to get the Opera, and Klimt's University paintings were rejected by the professors who had commissioned them.
sources: Carl E. Schorske, Fin-de-siècle Vienna: Politics and Culture (1980)
Grove Music Online, 'Mahler, Gustav'
Peter Gay, Freud: A Life for Our Time (1988)
Tobias G. Natter (ed.), Gustav Klimt: The Complete Paintings (2012)

items.title: The end of the old Europe
facts: Franz Joseph died at Schönbrunn on 21 November 1916 after sixty-eight years. His great-nephew Karl signed, on 11 November 1918, a declaration renouncing any part in the affairs of state, which was not an abdication, and left Schönbrunn that night; the Republic of German-Austria was proclaimed the next day.

The Habsburg Law of 3 April 1919 banished the family unless they renounced their claims, and a law of the same day abolished the nobility: titles and the particle 'von' became illegal in Austria, and still are.

Nicholas II abdicated in March 1917 and was shot with his family at Ekaterinburg on 17 July 1918; Wilhelm II's abdication was announced on 9 November 1918 and he lived out his life at Doorn in the Netherlands. Klimt died in February 1918 and Schiele in October, of the influenza.

Stefan Zweig, born in Vienna in 1881, finished Die Welt von Gestern (The World of Yesterday) in exile in 1941 and sent the manuscript to his publisher shortly before he and his wife took their own lives at Petrópolis in Brazil on 22 February 1942; its first chapter is called 'The World of Security'.

Elgar's Cello Concerto, his last major work, was premiered at the Queen's Hall on 27 October 1919 by Felix Salmond, under-rehearsed because Albert Coates had used up the time, and was a failure on the night. Ravel's Le Tombeau de Couperin (1919) dedicates each of its six movements to a friend killed in the war, and he denied that La Valse (1920) was about the fall of Vienna, though everyone hears it that way.
items.remark: Klimt died in February 1918, Schiele in October, the last emperor left Schönbrunn in November, and the republic abolished 'von' the following April; Zweig called the world before all that 'the world of security', and killed himself in Brazil in 1942.
items.gaffe: Saying Karl abdicated. He signed a renunciation of any part in the government on 11 November 1918 and never gave up the throne, which is why the republic had to legislate the family out of the country the following April.
sources: Stefan Zweig, The World of Yesterday (1942; trans. Anthea Bell, 2009)
Gordon Brook-Shepherd, The Last Habsburg (1968)
Grove Music Online, 'Elgar, Sir Edward' and 'Ravel, Maurice'
Jerrold Northrop Moore, Edward Elgar: A Creative Life (1984)

items.title: Maria Theresa
facts: Born in Vienna on 13 May 1717, the eldest surviving child of Charles VI, who spent his reign getting Europe to accept that a daughter could inherit; she succeeded on 20 October 1740, and Frederick the Great invaded Silesia within two months.

She was never Holy Roman Empress in her own right: the title came from her husband, Francis Stephen of Lorraine, elected Emperor in 1745, and what she held was Hungary, Bohemia and the Austrian lands. She fought Frederick twice for Silesia, in the War of the Austrian Succession and the Seven Years' War, and lost it both times.

In September 1741 the Hungarian Diet at Pressburg voted her their 'life and blood'; the prints that show her holding up the infant Joseph while they cheer conflate two sittings. Sixteen children, among them Joseph II, Leopold II and Maria Antonia, who became Marie Antoinette.

She had Pacassi rebuild Schönbrunn from 1743 as the summer palace; there, on 13 October 1762, the six-year-old Mozart played to her, and by Leopold Mozart's letter home jumped into her lap and kissed her. Gluck's Orfeo had opened at the Burgtheater eight days earlier.

Martin van Meytens, her court painter, made the standard portraits; the Theresianum (1746), compulsory schooling (1774) and the alliance with France that sent her daughter to Versailles are hers. She died on 29 November 1780.
items.remark: She was never empress in her own right; the title came from her husband's election in 1745, and what she actually held was Hungary, Bohemia and the Austrian lands, which she kept by fighting Frederick the Great twice over Silesia and losing it both times.
items.gaffe: Calling her Holy Roman Empress as though she had been elected, or muddling the Hofburg with Schönbrunn. Schönbrunn is the summer palace she had Pacassi rebuild, where the six-year-old Mozart played in October 1762.
sources: Edward Crankshaw, Maria Theresa (1969)
Barbara Stollberg-Rilinger, Maria Theresia: Die Kaiserin in ihrer Zeit (2017)
Otto Erich Deutsch, Mozart: A Documentary Biography (1965), Leopold Mozart's letter of 16 October 1762

items.title: Metternich
facts: Klemens von Metternich was born at Koblenz on 15 May 1773, a Rhinelander whose family lost its lands to the French Revolution; he was Austrian ambassador in Paris from 1806 to 1809, foreign minister from October 1809, and arranged Napoleon's marriage to the Emperor's daughter Marie Louise in 1810.

He hosted the Congress of Vienna, and Francis I paid him in 1816 with Schloss Johannisberg on the Rhine, which is why a sparkling wine still carries the name Fürst von Metternich; he was made State Chancellor in 1821.

The Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 put the universities and the press under police watch across the German Confederation; the 'Metternich system' is the name for the censorship and congress diplomacy of the thirty years after 1815. 'Italy is a geographical expression' is his, from 1847.
Thomas Lawrence painted him for the Prince Regent's Waterloo Chamber at Windsor, among the sovereigns and ministers who had beaten Napoleon.
He resigned on 13 March 1848, the day the barricades went up, fled to England, came back to Vienna in 1851 and died there on 11 June 1859.
items.remark: He held the job for thirty-nine years, from 1809 to the afternoon of 13 March 1848, and the Emperor paid him for the Congress with Schloss Johannisberg on the Rhine, which is why his name is on a bottle of Sekt.
items.gaffe: Saying he was Prussian, or that he fell at the Congress. He was a Rhinelander in Austrian service who ran the Congress and lasted another thirty-three years; it was the barricades of March 1848 that put him on the road to England.
sources: Alan Sked, Metternich and Austria: An Evaluation (2008)
Wolfram Siemann, Metternich: Strategist and Visionary (2019)

items.title: Franz Joseph I
facts: Born at Schönbrunn on 18 August 1830; emperor at eighteen on 2 December 1848, when his uncle Ferdinand abdicated at Olomouc; died at Schönbrunn on 21 November 1916, after sixty-eight years, the longest reign in Habsburg history.
He went to Bad Ischl in August 1853 to meet his cousin Helene of Bavaria and chose her younger sister Elisabeth instead; they married in the Augustinerkirche on 24 April 1854.
Beaten by Prussia at Königgrätz in July 1866, he accepted the Compromise of 1867 that made Austria-Hungary, and was crowned King of Hungary in Buda on 8 June 1867 to Liszt's Coronation Mass.

His decree of December 1857 ordered the city walls down, and the Ringstrasse was his: the Opera opened in 1869, the Burgtheater in 1888, the Kunsthistorisches Museum in 1891. He worked from a desk from five in the morning, slept on an iron bedstead, and from 1886 had the Burgtheater actress Katharina Schratt as his companion, with the Empress's blessing.

He lost his brother Maximilian to a Mexican firing squad in 1867, his son Rudolf at Mayerling in 1889, his wife to an assassin in 1898 and his heir Franz Ferdinand at Sarajevo in 1914, and he outlived them all.
items.remark: He came to the throne at eighteen in 1848 and was still on it in 1916; the Ringstrasse, the Opera and the Kunsthistorisches Museum are his, and he buried a brother, a son, a wife and an heir on the way.
items.gaffe: Mixing him up with Franz Ferdinand. Franz Joseph is the whiskers and the sixty-eight years; Franz Ferdinand was his nephew, the heir shot at Sarajevo in 1914, and the old man outlived him by two years.
sources: Jean-Paul Bled, Franz Joseph (1992)
Steven Beller, Francis Joseph (1996)
Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Sisi Museum, catalogue entry for Winterhalter's portrait of Franz Joseph I (1865)

items.title: Empress Elisabeth (Sisi)
facts: Born in Munich on Christmas Eve 1837, a daughter of Duke Max in Bavaria; married her cousin Franz Joseph at sixteen on 24 April 1854, having gone to Bad Ischl in August 1853 only to accompany her mother and her elder sister Helene, the intended bride.

Winterhalter painted her in 1865 in white tulle with diamond stars in her hair; the stars were real, made by the court jeweller Köchert, and the portrait hangs in the Hofburg. She refused to be photographed after her early thirties, so it is the face the world kept.

She kept a waist of about fifty centimetres with riding, walking and a set of gymnastic rings in her apartments; her hair took hours a day; she learned Hungarian, championed the Compromise of 1867, was crowned Queen of Hungary that June and was given Gödöllő as a coronation present.
She read Heine, wrote verse, built the Achilleion on Corfu about 1890 and then tired of it; after Mayerling she wore black and travelled almost without pause.

On 10 September 1898, walking to a lake steamer on the quay at Geneva, she was stabbed through the heart with a sharpened file by the anarchist Luigi Lucheni and died within the hour. The 1950s films with Romy Schneider spell her 'Sissi'; the family spelling is Sisi.
items.remark: The diamond stars in the Winterhalter portrait were real, made by Köchert, and the waist underneath was about fifty centimetres; she stopped allowing photographs in her early thirties, so the 1865 picture is the face the world kept.
items.gaffe: Spelling her Sissi. That is the Romy Schneider films of the 1950s; the family spelling is Sisi, and she was Bavarian, not Austrian, a duchess in Bavaria married to her cousin at sixteen.
sources: Brigitte Hamann, The Reluctant Empress: A Biography of Empress Elisabeth of Austria (1986)
Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Sisi Museum, catalogue entry for Winterhalter's portrait of Empress Elisabeth (1865)

items.title: The child Mozart proposes to Marie Antoinette
facts: The Mozarts, on their first tour, were received by Maria Theresa at Schönbrunn on 13 October 1762; Leopold's letter home of 16 October reports the Empress's kindness and the boy jumping into her lap, and says nothing of a proposal.
Maria Antonia, the future Marie Antoinette, was born on 2 November 1755 and was six that October, as was Mozart, born on 27 January 1756; she left for France and the Dauphin in 1770.
Gluck's Orfeo ed Euridice had opened at the Burgtheater on 5 October 1762, the week before the Mozarts arrived.
items.remark: What Leopold actually wrote home in October 1762 was that Wolferl jumped into the Empress's lap and kissed her; the slip on the floor and the proposal to the future Marie Antoinette came later, when both children were famous for other reasons.
items.gaffe: Telling it as Mozart proposing to the Queen of France. In 1762 she was Maria Antonia, the Empress's fifteenth child, aged six, and the French marriage was eight years off; and the proposal is not in the one letter that describes the day.
sources: Emily Anderson (ed.), The Letters of Mozart and His Family (3rd ed., 1985), Leopold Mozart to Lorenz Hagenauer, 16 October 1762
Otto Erich Deutsch, Mozart: A Documentary Biography (1965)
Maynard Solomon, Mozart: A Life (1995)
items.claim: At Schönbrunn in 1762 the six-year-old Mozart slipped on the polished floor, was picked up by the little Archduchess Maria Antonia, and announced that he would marry her when he grew up.
items.truth: The visit happened: Leopold Mozart's letter of 16 October 1762 describes Wolfgang playing at Schönbrunn on 13 October, jumping into the Empress's lap and kissing her. The slip on the floor and the proposal are not in the letter, the only contemporary account, and appear only in later biography; they cannot be verified.

items.title: Salieri poisoned Mozart
facts: Seven weeks before he died Mozart took Salieri to Die Zauberflöte, and wrote to Constanze on 14 October 1791 that Salieri had called out bravo at every number.
Salieri taught Beethoven, Schubert, Liszt and Mozart's own younger son Franz Xaver; he was Kapellmeister to the imperial court from 1788 until 1824 and died on 7 May 1825.

Peter Shaffer's Amadeus opened at the National Theatre in London in 1979, and Milos Forman's film of 1984 won eight Academy Awards; Pushkin's little tragedy of 1830 had already put the poison in Salieri's hand.
items.remark: Salieri taught Beethoven, Schubert, Liszt and Mozart's own younger son, which is not what you do with the family of a man you have murdered; the poison is Pushkin's, from 1830, and Shaffer's, from 1979.
items.gaffe: Taking Amadeus for biography. The register says fever, the poisoning story was gossip within a month, and Salieri's supposed confession is a rumour from his dementia in 1823, denied by him and preserved second-hand in Beethoven's conversation books.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Salieri, Antonio'
H. C. Robbins Landon, 1791: Mozart's Last Year (1988)
Otto Erich Deutsch, Mozart: A Documentary Biography (1965)
Emily Anderson (ed.), The Letters of Mozart and His Family (3rd ed., 1985), Mozart to Constanze, 14 October 1791
items.claim: Antonio Salieri, the court Kapellmeister, poisoned Mozart out of jealousy and confessed to it on his deathbed.
items.truth: Mozart died on 5 December 1791 after about two weeks of illness; the death register gives 'hitziges Frieselfieber', an acute fever with a rash. A Berlin paper printed the poisoning rumour within the month, with no evidence. In 1823, old and in mental decline, Salieri was said to have accused himself; he denied it to Moscheles on his word of honour, and the rumour survives mostly in Beethoven's conversation books. Pushkin's play Mozart and Salieri (1830), Rimsky-Korsakov's opera (1898) and Shaffer's Amadeus (1979) made the story permanent.

items.title: Ecco la primavera
items.creator: Francesco Landini
facts: A two-voice ballata by Francesco Landini (c. 1325–1397), the blind organist of San Lorenzo and the leading composer of the Italian Trecento; more than 150 of his pieces survive, almost all of them ballate.

Landini's music is preserved chiefly in the Squarcialupi Codex, an illuminated manuscript of the early 1400s now in the Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana in Florence, which gives him nearly 150 pieces and a portrait with his portative organ.
The 'Landini cadence', in which the melody dips to the sixth before rising to the octave, is named after him, though he did not invent it.
items.remark: Landini was blinded by smallpox as a child and became the most famous organist in Florence; his tomb slab in San Lorenzo shows him holding the little portative organ he played.
items.gaffe: Hearing 'Trecento' and thinking of the thirteenth century. It is Italian for the 1300s: the century of Landini, Petrarch and Boccaccio.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Landini, Francesco'
Grove Music Online, 'Squarcialupi Codex'

items.title: The Florentine intermedi of 1589 (La Pellegrina)
items.creator: Cristofano Malvezzi, Luca Marenzio, Emilio de' Cavalieri and others
facts: Six musical interludes performed between the acts of Girolamo Bargagli's comedy La Pellegrina in the Uffizi theatre on 2 May 1589, for the wedding of Grand Duke Ferdinando I de' Medici and Christine of Lorraine.

Count Giovanni de' Bardi devised the programme on the power of music; Bernardo Buontalenti designed the sets and machines; the composers included Malvezzi, Marenzio, Cavalieri, Jacopo Peri and Giulio Caccini, and the music was printed in 1591.
The closing ballo, Cavalieri's 'O che nuovo miracolo', travelled across Europe as the 'Aria di Fiorenza' or 'Ballo del Granduca' and served keyboard composers as a theme for variations for a century.
items.remark: The 1589 intermedi were a dress rehearsal for opera without anyone intending it: Peri sang Arion in the fifth, Caccini wrote for the fourth, and within eleven years both had composed an Euridice.
items.gaffe: Calling them the first opera. They are spectacle between the acts of a spoken comedy; the first operas came from the same circle a decade later.
sources: Nina Treadwell, Music and Wonder at the Medici Court: The 1589 Interludes for La pellegrina (2008)
Grove Music Online, 'Intermedio'

items.title: Amarilli, mia bella
items.creator: Giulio Caccini
facts: A solo song from Le nuove musiche, the collection Caccini published in Florence in 1602 with a preface that is the manifesto of the new style: one voice over a bass, the words ruling the rhythm, the ornaments written out and explained.
The poem is attributed to Alessandro Guarini; the song was copied, printed and arranged all over Europe within a generation and is in every singing student's Arie antiche.
Caccini's preface borrows Castiglione's word sprezzatura for the singer's studied nonchalance with the beat.
His daughter Francesca Caccini composed La liberazione di Ruggiero (Florence, 1625), generally called the first opera by a woman.
items.remark: Caccini's preface to Le nuove musiche borrows the courtier's word sprezzatura: sing it with a studied carelessness about the beat, over a bass that keeps its own counsel.
items.gaffe: Attributing the 'Caccini Ave Maria' to him. It was written around 1970 by the Soviet lutenist Vladimir Vavilov, who put it out as anonymous; Caccini's name attached itself later.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Caccini, Giulio'
Giulio Caccini, Le nuove musiche, ed. H. Wiley Hitchcock (1970)

items.title: Fiori musicali
items.creator: Girolamo Frescobaldi
facts: Three organ masses (for Sundays, for the Apostles, for the Madonna) made up of toccatas, Kyrie versets, canzonas and ricercars, published in Venice in 1635; a bergamasca and a capriccio on a popular tune close the book.

Frescobaldi, born in Ferrara in 1583, was organist of St Peter's in Rome from 1608; the Medici brought him to Florence in 1628 and he served Grand Duke Ferdinando II until 1634, returning to Rome the year before Fiori musicali appeared.
J. S. Bach owned a manuscript copy of the whole collection, signed and dated by him in Weimar in 1714; Froberger came from Vienna to study with Frescobaldi in Rome in the late 1630s.
items.remark: Bach owned a manuscript copy of the whole of Fiori musicali, signed and dated in Weimar in 1714, which tells you what he thought of it; the organ fugue's grandparents live in that book.
items.gaffe: Calling Frescobaldi a Florentine. He was from Ferrara and worked mostly in Rome; Florence had him for six years, 1628 to 1634, on the Grand Duke's payroll.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Frescobaldi, Girolamo'
Frederick Hammond, Girolamo Frescobaldi (1983)

Giovanni Gabrieli

items.title: Minuet from the String Quintet in E major, Op. 11 No. 5
items.creator: Luigi Boccherini
items.parent: String Quintet in E major, Op. 11 No. 5, G 275 (1771)
facts: The third movement of a quintet for two violins, viola and two cellos composed in 1771, one of a set of six; the quintet is in E major but the minuet is in A.
Boccherini was born in Lucca in 1743, a cellist who wrote his own cello part into the quintets; from 1770 he served the Infante Luis in Spain, and he died in Madrid in 1805.
In Alexander Mackendrick's The Ladykillers (1955) it is the record the criminals play while pretending to rehearse as a string quintet.
items.remark: The minuet everyone knows comes from a quintet with two cellos, because Boccherini was a cellist and wrote the quintets for himself to play; it is in A major though the quintet is in E.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Haydn. Boccherini was called 'Haydn's wife' by the violinist Giuseppe Puppo, which was unkind and inaccurate: he spent his career in Spain, not Esterháza, and his textures are lighter.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Boccherini, Luigi'
Elisabeth Le Guin, Boccherini's Body: An Essay in Carnal Musicology (2006)

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
