items.title: Jean-Baptiste Lully
facts: Born Giovanni Battista Lulli in Florence on 28 November 1632, a miller's son; taken to Paris in 1646 to serve the Grande Mademoiselle, and naturalised French in 1661.
Danced beside the young Louis XIV in the Ballet de la Nuit in 1653, wrote the comédies-ballets with Molière, including Le Bourgeois gentilhomme (1670), and from 1672 held the royal monopoly on opera.
Died in 1687 of gangrene after striking his foot with the long staff he used to beat time, while conducting his Te Deum for the king's recovery.
items.remark: The founder of French opera was a Florentine miller's son who did not become French until he was nearly thirty: Lulli turned into Lully by letters of naturalisation in 1661.
items.gaffe: Treating the story of his death as a legend. He really did strike his foot with his conducting staff and die of the gangrene, in 1687; the surprise is that it is attested.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Lully, Jean-Baptiste'
Jérôme de La Gorce, Jean-Baptiste Lully (2002)

items.title: Luigi Cherubini
facts: Born in Florence in September 1760; came to Paris in 1786 and, after one last Italian commission at Turin, settled there for good in 1788, directing the Conservatoire from 1822 until a month before his death in 1842.

His Requiem in C minor was written for the anniversary of Louis XVI's execution and first sung at Saint-Denis on 21 January 1817; his opera Médée (1797) is the one that returns to the stage, usually in the Italian version with Franz Lachner's recitatives of 1855.

Ingres painted him in 1842 with the Muse of Lyric Poetry holding a hand over his head; the picture is in the Louvre. Berlioz's Mémoires make him the villain of the Conservatoire, which is one side of the story.
Florence's conservatory, the Conservatorio Luigi Cherubini, is named after him.
items.remark: Cherubini was a Florentine who became the most powerful musician in Paris: Ingres painted him, Berlioz mocked him, Beethoven admired him, and Florence named its conservatory after him.
items.gaffe: Assuming Callas's Medea is the original. Cherubini's Médée is a French opera of 1797 with spoken dialogue; the sung recitatives are Franz Lachner's, added in 1855.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Cherubini, Luigi'
Basil Deane, Cherubini (1965)

items.title: Giacomo Puccini
facts: Born in Lucca on 22 December 1858, the fifth generation of a family that had run the music at Lucca's cathedral of San Martino since the eighteenth century.

Gianni Schicchi, the comedy that closes Il trittico (New York, 1918), is set in Florence in 1299 and takes its plot from a mention in Dante's Inferno; 'O mio babbino caro' names Porta Rossa, the Ponte Vecchio and the Arno.

He lived from the 1890s at Torre del Lago, on a lake near Lucca, shooting waterfowl between operas, and is buried in the villa there; he died in Brussels in 1924 leaving Turandot unfinished, and Franco Alfano completed it.
items.remark: Puccini was Lucchese, not Florentine, from a family that had run Lucca's cathedral music for over a century; his one Florentine piece is Gianni Schicchi, which puts a fraudster from Dante's Inferno on stage.
items.gaffe: Calling him a Florentine, or a Milanese because of La Scala. He was born in Lucca, lived by the lake at Torre del Lago, and the distinction matters in Tuscany.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Puccini, Giacomo'
Julian Budden, Puccini: His Life and Works (2002)

items.title: The Florentine Camerata
facts: A circle of noblemen, musicians and scholars who met at the house of Count Giovanni de' Bardi in Florence from about 1573 into the 1580s to discuss, among other things, how the ancient Greeks had sung their tragedies.

Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, was its leading theorist; his Dialogo della musica antica et della moderna (1581) argued that counterpoint smothered the words and that a single voice over a simple accompaniment moved the passions better.

Giulio Caccini belonged to it; Peri's membership is likely but undocumented. The first operas, Dafne (1598) and Euridice (1600), came from a later circle around Jacopo Corsi, after Bardi had gone to Rome in 1592.
items.remark: The Camerata did not invent opera, whatever the programme note says; it was a talking shop at Bardi's house about how the Greeks sang their tragedies, and Galileo's father was its loudest voice.
items.gaffe: Saying the Camerata wrote the first opera. Dafne and Euridice came from Jacopo Corsi's circle in the 1590s, after Bardi had left Florence for Rome.
sources: Claude V. Palisca, The Florentine Camerata: Documentary Studies and Translations (1989)
Grove Music Online, 'Camerata'

items.title: Maggio Musicale Fiorentino
facts: Italy's oldest music festival, founded in 1933 by the conductor Vittorio Gui, who had set up the city's permanent orchestra five years earlier; it began as a festival for the month of May and now runs into the summer.

Its home for eighty years was the Teatro Comunale on the Corso Italia, a nineteenth-century politeama; in 2014 it moved to a new house by the Cascine park, opened in stages from December 2011 and now called the Teatro del Maggio.
Riccardo Muti was its principal conductor from 1968 to 1980 and Zubin Mehta from 1985 for more than thirty years.
items.remark: Maggio means May: Vittorio Gui started it as a May festival in 1933, which makes it the oldest in Italy, and Muti and then Mehta ran its orchestra for most of the last half-century.
items.gaffe: Saying 'the Florence opera house' and meaning La Pergola. The Teatro della Pergola is the old court theatre where Verdi's Macbeth had its premiere in 1847; the Maggio's home is the new Teatro del Maggio by the Cascine.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Florence'
Teatro del Maggio Musicale Fiorentino, official history

items.title: Madrigal
facts: It began in Florence and Rome in the 1520s and 1530s with Verdelot and Arcadelt, both of whom worked in Florence, and reached its height with Marenzio, Gesualdo and Monteverdi.
Word-painting is its signature: the line climbs on 'heaven', stops on 'death', sighs on 'sospiri'.

Monteverdi's eight books of madrigals (1587 to 1638) trace the form's whole passage from unaccompanied polyphony to voices with continuo; the fourteenth-century madrigal of Landini's time is a different form that shares only the name.
items.remark: The madrigal is where word-painting lives, a rising line on 'heaven' and a discord on 'death'; Marenzio did it best and Gesualdo did it strangest.
items.gaffe: Confusing it with the motet. A motet is sacred and Latin; a madrigal is secular and Italian, or, after Musica transalpina in 1588, English.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Madrigal'
Alfred Einstein, The Italian Madrigal (1949)

term: A sacred Latin motet for the Mass, sung by a choir without instruments.
A strophic Neapolitan street song in three parts with a refrain, deliberately rustic in style.
A solo song with lute accompaniment fashionable at the Elizabethan court.

items.definition: A secular Italian part-song of the sixteenth century, usually for four to six unaccompanied voices, setting a serious poem line by line so that the music follows the sense of the words.

items.title: Basso continuo
facts: Figured bass first appeared in print around 1600, in Cavalieri's Rappresentatione di Anima, et di Corpo in Rome and Peri's Euridice in Florence; Caccini's Le nuove musiche followed in 1602.
The figures are intervals above the bass; the keyboard player realises them on the spot, so two performances of the same continuo part need never sound the same.
Historians have called the Baroque 'the thoroughbass era' because the practice bounds it so neatly: it arrives around 1600 and fades after 1750.
items.remark: Continuo is why a Baroque band always has a harpsichordist who never seems to have a tune: they are reading a bass line with numbers under it and inventing the chords.
items.gaffe: Assuming the figures under the bass are fingering. They are intervals above the bass, and the player is improvising the chords from them, not reading a written part.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Continuo'
F. T. Arnold, The Art of Accompaniment from a Thorough-Bass (1931)

term: A short bass melody repeated over and over while the upper parts vary, as in a chaconne or passacaglia.
The lowest voice part in an opera chorus, sung throughout without rests.
The sustained pedal note held under a cadenza in a concerto.

items.definition: The continuous bass line under most music from about 1600 to 1750, played by a bass instrument together with a chord instrument such as harpsichord, organ or lute, whose player improvises the harmonies, often from figures written under the notes.

items.title: Monody
facts: Caccini's Le nuove musiche (Florence, 1602) is the first large printed collection of monodies, with a preface explaining how they should be sung.
The Florentines called the speech-like kind stile recitativo or stile rappresentativo; 'monody' is the historians' word, not theirs.
Monteverdi's Lamento d'Arianna (1608), the one surviving piece of his lost opera Arianna, is the most famous monody of all; he later reworked it as a five-voice madrigal.
items.remark: Monody is one voice and a bass, with the rhythm of speech; the Florentines believed that was how Greek tragedy had sounded, and it is the difference between a madrigal and an opera.
items.gaffe: Using 'monody' to mean 'monophony'. Plainchant is monophony, one line and nothing else; monody has a bass under the voice, which is the whole point.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Monody'
Nigel Fortune, 'Italian Secular Monody from 1600 to 1635: An Introductory Survey', Musical Quarterly (1953)

term: Music in a single unaccompanied line, such as plainchant.
A polyphonic texture in which every voice sings the same words in the same rhythm.
A canon in which one melody is sung by two voices entering at different times.

items.definition: Italian solo song of around 1600 to 1640: one voice over a basso continuo, with the singer's rhythm following the words like heightened speech; the style in which the first operas were written.

items.title: Zadok the Priest, HWV 258
items.creator: George Frideric Handel
facts: One of four anthems Handel wrote for the coronation of George II and Queen Caroline in Westminster Abbey on 11 October 1727; it has been sung at every coronation since.
The words, from 1 Kings 1, describe the anointing of Solomon and have been used at English coronations since King Edgar's in 973.
Handel had been made a British subject by Act of Parliament in February 1727, eight months before the coronation.
The UEFA Champions League anthem of 1992 is an arrangement of it by Tony Britten.
items.remark: Handel wrote it for George II's coronation in October 1727, eight months after an Act of Parliament made him a British subject, and it has been sung at every coronation since.
items.gaffe: Assuming it was written for George I. He died in June 1727; the anthem is for his son's crowning in October, and the Champions League tune is a 1992 arrangement of it, not the other way round.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Handel, George Frideric'
Donald Burrows, Handel and the English Chapel Royal (2005)

items.title: Water Music, HWV 348–350
items.creator: George Frideric Handel
facts: Played on the Thames on 17 July 1717 from a barge alongside George I's, between Whitehall and Chelsea, by about fifty musicians; the Daily Courant reported that the king had it played over three times 'in going and returning', and the Prussian envoy Friedrich Bonet added that this was twice before supper and once after.
Survives as three suites, in F, D and G major; the autograph is lost and the original order of the movements is not known.
The well-known 'Alla Hornpipe' belongs to the D major suite, the one with trumpets.
Handel's other outdoor piece, the Music for the Royal Fireworks, was for George II's peace celebration in Green Park on 27 April 1749, at which part of the fireworks pavilion caught fire.
items.remark: The Daily Courant reported that George I had it played three times on the river that night, 'in going and returning'; the tale that Handel wrote it to win back the king's favour comes from Mainwaring in 1760 and is doubted.
items.gaffe: Calling it the Royal Fireworks music. That is a different piece, for a different king, thirty-two years later.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Handel, George Frideric'
Donald Burrows, Handel (Master Musicians, 2nd ed., 2012)
Daily Courant, 19 July 1717

items.title: Hallelujah, from Messiah
items.creator: George Frideric Handel
facts: Messiah was composed in about twenty-four days in August and September 1741, to a text compiled by Charles Jennens from the Bible and the Prayer Book psalms.
First performed in Dublin on 13 April 1742; the London premiere was at Covent Garden on 23 March 1743.

The chorus ends Part Two of three; the words are from Revelation, and it is where the timpani first enter: until then the trumpets have sounded only briefly, 'from a distance', in 'Glory to God' in Part One.
The story that George II stood for it first appears in a letter of 1780; no contemporary account puts the king at the performance.
items.remark: It closes Part Two, not the work, and the story of George II rising to his feet rests on a letter written in 1780, thirty-seven years after the London premiere.
items.gaffe: Saying 'The Messiah', or calling it an opera. Handel's title has no article, and an oratorio is sung in concert with no staging.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Messiah'
Donald Burrows, Handel: Messiah (Cambridge Music Handbooks, 1991)

creator: Johann Sebastian Bach

items.title: Nimrod, from the Enigma Variations
items.creator: Edward Elgar
items.parent: Variations on an Original Theme ('Enigma'), Op. 36 (1899)
facts: Variation IX of fourteen; the set was first performed at St James's Hall, London, on 19 June 1899, conducted by Hans Richter.
A portrait of August Jaeger, Elgar's editor at the publisher Novello: Jäger is German for hunter, and Nimrod is the mighty hunter of Genesis.
Elgar wrote that the opening bars were meant to recall the slow movement of Beethoven's Pathétique Sonata, after an evening in which Jaeger talked about Beethoven's slow movements.
Played at the Cenotaph in Whitehall every Remembrance Sunday.
items.remark: It is a portrait of August Jaeger, his editor at Novello: Jäger is German for hunter, and Nimrod is the mighty hunter of Genesis, so the most solemn tune in English music is named after a pun on a friend's surname.
items.gaffe: Calling it a funeral piece. Elgar wrote it about a living friend and a summer-evening talk about Beethoven's slow movements; the Cenotaph came later.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Elgar, Edward'
Julian Rushton, Elgar: Enigma Variations (Cambridge Music Handbooks, 1999)
Jerrold Northrop Moore, Edward Elgar: A Creative Life (1984)

items.title: Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 in D, Op. 39
items.creator: Edward Elgar
facts: First played in Liverpool on 19 October 1901; three days later Henry Wood conducted it at the Queen's Hall Proms and, by his own account, the audience made him play it three times.
The title is from Othello: 'Pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war.'
The trio tune became 'Land of Hope and Glory' in the Coronation Ode of 1902, with words by A. C. Benson; the coronation gala was cancelled when Edward VII fell ill with appendicitis.
There are five Pomp and Circumstance marches (1901 to 1930); a sixth was completed from sketches by Anthony Payne in 2006.
items.remark: The tune came first and the words a year later: Elgar had the trio in 1901, and A. C. Benson fitted 'Land of Hope and Glory' to it for the Coronation Ode of 1902.
items.gaffe: Calling the whole march 'Land of Hope and Glory', or crediting Elgar with the words. Benson wrote them, and there are five Pomp and Circumstance marches, not one.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Elgar, Edward'
Henry Wood, My Life of Music (1938)
Jerrold Northrop Moore, Edward Elgar: A Creative Life (1984)

items.title: The Lark Ascending
items.creator: Ralph Vaughan Williams
facts: Written for violin and piano in 1914, revised and orchestrated after the war; the orchestral version was first heard at the Queen's Hall, London, on 14 June 1921, with Marie Hall and Adrian Boult.
Subtitled 'Romance'; it is a single movement of about a quarter of an hour, and takes its title and prefatory lines from George Meredith's poem.
The solo violin's opening and closing cadenzas are written without bar lines.
Regularly voted first in Classic FM's annual Hall of Fame poll.
items.remark: It was sketched in 1914 and finished after the war, so the pastoral is a memory rather than a description; the violin's opening cadenza has no bar lines at all.
items.gaffe: Calling it a violin concerto. It is a single-movement romance for violin and orchestra, a quarter of an hour long, with no fast movement to show off in.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Vaughan Williams, Ralph'
Michael Kennedy, The Works of Ralph Vaughan Williams (2nd ed., 1980)

Fantasia on Greensleeves
A London Symphony

items.title: Jupiter, the Bringer of Jollity, from The Planets
items.creator: Gustav Holst
facts: The fourth of seven movements; the suite was written between 1914 and 1916 and first heard privately at the Queen's Hall on 29 September 1918, conducted by Adrian Boult.
Holst's planets are astrological characters, an interest he took up in 1913, which is why Earth is absent and each title names a temperament.
The broad central tune became the hymn 'I vow to thee, my country' in 1921 and takes its hymn-book name, Thaxted, from the Essex village where Holst lived.
Holst taught for most of his working life at St Paul's Girls' School in Hammersmith, from 1905 until his death, and at Morley College from 1907 to 1924.
items.remark: The planets are astrological characters, not astronomy, which is why there is no Earth; the big tune in the middle only became 'I vow to thee, my country' in 1921, five years after the suite was finished.
items.gaffe: Asking why Pluto is missing. It was discovered in 1930, sixteen years after Holst began the suite, and Earth is missing too, because the planets are astrological.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Holst, Gustav'
Imogen Holst, The Music of Gustav Holst (3rd ed., 1986)
Michael Short, Gustav Holst: The Man and His Music (1990)

items.title: God Save the King
items.creator: Anonymous
facts: First printed, without an author, in the collection Thesaurus Musicus in London in 1744.
Taken up at Drury Lane and Covent Garden in September 1745, in the alarm after the Jacobite victory at Prestonpans; Thomas Arne made the Drury Lane arrangement.
Henry Carey's son claimed the song for his father fifty years after Carey's death; John Bull has also been proposed; no attribution has been proved.
Beethoven wrote seven piano variations on it (WoO 78, 1803), and Haydn, who heard it in London, wanted an equivalent for Austria and wrote the Emperor's Hymn of 1797.
items.remark: Nobody knows who wrote it: it was printed anonymously in 1744 and taken up by the London theatres in September 1745 as the Jacobites marched south, and Beethoven later wrote a set of variations on it.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Handel, or to Henry Carey as fact. Carey's son claimed it for his father half a century after his death, and nobody's authorship has ever been proved.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'God Save the King'
Percy Scholes, God Save the Queen! The History and Romance of the World's First National Anthem (1954)

theme.note: The first six bars, melody only, in the usual key of G.

items.title: Henry Purcell
facts: Born in Westminster in 1659; organist of Westminster Abbey from 1679 and of the Chapel Royal from 1682; died on 21 November 1695, aged thirty-six, and was buried in the Abbey beside the organ.

Wrote the March and Canzona for four 'flatt' (slide) trumpets and the anthem 'Thou knowest, Lord' for Queen Mary II's funeral in Westminster Abbey on 5 March 1695; the same music was performed at his own funeral that November.
Dido and Aeneas, his one true opera, was performed at a girls' boarding school in Chelsea in about 1689; its closing lament is built over a repeating descending bass, a ground bass.
Britten's Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra (1946) is a set of variations on a rondeau from Purcell's music for the play Abdelazer.
items.remark: He was buried beneath the organ he had played at Westminster Abbey, and the music he wrote for Queen Mary's funeral in March 1695 was sung again at his own that November.
items.gaffe: Saying pur-SELL, or crediting him with the Trumpet Voluntary. The stress is on the first syllable, and the Trumpet Voluntary is Jeremiah Clarke's Prince of Denmark's March, published under Purcell's name from the 1870s and not given back to Clarke until the mid-twentieth century.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Purcell, Henry'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Purcell, Henry'
Peter Holman, Henry Purcell (Oxford Studies of Composers, 1994)

image.source: John Closterman, portrait of Henry Purcell (1695), National Portrait Gallery, London, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (artist died 1711); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: William Byrd
facts: Born about 1540, probably a pupil of Thomas Tallis; organist of Lincoln Cathedral from 1563 and a Gentleman of the Chapel Royal from 1572; died at Stondon Massey, Essex, on 4 July 1623.
In 1575 Elizabeth I granted Tallis and Byrd a twenty-one-year monopoly on printing music in England; their first joint publication, the Cantiones sacrae of 1575, was dedicated to her.
A Catholic recusant who wrote three Latin Masses (for three, four and five voices, about 1592 to 1595) and the Gradualia for clandestine worship, while also writing the Anglican Great Service.
Tallis (about 1505 to 1585) served under Henry VIII, Edward VI, Mary and Elizabeth; his forty-part motet Spem in alium is his, not Byrd's.
items.remark: He was a Catholic who wrote Latin masses for illegal household chapels under Elizabeth and kept his place in her Chapel Royal throughout; the Queen evidently preferred good music to consistency.
items.gaffe: Crediting him with Spem in alium. The forty-part motet is Tallis's, his teacher and business partner; Byrd's are the three Masses and the Great Service.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Byrd, William'
Kerry McCarthy, Byrd (Master Musicians, 2013)
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Byrd, William'

items.title: Royal Albert Hall
facts: Opened by Queen Victoria on 29 March 1871 in memory of Prince Albert, who had died in 1861; she was too overcome to speak, and the Prince of Wales declared it open for her. Designed by two Royal Engineers, Francis Fowke and Henry Scott.
Home of the BBC Proms since 1941, after the Queen's Hall was destroyed by bombing; the Proms had begun there in 1895 under Robert Newman and Henry Wood, and the BBC took them over in 1927.
Its echo was notorious until fibreglass 'mushrooms' were hung from the dome in 1969.
The chamber-music hall is Wigmore Hall, opened as the Bechstein Hall in 1901 and renamed in 1917 after the German firm's property was seized in the war.
items.remark: The Proms only moved here in 1941 because a bomb destroyed the Queen's Hall; before the acoustic 'mushrooms' went up in 1969 the echo was such that, as the old joke went, a British composer could be sure of hearing his work twice.
items.gaffe: Assuming the Royal Opera performs here. Opera is at Covent Garden; the Albert Hall is a concert hall that also hosts boxing and tennis, and the Proms for eight weeks a summer.
sources: Royal Albert Hall, 'Our History' (archives pages)
David Cox, The Henry Wood Proms (1980)

items.title: Oratorio
facts: Named after the oratory, or prayer hall, of St Philip Neri in Rome, where the genre began around 1600.

Handel turned from Italian opera to English oratorio in the 1730s when opera stopped paying; Messiah (1742), Judas Maccabaeus (1747) and Israel in Egypt (1739) followed, given in Lent when the theatres could not stage opera.
Mendelssohn's Elijah was written for Birmingham in 1846 and Elgar's The Dream of Gerontius for Birmingham in 1900; the English choral festival kept the form alive.
items.remark: Handel more or less invented the English oratorio because Italian opera stopped paying: the same singers and theatres, no scenery to fund, and the weeks of Lent to fill when opera could not be staged.
items.gaffe: Asking who is singing Jesus in Messiah. There are no characters and no drama; the soloists narrate and reflect, they do not play anyone.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Oratorio'
Howard E. Smither, A History of the Oratorio (1977–2000)

term: A staged music drama sung throughout, with sets, costumes and action.
A short choral piece sung during the Anglican service, usually after the third collect.
A work for orchestra alone in four movements, the first in sonata form.

items.definition: A large-scale setting of a sacred or biblical text for solo voices, chorus and orchestra, performed in concert without staging, costumes or action; Handel's Messiah is the standard English example.

items.title: Anthem
facts: The word descends from 'antiphon'; the Prayer Book of 1662 fixed its place in the service with the rubric 'In quires and places where they sing, here followeth the anthem'.
Purcell wrote verse anthems for the Chapel Royal; Handel wrote four coronation anthems in 1727; Parry's 'I was glad' was written for the coronation of 1902.

'God Save the King' has been called the national anthem since the early nineteenth century and is generally reckoned the first song anywhere to be called one; 'Jerusalem' is a hymn, Parry's 1916 setting of Blake.
items.remark: In England an anthem is the choir's piece at Evensong long before it is anything to do with flags; the Prayer Book of 1662 says 'here followeth the anthem', and Handel's Zadok is a coronation anthem in exactly that sense.
items.gaffe: Calling 'Jerusalem' the national anthem. It is Parry's 1916 setting of Blake, sung as a hymn; the anthem is 'God Save the King', and 'anthem' in church means something else again.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Anthem'
Peter Le Huray, Music and the Reformation in England 1549–1660 (1967)

term: A solo song with orchestra sung by a character in an opera.
A German art song for solo voice and piano.
A piece for organ played while the congregation leaves the church.

items.definition: In English church music, a choral piece on a sacred English text sung during the Anglican service, a 'verse anthem' alternating soloists with full choir; only by extension a national or ceremonial song.

items.title: Symphonie fantastique, Op. 14
items.creator: Hector Berlioz
facts: First performed on 5 December 1830 in the hall of the Paris Conservatoire, conducted by François Habeneck; Berlioz had won the Prix de Rome that July, at his fourth attempt.

Five movements with a printed programme: Rêveries – Passions, Un bal, Scène aux champs, Marche au supplice, and Songe d'une nuit du sabbat, in which the artist, who has taken opium, dreams he is executed and then mocked at a witches' sabbath to the plainchant Dies irae.
The beloved is a tune, which Berlioz's programme calls the idée fixe; it returns in every movement, waltzing in the second, and in the finale it comes back as a shrill parody on the E-flat clarinet.

The beloved was real: the Irish actress Harriet Smithson, whom Berlioz had seen as Ophelia at the Odéon in September 1827 and had never met. They were introduced in December 1832 and married on 3 October 1833.
Liszt made the piano transcription in 1833, which is how much of Europe first heard it.
items.remark: It was written in 1830, three years after Beethoven died, and its idée fixe is a tune for a real woman, the actress Harriet Smithson, whom Berlioz had seen on stage and never met; they married three years later and it did not go well.
items.gaffe: Calling the idée fixe a leitmotif. Berlioz's is a whole tune that returns and is transformed, and idée fixe is his own term from the printed programme; Wagner's leitmotifs were decades away and work differently.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Berlioz, Hector'
David Cairns, Berlioz: The Making of an Artist, 1803–1832 (2nd ed., 1999)
Edward T. Cone (ed.), Berlioz: Fantastic Symphony (Norton Critical Score, 1971)

items.title: Nocturne in E-flat major, Op. 9 No. 2
items.creator: Frédéric Chopin
facts: The second of the three nocturnes of Op. 9, composed between 1830 and 1832 and dedicated to Madame Camille Pleyel: the pianist Marie Moke, who had been engaged to Berlioz and married the piano maker instead in April 1831.
Chopin settled in Paris in the autumn of 1831 and made his debut there at the Salle Pleyel on 26 February 1832; he stayed for the rest of his life and wrote twenty-one nocturnes in all.
The nocturne as a piano piece was the invention of the Irish pianist John Field, whose first ones were published in the 1810s; Chopin took the form and its singing right hand over a rocking left.
In 12/8 and marked Andante; the tune returns more ornamented each time, and Chopin wrote further variants of the ornaments into his pupils' copies, some of which survive.

Chopin's Funeral March, the slow movement of the B-flat minor Sonata, Op. 35, was written in 1837, two years before the rest of the sonata; it was played at his own funeral at the Madeleine in October 1849, orchestrated by Henri Reber.
items.remark: It is dedicated to Madame Camille Pleyel, the pianist Marie Moke, who had jilted Berlioz for the piano maker in the year Chopin arrived; musical Paris in 1831 was a very small town.
items.gaffe: Asking for 'the Chopin nocturne'. There are twenty-one; this is Op. 9 No. 2 in E-flat, and if you add anything, add that the form was invented by an Irishman, John Field, not by Chopin.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Chopin, Fryderyk Franciszek'
Jim Samson, Chopin (Master Musicians, 1996)
Jean-Jacques Eigeldinger, Chopin: Pianist and Teacher as Seen by his Pupils (1986)

items.title: Le Cygne (The Swan)
items.creator: Camille Saint-Saëns
facts: The thirteenth of the fourteen movements of Le Carnaval des animaux, a 'grand zoological fantasy' written in a few days in February 1886 for a private Shrove Tuesday concert given by the cellist Charles Lebouc on 9 March.

For cello and two pianos in the original; Saint-Saëns forbade public performance of the Carnival in his lifetime, fearing it would damage his reputation as a serious composer, and allowed only The Swan to be published, in 1887. The rest appeared in 1922, after his death.

The Carnival's jokes include Offenbach's galop from Orphée aux enfers slowed to a crawl for the tortoises, Berlioz's Dance of the Sylphs given to the elephant on a double bass, and Saint-Saëns's own Danse macabre rattled out on a xylophone in Fossils.
Michel Fokine made the solo The Dying Swan for Anna Pavlova to it in St Petersburg; he dated it 1905, and its first documented performance was in December 1907.
items.remark: It is the only piece of the Carnival that Saint-Saëns let out in his lifetime; the rest, with its tortoises dancing Offenbach's galop at a crawl, was a private joke he sat on for thirty-five years.
items.gaffe: Calling it The Dying Swan as if that were the title. Saint-Saëns wrote Le Cygne; the dying is Fokine's and Pavlova's, some twenty years later, and the composer had nothing to do with it.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Saint-Saëns, Camille'
Brian Rees, Camille Saint-Saëns: A Life (1999)
Sabina Teller Ratner, Camille Saint-Saëns, 1835–1921: A Thematic Catalogue of his Complete Works, vol. 1 (2002)

items.title: Gymnopédie No. 1
items.creator: Erik Satie
facts: The first of three Gymnopédies for piano written in 1888, when Satie was twenty-two and earning his living as a pianist at the cabaret Le Chat Noir in Montmartre; it is marked 'Lent et douloureux', slow and sorrowful.

The word refers to the gymnopaedia, a festival of ancient Sparta at which naked youths danced; where Satie found it is disputed, and he is said to have introduced himself at the Chat Noir as a 'gymnopédiste'.

Debussy orchestrated the first and third in 1896 and swapped their numbers, so that Debussy's 'first' Gymnopédie is Satie's third; the orchestral versions were first played at the Société nationale in February 1897.
One tune over a rocking accompaniment of two chords, in 3/4, in D major; the second and third Gymnopédies use the same shape, which is why they are often mistaken for one another.
items.remark: The word means the naked-boy dances of Sparta and nobody knows why Satie chose it; Debussy orchestrated two of the three in 1896 and swapped their numbers, so his first Gymnopédie is Satie's third.
items.gaffe: Calling it Impressionist because it is quiet and French. It is six years older than Debussy's Faune and the opposite of it: no wash of colour, one tune, two chords. Les Six took their plainness from Satie, not from Debussy.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Satie, Erik'
Robert Orledge, Satie the Composer (1990)
Steven Moore Whiting, Satie the Bohemian: From Cabaret to Concert Hall (1999)

items.title: Clair de lune, from Suite bergamasque
items.creator: Claude Debussy
facts: The third of the four movements of the Suite bergamasque for piano (Prélude, Menuet, Clair de lune, Passepied), begun around 1890 and revised for publication by Fromont in 1905, when Debussy had become famous and the publisher held the rights.

The title is Verlaine's, from the poem 'Clair de lune' in Fêtes galantes (1869), which begins 'Votre âme est un paysage choisi' and speaks of 'masques et bergamasques'; Debussy set the poem as a song twice, in 1882 and 1891.
In the 1890 manuscript the movement was called 'Promenade sentimentale', after another Verlaine poem; the present title came with the revision of 1905.
In D-flat major and 9/8, marked 'Andante très expressif'; Debussy had won the Prix de Rome in 1884 and was, at the time he wrote it, a struggling composer of songs.
items.remark: Bergamasque is Verlaine's word, from a poem about masks in moonlight, and the piece was called Promenade sentimentale until Debussy revised it for publication in 1905, fifteen years after he wrote it.
items.gaffe: Calling it Debussy's Moonlight Sonata, or attributing it to Chopin. It is one movement of a four-movement suite; and the nickname Moonlight was not even Beethoven's, but a critic's, five years after his death.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Debussy, Claude'
François Lesure, Claude Debussy: A Critical Biography, trans. Marie Rolf (2019)
Roger Nichols, The Life of Debussy (1998)
