items.title: Boléro
items.creator: Maurice Ravel
facts: Commissioned by the dancer Ida Rubinstein and first performed at the Paris Opéra on 22 November 1928, with Rubinstein dancing on a table in a Spanish tavern, choreography by Bronislava Nijinska, sets by Alexandre Benois, and Walther Straram conducting.
Ravel had meant to orchestrate pieces from Albéniz's Iberia for her, found that the orchestration rights belonged to Enrique Fernández Arbós, and wrote an original piece instead.

One rhythm on the side drum from the first bar to the last, two sixteen-bar tunes alternating over it, a single crescendo, and C major throughout until one change of key just before the end; Ravel told the Daily Telegraph in 1931 that it was 'orchestral tissue without music'.
Ravel wanted it slow, about a quarter of an hour; when Toscanini took it faster with the New York Philharmonic in Paris in May 1930 the two men quarrelled about it.
Ravel's other tune that everyone knows, the Pavane pour une infante défunte, was written for piano in 1899 while he was still a Conservatoire student and orchestrated in 1910.
items.remark: Ravel wrote it for Ida Rubinstein to dance on a tavern table in 1928, and told the Daily Telegraph it was 'orchestral tissue without music': one rhythm, two tunes, one crescendo, one change of key just before the end.
items.gaffe: Complaining that it is repetitive. That is the whole design and Ravel said so himself; the informed complaint is about the tempo, which Toscanini took too fast in 1930 and was told so.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Ravel, Maurice'
Arbie Orenstein, Ravel: Man and Musician (1975)
Roger Nichols, Ravel (2011)

items.title: Le Sacre du printemps (The Rite of Spring)
items.creator: Igor Stravinsky
facts: First performed on 29 May 1913 at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, which had opened that April, by Diaghilev's Ballets Russes: choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky, designs by Nicholas Roerich, Pierre Monteux conducting.

Subtitled 'Pictures of pagan Russia in two parts'; a chosen maiden dances herself to death. The audience laughed, shouted and fought until the orchestra could not be heard; Stravinsky left his seat and watched from the wings, where Nijinsky stood on a chair shouting the counts to the dancers.
The music itself won within a year: Monteux conducted it in concert at the Casino de Paris on 5 April 1914 and Stravinsky was carried out on the crowd's shoulders.
Nijinsky's choreography was lost after a handful of performances in Paris and London and was reconstructed by Millicent Hodson and Kenneth Archer for the Joffrey Ballet in 1987.
Debussy and Stravinsky played it through as a piano duet at Louis Laloy's house at Bellevue on 9 June 1912, a year before the premiere.
items.remark: The riot was at the ballet, not the music: a year later Monteux conducted it in concert at the Casino de Paris and Stravinsky was carried out on the crowd's shoulders. It was Nijinsky's steps that people could not bear.
items.gaffe: Repeating that Saint-Saëns stormed out over the bassoon's first note. The story is Stravinsky's own, told years later, and there is no evidence that Saint-Saëns was in the theatre that night.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Stravinsky, Igor'
Thomas Forrest Kelly, First Nights: Five Musical Premieres (2000)
Richard Taruskin, Stravinsky and the Russian Traditions (1996)

items.title: Gabriel Fauré
facts: Born in Pamiers, in the Ariège, on 12 May 1845; trained not at the Conservatoire but at the École Niedermeyer in Paris, a school for church musicians, where Saint-Saëns taught him the piano and showed him Schumann, Liszt and Wagner.

Choirmaster at the Madeleine from 1877 and its organist from 1896; director of the Paris Conservatoire from 1905 to 1920, where his reforms and sackings earned him the nickname Robespierre, and his pupils included Ravel, Enescu, Koechlin and Nadia Boulanger.

His Requiem was first sung at the Madeleine on 16 January 1888, at the funeral of an architect, and grew to its final form by 1900; it leaves out the Dies irae sequence, and he wrote in 1910 that someone had called it 'a lullaby of death'.
The Pavane of 1887 has words by Robert de Montesquiou and is dedicated to the Comtesse Greffulhe, the two people Proust would later turn into the Baron de Charlus and the Duchesse de Guermantes.
Deaf and hearing pitches distorted from about 1903, he went on composing; he died in Paris on 4 November 1924 and was given a state funeral at the Madeleine.
items.remark: The Pavane's words are by Robert de Montesquiou and it is dedicated to the Comtesse Greffulhe: that is, to the models for Proust's Charlus and his Duchesse de Guermantes, a quarter of a century before Proust wrote them down.
items.gaffe: Expecting the Requiem to sound like Verdi's. It leaves out the Dies irae sequence that Verdi and Berlioz put at the centre of theirs; Fauré reported that someone had called it a lullaby of death and did not object.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Fauré, Gabriel'
Jean-Michel Nectoux, Gabriel Fauré: A Musical Life, trans. Roger Nichols (1991)
Robert Orledge, Gabriel Fauré (1979)

items.title: Francis Poulenc
facts: Born in Paris on 7 January 1899, the son of a pharmaceutical manufacturer whose firm became Rhône-Poulenc; he never attended the Conservatoire, studied the piano with Ricardo Viñes, and took his only composition lessons from Charles Koechlin in the early 1920s.
The youngest of Les Six, named by the critic Henri Collet in 1920; Rapsodie nègre (1917) made his name at eighteen, and Diaghilev staged his ballet Les Biches in 1924.

After the death of his friend Pierre-Octave Ferroud in 1936 and a visit to the shrine of Rocamadour he returned to the Catholic faith; the Litanies à la Vierge noire (1936), the Stabat Mater (1950), Dialogues des Carmélites (La Scala, 1957) and the Gloria (1959) followed.
From 1934 he wrote and toured his songs with the baritone Pierre Bernac; in 1950 the critic Claude Rostand called him 'moine et voyou', monk and guttersnipe, and the phrase has stuck.
Died in Paris on 30 January 1963; his last opera, La Voix humaine (1959), is a forty-minute telephone call for one soprano, to a text by Cocteau.
items.remark: He was a pharmaceutical manufacturer's son who never went to the Conservatoire, and Claude Rostand's 'moine et voyou' covers him: the Gloria and the Carmelites on one side, the naughty songs and Les Biches on the other.
items.gaffe: Treating Les Six as a school with a doctrine that Poulenc followed. They were six friends bundled together by a critic in 1920, with no manifesto of their own; Cocteau's Le Coq et l'Arlequin was the nearest thing, and it was Cocteau's.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Poulenc, Francis'
Roger Nichols, Poulenc: A Biography (2020)
Carl B. Schmidt, Entrancing Muse: A Documented Biography of Francis Poulenc (2001)

items.title: Les Six
facts: Named by the critic Henri Collet in the newspaper Comœdia on 16 January 1920, in an article that set six young French composers beside the Russian Five and Erik Satie: Georges Auric, Louis Durey, Arthur Honegger, Darius Milhaud, Francis Poulenc and Germaine Tailleferre.

Jean Cocteau was their publicist and Satie their elder; Cocteau's pamphlet Le Coq et l'Arlequin (1918) had called for a French music of the circus, the music hall and the street, against Wagner and against Debussy's mists.

They wrote one work together, the Album des Six for piano in 1920, and one stage piece, Cocteau's Les Mariés de la tour Eiffel of 1921, to which only five contributed; Durey left in 1921 and by the mid-1920s the rest had gone their own ways.

Milhaud's ballet Le Bœuf sur le toit (1920) gave its name to the bar on the rue Boissy d'Anglas, opened in 1922, where the group and its friends met; Honegger, a Swiss, wrote Pacific 231 (1923) about a locomotive.
items.remark: Henri Collet made them up in a newspaper in January 1920 by counting them against the Russian Five; they wrote exactly one stage work together, Cocteau's Les Mariés de la tour Eiffel, and only five of them did that.
items.gaffe: Counting Satie among Les Six. He was their patron saint, not a member, and Collet's article named him separately; the six are Auric, Durey, Honegger, Milhaud, Poulenc and Tailleferre, and Tailleferre is the one everyone forgets.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Six, Les'
Robert Shapiro (ed.), Les Six: The French Composers and Their Mentors Jean Cocteau and Erik Satie (2011)
Jean Cocteau, Le Coq et l'Arlequin (1918)

items.title: Impressionism (in music)
facts: The word was first applied to Debussy in 1887 by the Académie des Beaux-Arts, as a reproach, in its report on Printemps, the piece he had sent back from Rome as a Prix de Rome winner; it warned him against 'vague impressionism'.

Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune, after Mallarmé's poem, was first played at the Société nationale on 22 December 1894; Boulez later wrote that modern music was awakened by it. La Mer, three symphonic sketches, followed at the Concerts Lamoureux on 15 October 1905, with Hokusai's Great Wave on the cover of the score.
Debussy wrote to his publisher Durand in March 1908 that he was trying to make 'something different, realities in a way: what imbeciles call impressionism'.
Ravel, who wrote sonatas, a string quartet and Le Tombeau de Couperin, resisted the label, and the two composers' partisans quarrelled for years over who had borrowed from whom.
items.remark: Debussy hated the word: he wrote to his publisher in 1908 that he was after 'what imbeciles call impressionism', and the first people to apply it to him, the Académie des Beaux-Arts in 1887, meant it as a reproach.
items.gaffe: Lumping Ravel in with Debussy as 'the Impressionists' in front of a musician. Ravel wrote sonatas, a string quartet and a Tombeau de Couperin; the two men's admirers quarrelled over who had borrowed from whom, and neither man liked the word.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Impressionism'
François Lesure, Claude Debussy: A Critical Biography, trans. Marie Rolf (2019)
Roger Nichols, The Life of Debussy (1998)

term: The German movement of about 1905 to 1925 that expressed extreme inner states through dissonance and the abandonment of key, as in early Schoenberg and Berg.
The revival of eighteenth-century forms, clear textures and small orchestras in the 1920s, as in Stravinsky's Pulcinella.
The nineteenth-century idea that orchestral music should tell a story or paint a scene, as in Liszt's symphonic poems.

items.definition: The label borrowed from painting for the music of Debussy and, less happily, Ravel: colour and atmosphere over argument, whole-tone and modal scales, chords chosen for their sound rather than their function, and titles about water, weather and light. Debussy disliked the word.

items.title: The salon
facts: Chopin gave about thirty public concerts in his life and played the rest in drawing rooms; after his Salle Pleyel debut of 26 February 1832 he was taken up by the Rothschilds and the Faubourg Saint-Germain, and his pupils, at twenty francs a lesson, came from there.

Liszt and Thalberg played against each other at the Princess Belgiojoso's on 31 March 1837; her reported verdict, that Thalberg was the first pianist in the world and Liszt the only one, is the most quoted line a salon ever produced.

The tradition ran on into the twentieth century: the Princesse de Polignac, born Winnaretta Singer of the sewing-machine fortune, commissioned Stravinsky's Renard, Satie's Socrate, Falla's El retablo de maese Pedro and Poulenc's Organ Concerto for her salon on the avenue Henri-Martin.
Fauré's songs, Debussy's early works and much of Ravel were first heard in private rooms; Proust's Madame Verdurin is a satire of the hostesses who ran them.
items.remark: Chopin gave about thirty public concerts in eighteen years in Paris and did the rest in drawing rooms; the salon was his concert hall, his publicity and his employment exchange, since that is where the pupils at twenty francs a lesson came from.
items.gaffe: Saying 'salon music' as a compliment, or muddling the salon with the Salon. The Salon, capital S, is the state art exhibition named after a room in the Louvre; and since about 1870 'salon music' has meant pretty and shallow, so do not say it of a Chopin nocturne in front of a pianist.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Salon music'
Jean-Jacques Eigeldinger, Chopin: Pianist and Teacher as Seen by his Pupils (1986)
Sylvia Kahan, Music's Modern Muse: A Life of Winnaretta Singer, Princesse de Polignac (2003)
Alan Walker, Franz Liszt: The Virtuoso Years, 1811–1847 (rev. ed., 1987)

term: The official state exhibition of living artists in Paris, held from 1667 and named after a room in the Louvre.
A public concert series with a paid orchestra and printed programmes, such as the Concerts Lamoureux or the Concerts Colonne.
A café with a small stage where singers and pianists entertained a paying crowd, such as Le Chat Noir in Montmartre.

items.definition: The private drawing-room gathering, presided over by a hostess, at which music was played to an invited audience of society, artists and writers. In nineteenth-century Paris it was where Chopin chose to be heard, where reputations were made and pupils found, and where much of the piano repertoire was first played; 'salon music' later became a sneer for the pretty pieces written for it.

items.title: The Conservatoire
facts: Founded by decree of the Convention on 3 August 1795, merging the old École royale de chant with the National Guard's music school, under Bernard Sarrette; it stood on the rue Bergère until 1911, then on the rue de Madrid, and since 1990 at the Cité de la musique at La Villette.

Its directors included Cherubini (1822 to 1842), Auber, Ambroise Thomas, Théodore Dubois and Fauré (1905 to 1920); its Société des Concerts, founded by François Habeneck in 1828, brought Beethoven's symphonies to Paris and became the Orchestre de Paris in 1967.

The Prix de Rome, judged by the Académie des Beaux-Arts, sent the winner to the Villa Medici: Berlioz won it in 1830 at the fourth attempt, Bizet in 1857, Debussy in 1884; Saint-Saëns failed twice and Ravel five times.

When the jury eliminated Ravel in the first round in 1905, and it emerged that the finalists were all pupils of one juror, the scandal forced Dubois out of the directorship and put Fauré, who had never studied there, in his place.
items.remark: Berlioz won the Prix de Rome at the fourth attempt and Ravel lost it five times; when the jury threw Ravel out in the first round in 1905, the scandal cost the director his job and gave it to Fauré, who had never been a student there.
items.gaffe: Saying 'the Conservatory'. In Paris it is the Conservatoire, founded in 1795 by the Convention and not by any king; and the Prix de Rome was not even its prize, but the Académie's, which is why the row of 1905 was so hard to contain.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Paris' and 'Conservatories'
Roger Nichols, Ravel (2011)
Constant Pierre, Le Conservatoire national de musique et de déclamation: documents historiques et administratifs (1900)

term: The Paris Opéra's own ballet school, which trains the company's dancers from childhood.
A private school founded in 1853 to train church organists and choirmasters, at which Fauré studied under Saint-Saëns.
The concert hall built by the piano firm Pleyel on the rue du Faubourg Saint-Honoré in 1927.

items.definition: The Paris Conservatoire, the state school of music founded by the Convention in 1795; for two centuries the gate through which French composers and players had to pass, with its own concert society, its published methods, its prizes, and the students who competed for the Prix de Rome, which Berlioz won and Ravel lost five times.

items.title: Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67, first movement
items.creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
facts: Premiered on 22 December 1808 at the Theater an der Wien, on the same marathon programme as the Sixth Symphony and the Fourth Piano Concerto.
Composed between 1804 and 1808, alongside the Fourth Symphony and the Violin Concerto.
items.remark: The 'fate knocking at the door' line comes from Beethoven's secretary Schindler, whose reliability scholars doubt; say that, and you sound like you have read something.
items.gaffe: Calling it the Fifth Piano Concerto. That is the Emperor, and it is a different piece.
sources: Lewis Lockwood, Beethoven: The Music and the Life (2003)
Grove Music Online, 'Beethoven, Ludwig van'

theme.note: Opening motif, strings and clarinets in unison. Fermatas approximated as long notes.

items.title: Lied
facts: Schubert wrote more than six hundred Lieder, including the cycles Die schöne Müllerin and Winterreise.
Schumann, Brahms, Wolf, Mahler and Strauss carried the form to the end of the nineteenth century.
items.remark: The point of a Lied is that the piano is telling the story too; listen to what it does under the voice, not just to the tune.
items.gaffe: Saying 'a Lieder'. Lied is the singular; Lieder is the plural.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Lied'

term: A short instrumental piece for solo piano in a single mood, often published in sets.
A German dance in triple time that preceded the waltz.
The German term for a choral movement in an oratorio.

items.definition: A German art song for solo voice and piano, in which the piano is a partner rather than an accompaniment; the plural is Lieder.

items.title: The Florentine Camerata
facts: A circle of noblemen, musicians and poets who met at the Florentine house of Count Giovanni de' Bardi from about 1573 into the late 1580s; Vincenzo Galilei and Giulio Caccini were members.

Vincenzo Galilei, Galileo's father, set out the group's case in his Dialogo della musica antica et della moderna (1581): counterpoint smothered the words, and ancient Greek drama had been sung by a single voice.
Caccini wrote in the preface to Le nuove musiche (1602) that he had learned more from the Camerata's conversations than from thirty years of counterpoint.
The Camerata staged no opera: Peri's Dafne (1598) and Euridice (1600) came out of the rival circle of Jacopo Corsi, after Bardi had gone to Rome in 1592.
items.remark: The Camerata were trying to bring back Greek tragedy and invented opera by mistake; their theorist was Vincenzo Galilei, whose son had the better career.
items.gaffe: Saying the Camerata wrote the first opera. They argued about Greek music at Bardi's house; the first operas came out of Jacopo Corsi's circle after Bardi had left for Rome.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Camerata'
Claude V. Palisca, The Florentine Camerata: Documentary Studies and Translations (1989)

items.title: Dafne
items.creator: Jacopo Peri
facts: Performed at the Florentine palazzo of Jacopo Corsi during Carnival 1598, on a libretto by Ottavio Rinuccini; Corsi wrote some of the music himself.
Usually counted as the first opera, but almost all the music is lost; only a few short fragments survive.
Rinuccini's libretto had a long afterlife: Marco da Gagliano reset it for Mantua in 1608, and Heinrich Schütz set Martin Opitz's German version in 1627 as the first German opera.
items.remark: The first opera is one nobody has heard: Peri's Dafne of 1598 survives only in scraps, so the earliest opera you can actually sit through is Euridice, two years later.
items.gaffe: Talking about the score. Almost none of it exists; anyone who claims to have heard Dafne has heard Gagliano's 1608 setting or a modern reconstruction.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Peri, Jacopo'
Tim Carter, Jacopo Peri (1561–1633): His Life and Works (1989)

creator: Giulio Caccini
Emilio de' Cavalieri
Claudio Monteverdi
title: Euridice
L'Orfeo
Rappresentatione di Anima, et di Corpo

items.title: Euridice
items.creator: Jacopo Peri
facts: Performed on 6 October 1600 in the Palazzo Pitti during the celebrations for the marriage of Maria de' Medici to Henri IV of France; libretto by Ottavio Rinuccini.
The earliest opera whose music survives complete; Peri, a tenor, sang Orfeo himself.
Giulio Caccini set the same libretto and rushed his version into print in December 1600, ahead of Peri's; at the 1600 performance Caccini's pupils sang his music for their own parts.
Rinuccini gave the myth a happy ending for the wedding: Euridice is returned to Orfeo and nobody looks back.
items.remark: The two Euridices are a race: Caccini set the same words and got his score into print first, but Peri's is the one that was sung at the Medici wedding, with Peri himself as Orfeo.
items.gaffe: Expecting a tragedy. It was written for a royal wedding, so Euridice comes back and nobody looks over his shoulder.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Euridice'
Tim Carter, Jacopo Peri (1561–1633): His Life and Works (1989)

items.title: L'Orfeo
items.creator: Claudio Monteverdi
facts: First performed on 24 February 1607 at the Gonzaga court in Mantua, for the Accademia degli Invaghiti, on a libretto by Alessandro Striggio.
Published in Venice in 1609 with a list of the instruments required, which is rare for the period; a second edition followed in 1615.
Opens with a Toccata for trumpets that Monteverdi reused to open his Vespers of 1610.
The printed score ends with Apollo carrying Orfeo to heaven; the 1607 libretto ended instead with a chorus of Bacchantes threatening him, as in Ovid, and his fate left offstage.
items.remark: L'Orfeo is the first opera anyone stages for pleasure rather than piety, and it was written for Mantua, not Florence; the Gonzagas were catching up with the Medici seven years after Euridice.
items.gaffe: Calling it the first opera. It is the first great one; Peri's Dafne and Euridice are older, and Striggio's libretto leans on Rinuccini's.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Orfeo'
John Whenham (ed.), Claudio Monteverdi: Orfeo (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1986)

items.title: Macbeth
items.creator: Giuseppe Verdi
facts: Premiered at the Teatro della Pergola, Florence, on 14 March 1847, on a libretto by Francesco Maria Piave after Shakespeare; Verdi's first opera on a Shakespeare play.
Revised for Paris in 1865, which added Lady Macbeth's 'La luce langue' and a ballet; most houses now play the revision.
Verdi told the librettist Cammarano in 1848 that the Naples soprano Tadolini sang too beautifully for Lady Macbeth, whose voice he wanted harsh, stifled and hollow.
Dedicated to Antonio Barezzi, the Busseto merchant who had paid for Verdi's education and became his father-in-law.
items.remark: Verdi wanted his Lady Macbeth to sound ugly; he wrote to Cammarano that the Naples soprano sang too well for the part, which is not a complaint composers often make.
items.gaffe: Assuming it premiered at La Scala. Florence's Pergola had it first, in 1847, and Paris got the revised version in 1865.
sources: Julian Budden, The Operas of Verdi, vol. 1 (1973)
David Rosen and Andrew Porter (eds), Verdi's Macbeth: A Sourcebook (1984)
Grove Music Online, 'Macbeth'

items.title: O mio babbino caro
items.creator: Giacomo Puccini
facts: Lauretta's aria from Gianni Schicchi, the comic third panel of Il trittico, which opened at the Metropolitan Opera, New York, on 14 December 1918.
The opera is set in Florence in 1299 and grows out of a few lines in Dante's Inferno, Canto XXX, where Schicchi is damned for impersonating the dead Buoso Donati to forge his will.
Lauretta sings it to her father, Schicchi, to make him help her marry Rinuccio; she threatens to throw herself from the Ponte Vecchio into the Arno if he refuses.
The libretto is by Giovacchino Forzano; the aria names Porta Rossa, where she means to buy the ring.
items.remark: It is emotional blackmail set to a lovely tune: Lauretta threatens to jump off the Ponte Vecchio unless her father forges a will, and the opera it comes from is a comedy about fraud.
items.gaffe: Treating it as a love song. Babbino means daddy; she is wheedling her father, not serenading a lover.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Gianni Schicchi'
Julian Budden, Puccini: His Life and Works (2002)
Dante, Inferno, Canto XXX

items.title: Cavalleria rusticana
items.creator: Pietro Mascagni
facts: Won the publisher Sonzogno's competition for one-act operas and opened at the Teatro Costanzi, Rome, on 17 May 1890; Mascagni was twenty-six and running a municipal music school in Cerignola.
From Giovanni Verga's Sicilian story of 1880 and the play he made of it in 1884; libretto by Giovanni Targioni-Tozzetti and Guido Menasci.
The Intermezzo sinfonico divides a single act set on Easter Sunday; the opera ends with a shout from offstage that Turiddu has been killed.
Mascagni was born in Livorno in 1863 and never repeated the success; the piece is usually paired with Leoncavallo's Pagliacci as 'Cav and Pag'.
items.remark: Mascagni was twenty-six and running a music school in Puglia when it won Sonzogno's competition; the Intermezzo is the part everyone knows, and it is the only stretch of the piece in which nobody is threatening anybody.
items.gaffe: Saying Cav and Pag are by the same composer. Leoncavallo wrote Pagliacci two years later; the pairing is a box-office habit, not a joint work.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Cavalleria rusticana'
Grove Music Online, 'Mascagni, Pietro'

items.title: Giulio Caccini
facts: A singer at the Medici court in Florence from the 1560s until his death in 1618, and a member of Bardi's Camerata.
Le nuove musiche (1602) collects his solo songs with a preface on how to sing them; 'Amarilli, mia bella' is in it.
Set Rinuccini's Euridice in competition with Peri, printed it first, in 1600, and saw it staged in 1602.
His daughter Francesca Caccini wrote La liberazione di Ruggiero (1625), the earliest surviving opera by a woman.
The 'Ave Maria' sold under his name is by Vladimir Vavilov, a Soviet guitarist and lutenist, from about 1970.
items.remark: Caccini's most famous piece is one he did not write: the Ave Maria on every wedding playlist is by a Soviet guitarist called Vavilov, from around 1970.
items.gaffe: Praising Caccini's Ave Maria. Praise Amarilli instead; it is his, and it is in Le nuove musiche.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Caccini, Giulio'
H. Wiley Hitchcock (ed.), Giulio Caccini: Le nuove musiche (1970)

items.title: Ruggero Leoncavallo
facts: Born in Naples in 1857; died at Montecatini Terme, in Tuscany, in 1919.
Pagliacci opened at the Teatro Dal Verme, Milan, on 21 May 1892, conducted by Arturo Toscanini; he wrote the libretto himself.
Accused of plagiarism by Catulle Mendès, he replied that the plot came from a real murder tried by his father, a magistrate in Calabria.
His La bohème (1897) set the same Murger novel as Puccini's, a year later, and lost.
items.remark: Leoncavallo wrote his own words, which Italian composers almost never did, and set the same Murger novel as Puccini a year too late; Pagliacci is what he is remembered for and La bohème is what he was bitter about.
items.gaffe: Attributing Pagliacci to Mascagni because it always shares the bill with Cavalleria. Different composer, two years apart, same publisher.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Leoncavallo, Ruggero'
Konrad Dryden, Leoncavallo: Life and Works (2007)

items.title: Teatro della Pergola
facts: Built from 1656 to a design by Ferdinando Tacca for the Accademia degli Immobili, a society of Florentine nobles; the first opera staged there was Jacopo Melani's Il potestà di Colognole in 1657.
Usually credited as the first theatre built with superimposed tiers of boxes, the plan that Italian opera houses followed for two centuries.
Verdi's Macbeth had its premiere here on 14 March 1847; Donizetti's Parisina had opened here in 1833.
Florence's opera company now plays elsewhere; the Pergola is mainly a theatre for plays.
items.remark: The Pergola is why opera houses look the way they do: it was built in 1656 with stacked tiers of boxes, and every horseshoe from La Scala to Covent Garden descends from it.
items.gaffe: Booking it for opera. Verdi's Macbeth opened here, but Florence's opera now lives at the Maggio Musicale's house; the Pergola is mostly for plays.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Florence'
Teatro della Pergola, 'La storia del teatro' (the theatre's own history)

items.title: Stile recitativo
facts: Peri's preface to Euridice explains that he wanted a way of singing that lay between ordinary speech and melody, holding the bass still while the voice moved through the notes of the speech.
The phrase recitar cantando appears in the preface to Emilio de' Cavalieri's Rappresentatione di Anima, et di Corpo, printed in Rome in 1600.
Recitative became the connective tissue of opera; arias were the tunes that grew up between the stretches of it.
items.remark: The invention of opera was really the invention of speaking in pitch; Peri's preface says he was looking for the halfway house between talking and singing, and that is what recitative still is.
items.gaffe: Calling the first operas a string of arias. Euridice is almost all recitative; the tunes came later, and that was the point.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Recitative'
Claude V. Palisca, The Florentine Camerata: Documentary Studies and Translations (1989)

term: A florid, ornamented style of singing in which the performer improvises runs on the long vowels.
The eighteenth-century aria form in which the opening section returns after a contrasting middle.
The Baroque practice of doubling the vocal line with a solo violin or cornett.

items.definition: The 'recitative style' of the first Florentine operas: a single voice declaiming the words over a simple bass, following the pace and inflection of speech rather than the shape of a tune. The Florentines also called it recitar cantando, speaking in song.

items.title: Verismo
facts: The word came from Italian literary realism, above all Giovanni Verga, whose 1880 story Cavalleria rusticana became Mascagni's opera in 1890.
The strict list is short: Cavalleria rusticana, Pagliacci and a few others from the 1890s; Puccini is called verismo loosely, and only Il tabarro really fits.
The term is now applied loosely to the whole generation of Italian opera after Verdi.
items.remark: Verismo proper is a short list, Cavalleria, Pagliacci and a handful of others from the 1890s; calling all of Puccini verismo is the loose usage, and Il tabarro is about the only one that qualifies.
items.gaffe: Using it for anything Italian and loud. Verdi is not verismo; the word belongs to the 1890s and Mascagni's generation.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Verismo'

term: The bel canto ideal of an even, agile voice across the whole range.
The nineteenth-century Italian practice of casting a woman in a young man's role.
A Risorgimento opera in which the chorus stands for the nation.

items.definition: Literally 'realism': the Italian operatic fashion of the 1890s for contemporary, low-life, often violent subjects, after Verga's fiction; Cavalleria rusticana and Pagliacci are the models.

items.title: Bel canto
facts: The term was hardly used before the middle of the nineteenth century, when it became a nostalgic complaint that singing had declined since Rossini.
The bel canto revival of the 1950s is associated with Maria Callas and Joan Sutherland, who made the serious operas of Bellini and Donizetti repertory pieces again.
Chopin, who knew Bellini in Paris, admired his long melodic lines.
items.remark: Bel canto is a nostalgic term: hardly anyone used it while Bellini was alive, and it came into fashion in the middle of the nineteenth century as a way of complaining that singers had started shouting.
items.gaffe: Calling Verdi or Puccini bel canto. The label covers Rossini, Bellini and Donizetti; after that the orchestra gets louder and the term gets vaguer.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Bel canto'
Rodolfo Celletti, A History of Bel Canto (1991)

term: The Florentine style of declaiming a text in pitch over a sustained bass.
The tradition of unaccompanied choral singing in Italian churches.
The Neapolitan school of comic opera sung in dialect.

items.definition: Literally 'beautiful singing': the Italian style that prized an even, agile, legato voice, and by extension the operas of Rossini, Bellini and Donizetti written for it in the early nineteenth century.

items.title: Ombra mai fu
items.creator: George Frideric Handel
facts: Opens Serse, which premiered at the King's Theatre in the Haymarket, London, on 15 April 1738.
Known as 'Handel's Largo', though Handel marked it larghetto.
Sung by Xerxes, king of Persia, in praise of the shade of a plane tree.
items.remark: It is a love song to a tree: Xerxes is serenading a plane tree, in an opera that lasted five performances in 1738 and was not staged again for nearly two centuries.
items.gaffe: Calling it 'Handel's Largo' as if that were its name, or assuming it is addressed to a woman.
sources: Winton Dean, Handel's Operas, 1726–1741 (2006)
Grove Music Online, 'Serse'

items.title: Royal Opera House, Covent Garden
facts: The first theatre on the site opened in 1732 under John Rich; the present building, by E. M. Barry, opened in 1858 after fires in 1808 and 1856.
Handel wrote many of his operas and oratorios for the first Covent Garden theatre.
It has been called the Royal Opera House since 1892.
items.remark: Everyone calls it Covent Garden; the current house is the third on the site, the first two having burned down.
items.gaffe: Calling it 'the Royal Albert Hall' or 'the Coliseum', which is the other opera house a few streets away in St Martin's Lane, home of English National Opera.
sources: Royal Opera House, 'History of the Royal Opera House'

items.title: Lascia ch'io pianga
items.creator: George Frideric Handel
facts: Rinaldo opened at the Queen's Theatre in the Haymarket on 24 February 1711, the first Italian opera composed specifically for the London stage.
Sung in Act II by Almirena, a captive of the sorceress Armida, asking to be left to weep for her cruel fate and sigh for liberty.
The tune had already served as a sarabande in Almira (Hamburg, 1705) and as 'Lascia la spina' in Il trionfo del Tempo (Rome, 1707).
The libretto is by Giacomo Rossi, from a scenario by Aaron Hill after Tasso; Addison mocked the production's live sparrows in The Spectator.
items.remark: Handel had used the tune twice already, as a sarabande in Almira at Hamburg and as 'Lascia la spina' in Rome; London in 1711 got the third set of words and kept it.
items.gaffe: Calling it 'Handel's Largo'. That is 'Ombra mai fu' from Serse; this is a sarabande from Rinaldo, sung by a woman in captivity asking for the liberty to weep.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Rinaldo'
Winton Dean and John Merrill Knapp, Handel's Operas, 1704–1726 (1987)

items.title: Giulio Cesare in Egitto
items.creator: George Frideric Handel
facts: First performed at the King's Theatre in the Haymarket on 20 February 1724 by the Royal Academy of Music, the opera company Handel served as composer.
The title role was written for the castrato Senesino and Cleopatra for the soprano Francesca Cuzzoni; the libretto is by Nicola Francesco Haym.
Set in Egypt in 48 BC: Ptolemy has Pompey murdered and presents his head to Caesar, while Cleopatra, disguised as 'Lidia', sets out to win Caesar for herself.
Cleopatra's arias include 'V'adoro, pupille', 'Piangerò la sorte mia' and 'Da tempeste'; Caesar's 'Va tacito e nascosto' has a solo horn stalking alongside the voice.
items.remark: Caesar was written for the castrato Senesino, so today he is a countertenor or a mezzo; if the Caesar you hear is a baritone, someone has transposed it.
items.gaffe: Expecting Shakespeare. Haym's libretto is Caesar in Egypt in 48 BC: Pompey's severed head, Cleopatra and her brother Ptolemy, and no Brutus at all.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Giulio Cesare in Egitto'
Winton Dean and John Merrill Knapp, Handel's Operas, 1704–1726 (1987)

items.title: George Frideric Handel
facts: Born in Halle on 23 February 1685, in what was then the Duchy of Magdeburg under Brandenburg-Prussia; came to London in 1710, settled there in 1712, and was naturalised as a British subject by Act of Parliament in 1727.
Wrote more than thirty Italian operas for London, from Rinaldo in 1711 to Deidamia in 1741, before turning to English oratorio; Messiah was first heard in Dublin in 1742.
Lived at 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death on 14 April 1759; he went blind in his last years and is buried in Westminster Abbey.
items.remark: He was a Saxon who became a British subject by Act of Parliament in 1727, wrote more than thirty Italian operas for London, and turned to English oratorio only when the opera business failed him.
items.gaffe: Assuming he and Bach knew each other. They were born in the same year, 1685, in towns a few days' ride apart, and never met; Bach tried twice.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Handel, George Frideric'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Handel, George Frideric'
Donald Burrows, Handel (2nd ed., 2012)

items.title: When I am laid in earth (Dido's Lament)
items.creator: Henry Purcell
facts: The only performance we can document in Purcell's lifetime was at Josias Priest's boarding school for young gentlewomen in Chelsea, in or before 1689; the exact date is still argued over.
Built over a five-bar ground bass in G minor that descends by semitones from G to D and repeats, unchanged, under the whole lament.
Dido sings it after she has sent Aeneas away; the words end 'Remember me, but ah! forget my fate', and the chorus 'With drooping wings' follows.
The libretto is by Nahum Tate; no score in Purcell's hand survives, and the earliest copy dates from long after his death.
items.remark: The whole lament sits on a five-bar ground bass that sinks chromatically from G to D and simply repeats; the grief is in the bass line, and the voice is left to break across it.
items.gaffe: Attributing it to Handel. Purcell died in 1695, and Handel did not reach London until 1710.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Dido and Aeneas'
Curtis Price, Henry Purcell and the London Stage (1984)
Ellen T. Harris, Henry Purcell's Dido and Aeneas (1987)

items.title: Henry Purcell
facts: Born in 1659, almost certainly in Westminster; organist of Westminster Abbey from 1679 and of the Chapel Royal from 1682.
Wrote one opera sung throughout, Dido and Aeneas, and four semi-operas for the London theatres: Dioclesian (1690), King Arthur (1691), The Fairy-Queen (1692) and The Indian Queen (1695).
Died on 21 November 1695, aged about thirty-six, and was buried in Westminster Abbey beside the organ; the music he had written for Queen Mary's funeral that March was played at his own.
Playford published his songs after his death under the title Orpheus Britannicus (1698).
items.remark: Dido is his only opera sung throughout; King Arthur and The Fairy-Queen are semi-operas, in which the principal characters speak and the singing is left to spirits, shepherds and a drunken poet.
items.gaffe: Saying 'Pur-SELL'. The stress falls on the first syllable, as in 'purse'.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Purcell, Henry'
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Purcell, Henry'
Peter Holman, Henry Purcell (1994)

items.title: H.M.S. Pinafore
items.creator: Arthur Sullivan
facts: Opened at the Opera Comique, London, on 25 May 1878 and ran for 571 performances; the words are by W. S. Gilbert, the fourth of his collaborations with Sullivan.

Josephine, the captain's daughter, loves the able seaman Ralph Rackstraw but is promised to Sir Joseph Porter, First Lord of the Admiralty, who rose to rule the Queen's Navy without ever going to sea.
Little Buttercup resolves everything by confessing that she nursed Ralph and the captain as babies and mixed them up; the numbers include 'When I was a lad' and 'He is an Englishman'.
Unauthorised American productions in 1878 and 1879 earned the authors nothing, which is why their next piece opened in New York.
items.remark: Sir Joseph Porter, who polished up the handle of the big front door and never went to sea, was taken by everyone in 1878 to be W. H. Smith, the newsagent Disraeli had just made First Lord of the Admiralty.
items.gaffe: Calling Sullivan the librettist, or Gilbert the composer. Gilbert wrote the words and Sullivan the music, and the partnership nearly ended in 1890 in a quarrel over the cost of a carpet for the Savoy.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'H.M.S. Pinafore'
Arthur Jacobs, Arthur Sullivan: A Victorian Musician (1984)

items.title: The Pirates of Penzance
items.creator: Arthur Sullivan
facts: After a single copyright performance at Paignton in Devon on 30 December 1879, it opened at the Fifth Avenue Theatre, New York, on 31 December 1879, and reached the Opera Comique in London on 3 April 1880.
Frederic, apprenticed to the pirates until his twenty-first birthday, was born on 29 February and so has had only five birthdays; he will come of age in 1940.
Major-General Stanley's patter song 'I am the very model of a modern Major-General' lists everything he knows, none of it military; the pirates turn out to be noblemen who have gone wrong.
The other famous numbers are 'With cat-like tread', 'Poor wand'ring one' and the Sergeant of Police's 'A policeman's lot is not a happy one'.
items.remark: It is the one Gilbert and Sullivan opera that opened in New York, on the last day of 1879, because American managers had spent a year staging Pinafore without paying either of them a penny.
items.gaffe: Attributing the Major-General's song to The Mikado. It is from Pirates, and the joke is that Stanley knows everything except anything military.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Pirates of Penzance, The'
Arthur Jacobs, Arthur Sullivan: A Victorian Musician (1984)

items.title: The Mikado
items.creator: Arthur Sullivan
facts: Opened at the Savoy Theatre on 14 March 1885 and ran for 672 performances, the longest first run of any of the Gilbert and Sullivan operas; it was the ninth of their collaborations.
Set in the town of Titipu: Nanki-Poo, the Mikado's son disguised as a wandering minstrel, loves Yum-Yum, who is engaged to her guardian Ko-Ko, the Lord High Executioner.
Sullivan borrowed one genuine Japanese tune, the march 'Miya sama', for the Mikado's entrance; a Japanese village exhibition had opened in Knightsbridge two months before the premiere.
The numbers include 'A wand'ring minstrel I', 'Three little maids from school are we', 'The sun whose rays', 'Tit-Willow' and Ko-Ko's 'I've got a little list'.
items.remark: The Japan is fancy dress and the target is Victorian England, which is why Ko-Ko's little list of people who never would be missed has been rewritten with topical names since Gilbert's own day.
items.gaffe: Calling it Japanese music. Sullivan borrows one Japanese tune, the march 'Miya sama' for the Mikado's entrance, and the rest is a Victorian burlesque in kimonos.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Mikado, The'
Arthur Jacobs, Arthur Sullivan: A Victorian Musician (1984)

items.title: Peter Grimes
items.creator: Benjamin Britten
facts: First performed at Sadler's Wells Theatre, London, on 7 June 1945, a month after VE Day, with Peter Pears as Grimes and Joan Cross as Ellen Orford; Reginald Goodall conducted.
The libretto is by Montagu Slater, after George Crabbe's poem The Borough (1810); Britten found Crabbe through an article by E. M. Forster that he read in California in 1941.
Grimes is a fisherman in a Suffolk village whose apprentices keep dying; the Borough turns on him, and Balstrode tells him to sail out and sink his boat.
The orchestral interludes were published separately as the Four Sea Interludes, Op. 33a: Dawn, Sunday Morning, Moonlight and Storm; the Passacaglia is Op. 33b.
items.remark: It opened at Sadler's Wells a month after VE Day with Peter Pears as Grimes, and it is the first English opera since Purcell to hold the stage everywhere.
items.gaffe: Calling Grimes a villain, or a baritone. He is a tenor written for Pears, and the point is that the Borough condemns him without ever proving anything.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Peter Grimes'
Humphrey Carpenter, Benjamin Britten: A Biography (1992)

items.title: Glyndebourne
facts: Opened on 28 May 1934 with The Marriage of Figaro, in an opera house that John Christie had built on to his country house for his wife, the soprano Audrey Mildmay.

The first seasons were run by three men newly out of Germany: the conductor Fritz Busch, the producer Carl Ebert and and Rudolf Bing, who negotiated the singers' contracts in 1934, became general manager in 1936 and later ran the Metropolitan Opera.
Britten's The Rape of Lucretia (1946) and Albert Herring (1947) had their premieres there; the present house, by Michael Hopkins, opened in 1994.
The summer festival keeps its own customs: evening dress in the afternoon, and a dinner interval long enough for a picnic in the gardens.
items.remark: John Christie built it in 1934 for his wife, the soprano Audrey Mildmay, and staffed it with three men just out of Hitler's Germany: Fritz Busch, Carl Ebert and Rudolf Bing, who went on to run the Met.
items.gaffe: Turning up in a lounge suit, or complaining about the length of the interval. Evening dress and a picnic in the long dinner interval are the point, and it is in Sussex, not London.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Glyndebourne'
Spike Hughes, Glyndebourne: A History of the Festival Opera (1965)

items.title: Aria
facts: In a Handel opera almost every aria is a da capo aria, in the form A–B–A, and the singer was expected to ornament the repeat of the first section.
Recitative comes in two kinds: secco, accompanied by the continuo alone, and accompagnato, with the orchestra.
The English plural is arias; an arietta is a short one, and an arioso is something between recitative and aria.
items.remark: In a Handel opera the plot happens in the recitative and the feeling in the arias; if you find yourself following a story during an aria, you have missed something.
items.gaffe: Calling a duet or a chorus an aria, or asking where the tune is during a recitative: the recitative is not meant to have one.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Aria'
Grove Music Online, 'Recitative'

term: A passage of sung speech, following the rhythms of the words, in which the story is carried forward between the set numbers.
The spoken dialogue between musical numbers in a comic opera or Singspiel.
An instrumental piece played by the orchestra before the curtain rises.

items.definition: A self-contained song for one voice in an opera or oratorio, in which the action pauses so that a character can feel something at length; its opposite is recitative, the speech-like passages that carry the plot.

items.title: Castrato
facts: Handel wrote Rinaldo for Nicolini and Giulio Cesare for Senesino; Farinelli came to London in 1734 to sing for the rival company set up against Handel.
The last castrato of the Sistine Chapel choir, Alessandro Moreschi, made recordings in 1902 and 1904 and died in 1922.

A countertenor is a different thing: an intact man singing in a developed falsetto. Alfred Deller revived the voice in England in the 1940s, and Britten wrote Oberon in A Midsummer Night's Dream (1960) for him.
items.remark: Handel's Caesar and Rinaldo were castrato roles, and a countertenor is not the same thing: he is an intact man singing in a trained falsetto, which is why the sound is lighter.
items.gaffe: Calling a countertenor a castrato. The last of the castrati, Alessandro Moreschi, died in 1922 and can be heard on records made in 1902 and 1904.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Castrato'
Grove Music Online, 'Countertenor'

term: A tenor with an exceptionally high range, trained to sing above the stave in full voice rather than falsetto.
A bass singer who specialises in the comic roles of Italian opera.
A boy soprano in a cathedral choir, replaced when his voice breaks.

items.definition: A male singer castrated before puberty so that he kept a boy's high range with a grown man's lungs; the star of Italian opera from the mid-seventeenth century to about 1800, whose heroic roles now go to countertenors or to women.

items.title: The voice types
facts: Mimì, Violetta and Tosca are sopranos; Rodolfo, Alfredo and Cavaradossi, the men who love them, are tenors.
Mezzo-sopranos get the seductresses and the trouser roles: Carmen, and the young men Cherubino in The Marriage of Figaro and Octavian in Der Rosenkavalier.
Scarpia in Tosca, Iago in Otello and Rigoletto are baritones; Sarastro in The Magic Flute and Boris Godunov are basses.
items.remark: The rule of thumb is that sopranos and tenors fall in love and baritones and basses get in the way; Scarpia, Iago and Rigoletto are all baritones.
items.gaffe: Calling Scarpia 'the tenor'. He is a baritone, and the tenor is the man he has arranged to have shot in Act III.
sources: Grove Music Online, entries 'Soprano', 'Mezzo-soprano', 'Tenor', 'Baritone' and 'Bass'
The New Kobbé's Opera Book, ed. the Earl of Harewood and Antony Peattie (1997)

term: The ranks of an opera company, from principal to chorus, fixed by the terms of a singer's contract.
The three registers of a single voice, chest, middle and head, which a singer must learn to blend.
The clefs in which vocal parts were printed before the nineteenth century: soprano, alto, tenor and bass.

items.definition: From high to low: soprano, mezzo-soprano and contralto for women; countertenor, tenor, baritone and bass for men. Convention gives the heroine to the soprano, the lover to the tenor, and the fathers, villains and kings to baritones and basses.

items.title: L'amour est un oiseau rebelle (Habanera)
items.creator: Georges Bizet
facts: Carmen opened at the Opéra-Comique, Paris, on 3 March 1875; Bizet died on 3 June, three months later, aged 36, before the work had become a success.
Carmen sings it in Act 1, outside the cigarette factory in Seville, to a crowd of soldiers; Célestine Galli-Marié created the role, which is written for mezzo-soprano.

The tune is taken from 'El Arreglito', a habanera by the Spanish composer Sebastián Iradier, published in 1863; Bizet believed it was a folk song and, when told otherwise, added an acknowledgement to the vocal score.
The libretto is by Henri Meilhac and Ludovic Halévy, after Prosper Mérimée's novella of 1845.
items.remark: The tune is not Bizet's own; it is 'El Arreglito' by Sebastián Iradier, which Bizet took for a folk song and credited in the vocal score once someone told him.
items.gaffe: Calling Carmen a soprano. She is a mezzo, and the Habanera sits in the middle of the voice on purpose; the soprano in the opera is Micaëla.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Carmen'
Winton Dean, Georges Bizet: His Life and Work (1965)
Hugh Macdonald, Bizet (2014)

items.title: Votre toast, je peux vous le rendre (Toreador Song)
items.creator: Georges Bizet
facts: Escamillo, the bullfighter, sings it on his entrance in Act 2, at Lillas Pastia's tavern; the role is a baritone, first sung by the Belgian Jacques Bouhy.
The refrain, 'Toréador, en garde', is heard before the curtain rises, as the middle section of the Prelude, in F major.
The refrain returns at the very end: the crowd sings it inside the bullring while Don José stabs Carmen outside the gates.
Toréador is the French form of the word; a Spanish bullfighter is a torero, or, if he kills, a matador.
items.remark: Bizet saves the jolliest tune in the score for the murder; the crowd sings 'Toréador, en garde' inside the arena while Don José kills Carmen at the gate.
items.gaffe: Calling Escamillo a tenor. He is the baritone; the tenor is Don José, and he never sings a note of this.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Carmen'
Winton Dean, Georges Bizet: His Life and Work (1965)

Jacques Offenbach
Jules Massenet

La fleur que tu m'avais jetée

items.title: Ah! je ris de me voir si belle (Jewel Song)
items.creator: Charles Gounod
facts: Faust opened at the Théâtre Lyrique, Paris, on 19 March 1859, with spoken dialogue; sung recitatives came later, and the Walpurgis Night ballet was added when the work entered the Opéra in 1869.
Marguerite sings it in the garden in Act 3, having found a casket of jewels that Méphistophélès has left to tempt her; it is a waltz, and she sings it to a mirror.
The libretto is by Jules Barbier and Michel Carré, after Part One of Goethe's Faust; in Germany the opera is often billed as Margarethe.
The Metropolitan Opera opened its first season with Faust on 22 October 1883, with Christine Nilsson as Marguerite.
items.remark: It is a waltz sung to a mirror: Marguerite has just opened a box of jewels left by the devil, and it is the one aria Bianca Castafiore in Tintin ever sings.
items.gaffe: Calling the opera 'Goethe's Faust'. Gounod set only the Gretchen story from Part One, which is why the Germans bill it as Margarethe.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Faust' (Gounod)
Steven Huebner, The Operas of Charles Gounod (1990)

items.title: Belle nuit, ô nuit d'amour (Barcarolle)
items.creator: Jacques Offenbach
facts: Les contes d'Hoffmann opened at the Opéra-Comique on 10 February 1881; Offenbach had died on 5 October 1880 with the orchestration unfinished, and Ernest Guiraud completed the score.
The Barcarolle opens the Venetian act and is a duet for Giulietta, a courtesan, and Nicklausse, Hoffmann's companion, a trouser role for mezzo-soprano.
Offenbach took the tune from his own Die Rheinnixen (Vienna, 1864), where it was a song for elves.
It is in D major and a rocking 6/8: a barcarolle imitates the song of a Venetian gondolier.
items.remark: Offenbach never heard it in this opera; the tune was second-hand from his Rheinnixen of 1864, where elves sang it, and the score was finished by Guiraud after his death.
items.gaffe: Taking it for a love duet between a man and a woman. Both singers are women, and one of them is playing a man.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Contes d'Hoffmann, Les'
Alexander Faris, Jacques Offenbach (1980)

Charles Gounod
Léo Delibes

Scintille, diamant

items.title: Galop infernal (the Can-can)
items.creator: Jacques Offenbach
facts: Orphée aux enfers opened at Offenbach's own Théâtre des Bouffes-Parisiens on 21 October 1858, to a libretto by Hector Crémieux and Ludovic Halévy; an expanded four-act version followed at the Théâtre de la Gaîté in 1874.
The galop is the finale in Hades: the gods, bored with Olympus, dance it at Pluto's party, and Eurydice, who has no wish to go home with Orpheus, joins in; the chorus sings 'Ce bal est original'.
It became the music of the cancan later, in the dance halls; in the opera it is a galop, and nobody kicks.
Saint-Saëns quotes it, slowed to a crawl, for the tortoises in Le carnaval des animaux (1886).
items.remark: In the opera nobody kicks; it is a galop for bored Olympians at a party in Hades, and Saint-Saëns's joke in the Carnival of the Animals is to play it at tortoise speed.
items.gaffe: Calling it 'the Can-can by Offenbach' as if he had written a cancan. He wrote a galop for a mythological burlesque; the dance halls borrowed it.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Orphée aux enfers'
Alexander Faris, Jacques Offenbach (1980)

theme.note: The principal strain, sung to 'Ce bal est original', in G major as first heard; the galop's own opening bars are a different, less known tune.

items.title: Méditation (from Thaïs)
items.creator: Jules Massenet
facts: Thaïs opened at the Opéra, in the Palais Garnier, on 16 March 1894, with Sibyl Sanderson, the American soprano Massenet wrote the role for; the libretto is by Louis Gallet, after Anatole France's novel of 1890.
The Méditation is an intermezzo for solo violin and orchestra between the two scenes of Act 2; while it plays, Thaïs, a courtesan in Alexandria, resolves to follow the monk Athanaël into the desert.
Athanaël is a baritone; by the last act it is he who burns with desire and she who dies a saint.
Massenet's other repertory operas are Manon (Opéra-Comique, 1884) and Werther, first given in Vienna in 1892.
items.remark: It is the sound of a courtesan converting: the violin plays between the two scenes of Act 2 while Thaïs decides to follow the monk, and by the last act the monk wants her and she is dying a saint.
items.gaffe: Treating it as a stand-alone violin piece by 'the man who wrote the Méditation'. It is an entr'acte from Thaïs, and Massenet's reputation rests on Manon and Werther.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Thaïs'
Demar Irvine, Massenet: A Chronicle of His Life and Times (1994)

theme.note: Solo violin from its entry after the harp introduction, Andante religioso. The opening tied note is re-struck; the triplet in bar 1 and the five-note turn in bar 3 are approximated.

items.title: Pelléas et Mélisande
items.creator: Claude Debussy
facts: First performed at the Opéra-Comique on 30 April 1902, conducted by André Messager, with the Scottish soprano Mary Garden as Mélisande and Jean Périer as Pelléas.

The text is Maurice Maeterlinck's Symbolist play of 1892, set almost word for word; Maeterlinck wanted his companion Georgette Leblanc for Mélisande and, refused, attacked the production in print before the premiere.
Golaud finds Mélisande weeping by a spring in a forest and marries her; his half-brother Pelléas falls in love with her, and Golaud kills him.
Debussy's only completed opera. Fauré and Sibelius wrote incidental music for the same play, and Schoenberg a tone poem.
items.remark: Nobody in it raises their voice: the text is Maeterlinck's play set nearly word for word, and Debussy's only finished opera has no set-piece arias at all, which is the point rather than a defect.
items.gaffe: Confusing it with Fauré's or Sibelius's Pelléas, which are incidental music for the play, or with Schoenberg's tone poem. Only Debussy's is an opera.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Pelléas et Mélisande'
Roger Nichols and Richard Langham Smith, Claude Debussy: Pelléas et Mélisande (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1989)

items.title: Les Troyens
items.creator: Hector Berlioz
facts: Berlioz wrote his own libretto from Virgil's Aeneid and composed the score between 1856 and 1858; the Opéra declined to stage it.

Only the second half, as Les Troyens à Carthage, was performed in his lifetime, with cuts, at the Théâtre Lyrique on 4 November 1863; the first complete staging was at Karlsruhe in December 1890, over two evenings.
Covent Garden gave it in one evening under Rafael Kubelík in 1957; the Opéra Bastille opened its first season with it on 17 March 1990.
Cassandre in the Trojan acts and Didon in the Carthaginian acts are both mezzo-soprano roles; the 'Royal Hunt and Storm' is the orchestral interlude that turns up in concerts.
items.remark: Berlioz never saw the Trojan acts staged; Paris gave him half of it, cut, in 1863, and the whole thing waited for Karlsruhe in 1890 and Covent Garden in 1957.
items.gaffe: Calling it Berlioz's Faust. La damnation de Faust is a different work and not written for the stage; Les Troyens is Virgil, in five acts and about four hours.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Troyens, Les'
David Cairns, Berlioz: Servitude and Greatness, 1832–1869 (1999)
Hugh Macdonald, Berlioz (1982)

items.title: Jean-Baptiste Lully
facts: Born Giovanni Battista Lulli in Florence on 28 November 1632; brought to France as a boy in 1646 and naturalised in 1661.
Louis XIV's surintendant de la musique; in 1672 he acquired the privilege of the Académie Royale de Musique, which gave him a monopoly on sung drama in France.

With the poet Philippe Quinault he created the tragédie en musique: Cadmus et Hermione (1673), Alceste (1674), Atys (1676) and Armide (1686); before that he wrote the comédies-ballets with Molière, including Le Bourgeois gentilhomme (1670).
Struck his own foot with the long staff he beat time with while conducting a Te Deum for the king's recovery in January 1687, and died of the gangrene on 22 March.
items.remark: French opera was founded by a Florentine with a royal monopoly; Lully bought the privilege in 1672, and after that nobody in France could stage a sung drama without his leave.
items.gaffe: Calling him an Italian composer. He was born Lulli in Florence, but he was naturalised in 1661, and his operas are in French, for Louis XIV.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Lully, Jean-Baptiste'
Jérôme de La Gorce, Jean-Baptiste Lully (2002)

image.source: Paul Mignard, portrait of Jean-Baptiste Lully, Musée Condé, Chantilly, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (painter died 1691); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Jean-Philippe Rameau
facts: Baptised in Dijon on 25 September 1683; died in Paris on 12 September 1764.

Published the Traité de l'harmonie in 1722 and was known for years as a theorist and organist before his first opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, at the Académie Royale de Musique in 1733, when he was nearly fifty.
Les Indes galantes (1735), Castor et Pollux (1737), Dardanus (1739) and the comedy Platée (1745) followed; Les Boréades was never staged in his lifetime.
Saw two Native Americans from Louisiana dance at the Théâtre-Italien in 1725, wrote a harpsichord piece called Les Sauvages, and later reworked it for the last entrée of Les Indes galantes.
Attacked from both sides: by the partisans of Lully in the 1730s for too much harmony, and by Rousseau in the Querelle des Bouffons of the 1750s for not being Italian.
items.remark: He was nearly fifty before he wrote an opera, having been famous for a decade as the man who wrote the treatise on harmony; the Lullistes complained that Hippolyte et Aricie had too much of it.
items.gaffe: Filing him under Lully as more of the same. Rameau's first opera came forty-six years after Lully's death, and the Lullistes attacked it for being too modern.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Rameau, Jean-Philippe'
Cuthbert Girdlestone, Jean-Philippe Rameau: His Life and Work (rev. ed., 1969)

image.source: Attributed to Joseph Aved, portrait of Jean-Philippe Rameau (c. 1728), Musée des Beaux-Arts de Dijon, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Palais Garnier
facts: Charles Garnier, aged 35, won the competition for the new opera house in 1861; Napoleon III commissioned it as part of Haussmann's rebuilding of Paris, but it opened under the Third Republic, on 5 January 1875.

In 1896 a counterweight from the chandelier fell into the auditorium and killed a spectator; Gaston Leroux used the accident in Le Fantôme de l'Opéra (1910), along with the water tank beneath the stage.
Marc Chagall's ceiling, commissioned by André Malraux, was unveiled on 23 September 1964; it is painted on removable panels fixed over Lenepveu's original of 1872.
The Opéra Bastille, designed by Carlos Ott, was inaugurated on 13 July 1989; since then most opera is given there, and the Garnier is chiefly the house of the ballet.
items.remark: Napoleon III ordered it and never saw it finished; it opened in January 1875 under the Third Republic, five years after his empire had fallen.
items.gaffe: Booking the Garnier expecting an opera. Since the Bastille opened in 1989 the Garnier is mostly ballet; check the poster before you boast about your seats.
sources: Opéra national de Paris, 'The Paris Opera in the 19th century' and 'The Paris Opera in the 20th century'
Christopher Curtis Mead, Charles Garnier's Paris Opéra: Architectural Empathy and the Renaissance of French Classicism (1991)

items.title: Grand opéra
facts: Auber's La Muette de Portici (1828) and Rossini's Guillaume Tell (1829) set the pattern; Meyerbeer's Robert le diable (1831) and Les Huguenots (1836) and Halévy's La Juive (1835) made it the fashion of Europe.
Giacomo Meyerbeer (1791–1864), a Berlin banker's son, was the most performed opera composer of his age; Les Huguenots passed its thousandth performance at the Opéra in 1906.

The ballet was expected in Act 2, after the members of the Jockey Club had dined; Wagner put his Tannhäuser ballet in Act 1 for the Paris production of March 1861, the Jockey Club whistled, and the opera was withdrawn after three performances.
Verdi wrote Don Carlos (1867) for the Opéra in the form; Wagner's attack on Meyerbeer in 'Das Judenthum in der Musik' (1850) helped bury Meyerbeer's reputation.
items.remark: The ballet was contractual and it went in Act 2, because the Jockey Club dined first; Wagner put his in Act 1 in 1861 and Tannhäuser lasted three nights.
items.gaffe: Using 'grand opera' to mean any big serious opera. In Paris it names a form with rules: five acts, history, chorus, ballet, and usually Scribe.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Grand opéra'
David Charlton (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Grand Opera (2003)

term: An Italian tradition of florid singing in which the beauty of the vocal line matters more than dramatic truth.
A French opera with spoken dialogue between the musical numbers, whether or not the subject is comic.
A late nineteenth-century Italian school that put working-class violence on the stage in short, blunt acts.

items.definition: The Paris Opéra's house style from the 1830s: four or five acts, sung throughout in French, on a historical subject, with a large chorus, spectacular staging and an obligatory ballet, and usually a libretto by Eugène Scribe.

items.title: Opéra comique
facts: The Opéra-Comique is also the company and its theatre, the Salle Favart on the place Boieldieu; the present house, the third, opened in 1898 after a fire on 25 May 1887 killed 84 people.
Carmen (1875), Les contes d'Hoffmann (1881), Lakmé (1883), Manon (1884) and Pelléas et Mélisande (1902) all opened there.
Carmen was written with spoken dialogue; the sung recitatives usually heard instead were composed by Ernest Guiraud for Vienna in October 1875, after Bizet's death.
items.remark: Comique means the form, not the jokes: an opéra comique has spoken dialogue, and Carmen, which ends with a stabbing, opened at the Opéra-Comique in 1875.
items.gaffe: Saying Carmen 'is not really an opéra comique because it is not funny'. The term has nothing to do with comedy; it means spoken dialogue.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Opéra comique'
Hervé Lacombe, The Keys to French Opera in the Nineteenth Century (2001)

term: A comic opera in the Italian style, with recitative and an ensemble finale to each act.
A light French stage piece of the Second Empire with songs and dances, written for the boulevard theatres.
The Paris Opéra's spectacular five-act form, sung throughout, with an obligatory ballet.

items.definition: French opera with spoken dialogue between the musical numbers instead of recitative; the name describes the form, not the tone, and Carmen, which ends in a stabbing, is one.

items.title: Adieu, notre petite table
items.creator: Jules Massenet
facts: Manon opened at the Opéra-Comique on 19 January 1884, with Marie Heilbron as Manon and Jean-Alexandre Talazac as des Grieux; the libretto is by Henri Meilhac and Philippe Gille, after the Abbé Prévost's novel of 1731.

Manon sings it in Act 2, in the lovers' rooms in the rue Vivienne, having already agreed to leave des Grieux for the rich de Brétigny; des Grieux comes in, sings her his dream ('En fermant les yeux'), and is carried off by his father's men before the act ends.
Much of the dialogue is spoken over the orchestra rather than sung, a device called mélodrame; in Massenet's version Manon dies on the road to Le Havre, not, as in the novel, in Louisiana.
Puccini set the same novel as Manon Lescaut (Turin, 1 February 1893); Massenet answered with a one-act sequel, Le portrait de Manon, in 1894.
items.remark: She is saying goodbye to a table, not to a man: Manon has already agreed to go off with the rich de Brétigny, and des Grieux, who does not know, walks in and sings her his dream.
items.gaffe: Confusing it with Puccini's Manon Lescaut. Same novel, nine years later, in Italian; Massenet's Manon dies on the road to Le Havre, Puccini's in a Louisiana desert.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Manon'
Demar Irvine, Massenet: A Chronicle of His Life and Times (1994)

items.title: Pourquoi me réveiller
items.creator: Jules Massenet
facts: Massenet finished Werther in 1887; Léon Carvalho, director of the Opéra-Comique, turned it down as too gloomy, and the work opened instead at the Vienna Hofoper, in German, on 16 February 1892, with the Belgian tenor Ernest Van Dyck as Werther.
Paris heard it on 16 January 1893, given by the Opéra-Comique company at the Théâtre Lyrique while the Salle Favart was being rebuilt after the fire of 1887.

The libretto, by Édouard Blau, Paul Milliet and Georges Hartmann, follows Goethe's novel of 1774; the aria comes in Act 3, on Christmas Eve, when Werther reads Charlotte his translation of Ossian, the passage Goethe's Werther reads to Lotte in the book.

Charlotte is a mezzo-soprano; Werther shoots himself with pistols borrowed from her husband Albert and dies as children sing a carol outside; Massenet later arranged the title role for the baritone Mattia Battistini, who sang it in St Petersburg in 1902.
items.remark: The words are not the librettists' but Ossian's: Werther is reading Charlotte his translation of Macpherson's counterfeit Gaelic bard, which is exactly what Goethe has him read to Lotte before he shoots himself.
items.gaffe: Calling it a German opera because it opened in Vienna. It is French through and through; Vienna took it after the Opéra-Comique had refused it as too gloomy, and Paris caught up a year later.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Werther'
Demar Irvine, Massenet: A Chronicle of His Life and Times (1994)

items.title: Giacomo Meyerbeer
facts: Born Jakob Liebmann Beer near Berlin on 5 September 1791, the son of a Jewish banker; the Meyer came from his mother's family. He died in Paris on 2 May 1864.
Studied with the Abbé Vogler at Darmstadt alongside Carl Maria von Weber, then spent the years 1816 to 1824 in Italy writing Italian operas, ending with Il crociato in Egitto (Venice, 1824).

Robert le diable (1831), Les Huguenots (1836) and Le prophète (1849) at the Paris Opéra made him the most performed opera composer of the century; L'Africaine was staged in 1865, the year after his death. From 1842 he was also Prussian Generalmusikdirektor in Berlin.
His support helped get Wagner's Rienzi staged at Dresden in 1842; Wagner repaid him in 1850 with the anonymous pamphlet 'Das Judenthum in der Musik'.
items.remark: Wagner owed him Rienzi and repaid him with 'Das Judenthum in der Musik'; the most performed opera composer of the nineteenth century is now known chiefly through the attack on him.
items.gaffe: Calling him a French composer. He was a Berlin banker's son who wrote Italian operas for Venice before he ever wrote for Paris, and he held the Prussian court's music post while the Opéra lived off Les Huguenots.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Meyerbeer, Giacomo'
Robert Ignatius Letellier, The Operas of Giacomo Meyerbeer (2006)

image.source: Print after a photograph of Meyerbeer by Pierre Petit (1865), via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (nineteenth-century print; photographer Pierre Petit died 1909); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Les Huguenots
items.creator: Giacomo Meyerbeer
facts: Grand opéra in five acts, libretto by Eugène Scribe and Émile Deschamps; first performed at the Opéra, then in the Salle Le Peletier, on 29 February 1836.

Set in 1572 and ending in the St Bartholomew's Day massacre: the Protestant Raoul de Nangis loves the Catholic Valentine, and in the last act Raoul, Valentine and Raoul's old servant Marcel are shot by soldiers led by Valentine's own father, Saint-Bris.
Marcel, a bass, sings Luther's chorale 'Ein feste Burg', which runs through the score; the Act 4 'Bénédiction des poignards', in which the Catholic nobles bless their daggers, is the famous ensemble.

It needs seven leading singers, and in the 1890s the Metropolitan Opera's casts (Melba, Nordica, Scalchi, the brothers de Reszke, Plançon, Maurel) were billed as 'the nights of the seven stars'; it was also the first work to reach a thousand performances at the Paris Opéra, in 1906.
items.remark: It needs seven stars, which is why nobody stages it: the Met's Huguenots of the 1890s, with Melba, Nordica and both de Reszkes, were sold as the nights of the seven stars, and the phrase has outlived the opera's place in the repertory.
items.gaffe: Assuming the Huguenots come out of it alive. It ends in the massacre of 24 August 1572, and the hero, the heroine and the servant who sings Luther's chorale are all shot by the heroine's father's men.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Huguenots, Les'
Robert Ignatius Letellier, The Operas of Giacomo Meyerbeer (2006)
David Charlton (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Grand Opera (2003)

items.title: Jacques Offenbach
facts: Born Jacob Offenbach in Cologne on 20 June 1819, the son of a synagogue cantor who had taken the name of his home town, Offenbach am Main; he came to the Paris Conservatoire as a cellist in 1833 and died in Paris on 5 October 1880.

He opened his own theatre, the Bouffes-Parisiens, in 1855; its licence at first allowed only one-act pieces for a handful of singers, and Orphée aux enfers (1858) was his first full-length work once the rule was relaxed.

La belle Hélène (1864), La Vie parisienne (1866), La Grande-Duchesse de Gérolstein (1867) and La Périchole (1868) made him the composer of the Second Empire; he was naturalised French in 1860. Rossini is said to have called him the Mozart of the Champs-Élysées.
After the war of 1870 he was attacked in Paris as a German and in Germany as the man who had mocked the Empire; Les contes d'Hoffmann, his one serious opera, was unfinished when he died.
items.remark: He was the Second Empire's court jester and its one German: after 1870 France remembered where he was born and Germany remembered whom he had mocked, and the Hoffmann he did not live to finish was his bid to be taken seriously.
items.gaffe: Calling him a Viennese operetta composer. He is the Paris original; Johann Strauss took up the form after Offenbach's Vienna successes, and Die Fledermaus is 1874, sixteen years after Orphée.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Offenbach, Jacques'
Alexander Faris, Jacques Offenbach (1980)
Siegfried Kracauer, Jacques Offenbach and the Paris of His Time (1937)

image.source: Photograph of Jacques Offenbach by Nadar, Bibliothèque nationale de France, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (photographer Félix Nadar died 1910); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Sous le dôme épais (Flower Duet)
items.creator: Léo Delibes
facts: Lakmé opened at the Opéra-Comique on 14 April 1883, with the American soprano Marie van Zandt in the title role; the libretto is by Edmond Gondinet and Philippe Gille, after Pierre Loti.

The duet comes in Act 1: Lakmé, daughter of a Brahmin priest in British India, and her servant Mallika, a mezzo, gather flowers by a river, singing in thirds in a rocking 6/8; Gérald, the British officer Lakmé will die for, has not yet appeared.
The Act 2 'Bell Song' ('Où va la jeune Hindoue') is the coloratura showpiece; Lakmé dies at the end by eating a datura leaf.
Delibes was a ballet composer first: Coppélia (1870) and Sylvia (1876) were written for the Opéra. British Airways took the duet for its advertising from 1989.
items.remark: Delibes was a ballet composer first, and the duet, sung in thirds by a Brahmin's daughter and her servant picking flowers by a river, is the one page of Lakmé that an airline and everybody else took.
items.gaffe: Calling it a love duet. Both singers are women, mistress and servant, and the man Lakmé loves, a British officer, has not yet walked on.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Lakmé'
Grove Music Online, 'Delibes, Léo'

creator: Georges Bizet
Jules Massenet
Charles Gounod
title: Où va la jeune Hindoue (Bell Song)
Belle nuit, ô nuit d'amour (Barcarolle)
Les oiseaux dans la charmille (Doll Song)

items.title: Mon cœur s'ouvre à ta voix
items.creator: Camille Saint-Saëns
facts: Paris theatres were shy of biblical subjects on stage, so the opera was first given at Weimar, in German, on 2 December 1877, at Liszt's instigation; the libretto is by Ferdinand Lemaire.
France first heard it at Rouen in 1890; it entered the Paris Opéra on 23 November 1892, and is the only one of Saint-Saëns's dozen or so operas that stays in the repertory.

Dalila, a mezzo-soprano, sings it in Act 2 to seduce Samson, a tenor, into telling her the secret of his strength; the Act 3 Bacchanale in the temple of Dagon is the orchestral showpiece, and Samson brings the temple down at the end.
Saint-Saëns began the piece in 1867 as an oratorio and was talked into making it an opera.
items.remark: Paris would not put the Bible on the stage, so his one repertory opera opened in Weimar, in German, in 1877 because Liszt arranged it, and the Opéra waited fifteen years.
items.gaffe: Calling Dalila a soprano. The seduction sits low on purpose; it is the mezzo's aria, and Samson is the tenor she is working on.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Samson et Dalila'
Brian Rees, Camille Saint-Saëns: A Life (1999)

items.title: Dialogues des Carmélites
items.creator: Francis Poulenc
facts: Commissioned by Ricordi and first performed at La Scala, Milan, in Italian, on 26 January 1957; the French premiere followed at the Paris Opéra on 21 June 1957, with Denise Duval as Blanche and Régine Crespin as the new Prioress.
The text is Georges Bernanos's, written as a film script after Gertrud von Le Fort's novella Die Letzte am Schafott (1931), and set by Poulenc nearly as it stood.

The subject is the sixteen Carmelite nuns of Compiègne guillotined in Paris on 17 July 1794, ten days before Robespierre fell; Blanche de la Force, the frightened aristocrat who joins them at the scaffold, is invented.

In the final scene the nuns walk to the guillotine singing the Salve Regina, and the fall of the blade is written into the score, the voices dropping out one by one. Poulenc dedicated the work to the memory of his mother and to Monteverdi, Verdi, Mussorgsky and Debussy.
items.remark: The guillotine is in the score: the nuns walk out singing the Salve Regina and a voice drops out at each stroke, which is what happened at the place du Trône on 17 July 1794, ten days before Robespierre followed them.
items.gaffe: Assuming it opened in Paris. Ricordi commissioned it, so it opened at La Scala in Italian in January 1957; Paris heard it in French that June, with Denise Duval as Blanche.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Dialogues des Carmélites'
Carl B. Schmidt, Entrancing Muse: A Documented Biography of Francis Poulenc (2001)

items.title: Opéra Bastille
facts: One of Mitterrand's grands projets, meant as a modern, popular opera house; Carlos Ott won the competition in 1983, and the building went up on the site of the old Bastille railway station.
Inaugurated on 13 July 1989, the eve of the Revolution's bicentenary; the first opera performed in it was Berlioz's Les Troyens, on 17 March 1990. The main auditorium seats about 2,700.
Pierre Bergé, president of the Opéra, sacked its music director designate, Daniel Barenboim, in January 1989, before the house had opened; Myung-whun Chung took the post.
Since it opened, most opera in Paris is given here and the Palais Garnier is chiefly the house of the ballet; the two together form the Opéra national de Paris.
items.remark: It opened on the eve of the bicentenary, 13 July 1989, on the site of the old Bastille railway station, having already sacked its music director, Barenboim, six months before anyone sang in it.
items.gaffe: Praising the building at a Paris dinner. Parisians have been rude about Carlos Ott's design since the competition, and panels of its facade started coming loose within a few years; praise the stage machinery and the sightlines instead.
sources: Opéra national de Paris, 'The Opéra Bastille'
Grove Music Online, 'Paris', §6 (after 1945)

items.title: Opéra-Comique (Salle Favart)
facts: The company began in the fairground theatres of Paris around 1715 and merged with the Comédie-Italienne in 1762; the house is named after Charles-Simon Favart, the eighteenth-century librettist who ran it.
