Three theatres have stood on the site: the first Salle Favart of 1783 burned in 1838, the second, of 1840, burned on 25 May 1887 with 84 dead, and the third, by Louis Bernier, opened in December 1898.

Carmen (1875), Les contes d'Hoffmann (1881), Lakmé (1883), Manon (1884), Louise (1900) and Pelléas et Mélisande (1902) all had their premieres with the company; Werther's Paris premiere in 1893 was given at the Théâtre Lyrique while the house was being rebuilt.
It is a separate company from the Opéra, a few hundred metres from the Garnier on the boulevard des Italiens, and has been a théâtre national since 2005.
items.remark: Three theatres on the same spot: the Salle Favart of 1783 burned in 1838, its successor burned in 1887 with eighty-four dead, and the third, of 1898, is where Pelléas opened in 1902.
items.gaffe: Assuming the Opéra-Comique is part of the Opéra. It is a separate company with its own house a few hundred metres away, and Carmen, Manon and Pelléas were its premieres, not the Opéra's.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Opéra-Comique'
Nicole Wild and David Charlton, Théâtre de l'Opéra-Comique, Paris: répertoire 1762–1972 (2005)

items.title: Claque
facts: Paris put applause on a commercial footing in 1820, when a man named Sauton opened an agency selling it to managers and performers; the Opéra's chef de claque of the 1830s, Auguste Levasseur, attended rehearsals to plan where his people would clap.
A claque had specialists: rieurs to laugh, pleureurs to weep, bisseurs to demand the encore, and chatouilleurs to keep their neighbours in good humour.

The practice is older than opera: Nero kept a trained body of young applauders, the Augustiani. Mahler fought the claque at the Vienna Hofoper after 1897, and houses went on tolerating it well into the twentieth century.
items.remark: At the Opéra in the 1830s the applause was scored as carefully as the music: Levasseur, the chef de claque, went to rehearsals to plan where his people would clap, laugh, weep and call for the encore.
items.gaffe: Taking a warm reception at a Paris premiere as the verdict of the public. Well into the twentieth century some of it was paid for, seated in the middle of the parterre, and told when to start.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Claque'
The Oxford Companion to Music, 'Claque'

term: A group of critics and connoisseurs who sat together in the parterre and set the town's opinion of a new work.
The clatter made by the stage machinery of an old French theatre, used as a signal to the orchestra.
A rousing vocal flourish written into the end of an aria to draw an ovation.

items.definition: An organised body of paid applauders, seated through the house and directed by a chef de claque, who clapped, laughed, wept and called for encores to order; from claquer, to clap.

items.title: Divertissement (the ballet in French opera)
facts: Louis XIV danced himself, appearing as the rising sun in the Ballet royal de la Nuit in 1653 with Lully among the dancers; Lully's tragédies en musique kept a divertissement of dances and choruses in each act, and Rameau's Les Indes galantes (1735) is an opéra-ballet, a form held together by dancing.

The Romantic ballet was born inside an opera: the ballet of the dead nuns in Act 3 of Meyerbeer's Robert le diable (1831), choreographed by Filippo Taglioni for his daughter Marie, came a year before La Sylphide.

Verdi wrote ballets for the Opéra four times, for Les vêpres siciliennes (1855), Le trouvère (1857), Don Carlos (1867) and the Paris Otello of 1894; Gounod's Faust acquired its Walpurgis Night ballet when it moved to the Opéra in 1869.
items.remark: The Romantic ballet was born inside an opera: the dance of the dead nuns in Robert le diable in 1831, with Marie Taglioni, came a year before La Sylphide, and after that the Opéra expected a ballet from everyone, Verdi and Wagner included.
items.gaffe: Treating the ballet in a French opera as padding to cut. Verdi wrote one for Paris four times, and the whole opéra-ballet form of Rameau is nothing but the dancing.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Divertissement'
Marian Smith, Ballet and Opera in the Age of Giselle (2000)
David Charlton (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to Grand Opera (2003)

term: The comic intermezzo played between the acts of an Italian opera seria, from which opera buffa grew.
A spoken scene between the musical numbers of an opéra comique.
The orchestral prelude played before the curtain rises on a French grand opéra.

items.definition: The dance episode built into a French opera: a set of dances, usually with chorus, that halts the plot to show the company's ballet. Lully put one in every act, and the Opéra of the 1830s expected it in Act 2.

items.title: Le nozze di Figaro (The Marriage of Figaro)
items.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
facts: First performed at the Burgtheater, Vienna, on 1 May 1786, with a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte after Beaumarchais's play La Folle Journée, ou Le Mariage de Figaro (1784).
Joseph II had forbidden the play on the Vienna stage; Da Ponte's libretto dropped its political speeches, and the emperor let the opera through.
One 'mad day' at Count Almaviva's castle near Seville: Figaro and Susanna are to marry, the Count wants Susanna, and the Countess and Susanna conspire to catch him out.
Cherubino, the page, is a trouser role for a mezzo-soprano; Figaro's 'Non più andrai' closes Act I and Cherubino's 'Voi che sapete' comes in Act II.
items.remark: The play was banned in Vienna and the opera was not; Da Ponte cut Figaro's politics, kept the bedroom doors, and Joseph II let it through in 1786.
items.gaffe: Running it together with Rossini. The Barber of Seville is the earlier play and the later opera (1816); Mozart's Figaro is the sequel, with Figaro now the Count's valet and about to be married.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Nozze di Figaro, Le'
Tim Carter, W. A. Mozart: Le nozze di Figaro (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1987)

theme.note: 'Voi che sapete', Cherubino's arietta in Act II; the opening vocal phrase in the original key.

items.title: Don Giovanni
items.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
facts: First performed in Prague at the Nostitz (now Estates) Theatre on 29 October 1787; Vienna heard it at the Burgtheater on 7 May 1788 with numbers Mozart added for the Viennese cast.
For Vienna Mozart wrote 'Dalla sua pace' for the tenor Francesco Morella, who found 'Il mio tesoro' too hard, and 'Mi tradì quell'alma ingrata' for Caterina Cavalieri as Donna Elvira.
Da Ponte called it a dramma giocoso; the Commendatore, killed in the first scene, returns as a stone statue and drags the unrepentant Don down to hell.
Leporello's catalogue aria counts the Don's conquests by country: 640 in Italy, 231 in Germany, 100 in France, 91 in Turkey, and in Spain already 1,003.
items.remark: Prague had it first, in October 1787; Vienna got it seven months later with 'Dalla sua pace' added because the Viennese tenor could not manage 'Il mio tesoro'.
items.gaffe: Giving the catalogue aria to the Don. 'Madamina, il catalogo è questo' is Leporello's, the servant reading the list to Donna Elvira, and the Spanish total is 1,003.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Don Giovanni'
Julian Rushton, W. A. Mozart: Don Giovanni (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1981)

theme.note: 'Là ci darem la mano', the Act I duet; Don Giovanni's opening phrase, which he sings an octave below this and Zerlina answers at this pitch.

items.title: Così fan tutte
items.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
facts: First performed at the Burgtheater on 26 January 1790; the third and last Mozart and Da Ponte opera, subtitled La scuola degli amanti, the school for lovers.
Joseph II died on 20 February 1790 and the court theatres closed in mourning after a handful of performances; the run resumed that summer.

Two officers, Ferrando and Guglielmo, bet the cynic Don Alfonso that their fiancées Fiordiligi and Dorabella will stay faithful, then woo each other's fiancée in disguise; the maid Despina is in on it.
Nineteenth-century audiences thought the plot immoral and it was rewritten or left alone; its standing in the repertory dates from the twentieth century.
items.remark: It is the men who make the wager: Don Alfonso bets two officers that their fiancées will stray within a day, and the title, 'they all do it', is his verdict when they do.
items.gaffe: Pronouncing it 'cosy fan tootie'. It is ko-ZEE fahn TOOT-teh, and tutte is feminine: 'so do all women', which is the whole of Don Alfonso's argument.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Così fan tutte'
Bruce Alan Brown, W. A. Mozart: Così fan tutte (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1995)

items.title: Die Zauberflöte (The Magic Flute)
items.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
facts: First performed on 30 September 1791 at the Theater auf der Wieden, Emanuel Schikaneder's suburban theatre; Schikaneder wrote the words and played Papageno, and Mozart died on 5 December.
A Singspiel: sung numbers with spoken dialogue in German, not recitative.
The Queen of the Night's second aria, 'Der Hölle Rache kocht in meinem Herzen', climbs to F above high C; the role was created by Mozart's sister-in-law Josepha Hofer.

Papageno the bird-catcher has panpipes and a set of magic bells, Tamino the flute; Sarastro, the bass, sings 'O Isis und Osiris'. Mozart and Schikaneder were Freemasons, and the three chords and the trials are usually read as Masonic.
items.remark: It opened in a suburb, not at court: Schikaneder's Theater auf der Wieden, where the impresario wrote the words and played Papageno himself, some nine weeks before Mozart died.
items.gaffe: Taking the Queen of the Night for the heroine because she has the famous aria. By Act II she is the villain, and Sarastro, whom she wants murdered, is the good one.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Zauberflöte, Die'
Peter Branscombe, W. A. Mozart: Die Zauberflöte (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1991)

theme.note: 'Der Hölle Rache', the Queen of the Night's Act II aria; the vocal entry after one bar of orchestra.

items.title: Orfeo ed Euridice
items.creator: Christoph Willibald Gluck
facts: First performed at the Burgtheater, Vienna, on 5 October 1762, with a libretto by Ranieri de' Calzabigi.
Orfeo was written for the alto castrato Gaetano Guadagni; for Paris in 1774 Gluck rewrote the role for a high tenor and the work became Orphée et Eurydice.
Gluck and Calzabigi set out to rid opera of vocal display and da capo ornament, the programme Gluck spelled out in the preface to Alceste, published in 1769.
Orfeo loses Euridice a second time by looking back, sings 'Che farò senza Euridice', and is about to kill himself when Amore restores her; the ending is happy.
items.remark: The great lament is in C major and the ending is happy: Amore relents and hands Euridice back, because the Vienna of 1762 had no appetite for Ovid's version.
items.gaffe: Announcing that Orfeo is a tenor. In Vienna he was the castrato Guadagni, today he is a mezzo or a countertenor, and the tenor version is the Paris one of 1774.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Orfeo ed Euridice'
Patricia Howard (ed.), C. W. von Gluck: Orfeo (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1981)

theme.note: 'Che farò senza Euridice', Act III; the vocal line from its first entry, in the Vienna key of C major.

items.title: Fidelio
items.creator: Ludwig van Beethoven
facts: First performed at the Theater an der Wien on 20 November 1805, a week after Napoleon's troops had occupied Vienna; the audience was largely French officers and it closed after three nights.
Beethoven revised it in 1806 and again, thoroughly, in 1814; the 1814 version is the one performed, and the earlier title was Leonore.
Beethoven's only opera. It has four overtures, Leonore Nos. 1, 2 and 3 and the Fidelio overture of 1814; Mahler started the custom of playing Leonore No. 3 before the final scene.
Leonore disguises herself as the youth Fidelio to free her husband Florestan from Pizarro's prison; the libretto descends from Bouilly's Léonore, ou L'amour conjugal (1798).
items.remark: Its first audience in November 1805 was mostly French officers, because Napoleon's army had marched into Vienna the week before; it ran for three nights.
items.gaffe: Asking which of Beethoven's operas it is. There is only one, though it has four overtures, and the Leonore No. 3 often played before the finale was Mahler's habit, not Beethoven's.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Fidelio'
Paul Robinson (ed.), Ludwig van Beethoven: Fidelio (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1996)

theme.note: Fidelio overture (1814), the opening fanfare, top line; alla breve, the fermata approximated by rests.

items.title: Die Fledermaus
items.creator: Johann Strauss II
facts: First performed at the Theater an der Wien on 5 April 1874; the libretto by Carl Haffner and Richard Genée derives from Meilhac and Halévy's French play Le Réveillon.
Dr Falke pays Eisenstein back for once leaving him to walk home in daylight dressed as a bat: he lures him to Prince Orlofsky's ball, where Eisenstein flirts with his own masked wife.
Prince Orlofsky is a trouser role for a mezzo-soprano; Adele's laughing song 'Mein Herr Marquis' and the Act II 'Brüderlein und Schwesterlein' are the numbers people hum.
The Vienna State Opera plays it on New Year's Eve, a tradition of long standing.
items.remark: The Staatsoper puts it on every New Year's Eve, and the Russian prince throwing the party is sung by a woman; if Orlofsky sounds like a mezzo, that is the casting, not the acoustics.
items.gaffe: Calling Johann Strauss the father of Richard Strauss. Richard was from Munich and no relation; Johann's father was the other Johann Strauss, of the Radetzky March.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Fledermaus, Die'
Richard Traubner, Operetta: A Theatrical History (2nd ed., 2003)

theme.note: 'Ich lade gern mir Gäste ein' (Chacun à son goût), Orlofsky's couplets in Act II; the vocal entry, after the 1875 Schreiber vocal score.

items.title: Der Rosenkavalier
items.creator: Richard Strauss
facts: First performed at the Dresden Court Opera on 26 January 1911, with a libretto by Hugo von Hofmannsthal; the Vienna Court Opera followed in April 1911.

Set in Vienna in the 1740s, early in Maria Theresa's reign: the Marschallin gives up her young lover Octavian, who falls for Sophie while presenting the silver rose on behalf of the boorish Baron Ochs.
Octavian is a trouser role for a mezzo-soprano; the Marschallin, Octavian and Sophie end the opera with a trio, and then Octavian and Sophie with a duet.
The waltzes are an anachronism; the Viennese waltz belongs to the century after the opera's setting.
items.remark: The waltzes are an anachronism: the story is set in Maria Theresa's 1740s, two generations before the Viennese waltz, and it is still the most Viennese opera there is.
items.gaffe: Calling it a Vienna premiere. It opened in Dresden in January 1911, as Salome and Elektra had; Vienna's Court Opera got it that April.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Rosenkavalier, Der'
Alan Jefferson, Richard Strauss: Der Rosenkavalier (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1985)

items.title: Lorenzo Da Ponte
facts: Born Emanuele Conegliano in the Jewish community of Ceneda in the Veneto on 10 March 1749; the family converted when he was fourteen and took the name of the local bishop, and he was ordained a priest in 1773.
Banished from Venice in 1779 for adultery and for living in a brothel; came to Vienna in 1781 and in 1783 became poet to Joseph II's Italian opera company at the court theatre.
Wrote the librettos of Le nozze di Figaro (1786), Don Giovanni (1787) and Così fan tutte (1790) for Mozart, and Una cosa rara for Martín y Soler, which outsold them all at the time.

Left Vienna after Joseph II's death, spent years in London, and emigrated to America in 1805, where he kept a grocery in Pennsylvania and in 1825 became the first professor of Italian at Columbia College; he died in New York in 1838.
items.remark: A Venetian priest banished for adultery who wrote Figaro, Don Giovanni and Così, then ended as a grocer in Pennsylvania and the first professor of Italian at Columbia; the life outdid the librettos.
items.gaffe: Assuming he wrote The Magic Flute. That is Schikaneder's; Da Ponte's Mozart operas are the three Italian ones.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Da Ponte, Lorenzo'
Sheila Hodges, Lorenzo Da Ponte: The Life and Times of Mozart's Librettist (1985)

items.title: Richard Strauss
facts: Born in Munich on 11 June 1864, the son of Franz Strauss, principal horn of the Munich court orchestra; died at Garmisch-Partenkirchen on 8 September 1949.
Salome (Dresden, 1905), after Oscar Wilde's play, was kept off the Vienna Court Opera stage by the censor when Mahler wanted to give it; Vienna's opera did not stage it until 1918.
Elektra (1909) and Der Rosenkavalier (1911), both with Hugo von Hofmannsthal, followed at Dresden; the two worked together until the poet's death in 1929.
Co-director of the Vienna State Opera with Franz Schalk from 1919 to 1924; he liked to say that Salome's royalties had built his villa at Garmisch.
items.remark: No relation to the waltz Strausses: a Bavarian, son of Munich's principal horn, whose Salome the Vienna censor kept off the Court Opera stage from 1905 until 1918.
items.gaffe: Filing him with Johann Strauss as a Viennese. Richard was a Munich man, born in 1864, and Salome, Elektra and Der Rosenkavalier all opened in Dresden.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Strauss, Richard'
Michael Kennedy, Richard Strauss: Man, Musician, Enigma (1999)

items.title: Wiener Staatsoper (Vienna State Opera)
facts: Opened on the Ringstrasse on 25 May 1869 as the Court Opera (Hofoper) with Mozart's Don Giovanni; the architects, August Sicard von Sicardsburg and Eduard van der Nüll, both died in 1868 before the opening, van der Nüll by his own hand.
Gustav Mahler was its director from 1897 to 1907; it became the State Opera after the monarchy fell in 1918.
The auditorium was destroyed by bombing on 12 March 1945; the house reopened on 5 November 1955 with Fidelio under Karl Böhm.
The Vienna Opera Ball takes over the auditorium on the Thursday before Ash Wednesday, with the stalls floored over for dancing.
items.remark: It opened in 1869 with Don Giovanni and neither architect lived to see it: van der Nüll hanged himself after the design was ridiculed, and Sicardsburg died within weeks.
items.gaffe: Calling it the Volksoper. That is the other Vienna house, out by the Gürtel, for operetta and opera in German; the Staatsoper is the one on the Ring.
sources: Wiener Staatsoper, 'History of the Vienna State Opera'
Grove Music Online, 'Vienna'

items.title: Singspiel
facts: Joseph II founded a National Singspiel company at the Burgtheater in 1778 to promote opera in German; Mozart's Die Entführung aus dem Serail (1782) was written for it.
Die Zauberflöte (1791) is a Singspiel; so, technically, is Fidelio (1805), which keeps spoken dialogue; the line runs on to Weber's Der Freischütz (1821).
The plural is Singspiele.
items.remark: It simply means that they talk between the numbers: The Magic Flute and Fidelio are both Singspiele, and the spoken dialogue is what modern productions cut or rewrite.
items.gaffe: Treating it as a lesser form, or as a musical. Mozart and Beethoven wrote Singspiele; the word describes the spoken dialogue, not the ambition.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Singspiel'

term: An Italian comic opera in two acts with a buffo bass and a patter finale.
A short one-act German opera without chorus, performed as a curtain-raiser.
A song cycle for voice and piano staged with costumes and scenery.

items.definition: A German-language opera with spoken dialogue between the musical numbers instead of sung recitative; the Viennese form of the late eighteenth century, of which Die Zauberflöte is the summit.

items.title: Operetta
facts: Offenbach made the form in Paris in the 1850s and 1860s; Vienna's Golden Age is Strauss, Suppé and Millöcker, its Silver Age Lehár, Kálmán and Oscar Straus.
Lehár's Die lustige Witwe (The Merry Widow) opened at the Theater an der Wien on 30 December 1905, set in the Paris embassy of the invented Balkan state of Pontevedro, and went round the world.
Gilbert and Sullivan's Savoy operas are the English branch; the Volksoper, opened in 1898, is Vienna's operetta house today.
items.remark: The Merry Widow's Pontevedro is Montenegro with the name changed, and the plot is a bankrupt state trying to keep a widow's millions at home by marrying her to Danilo; that is Viennese operetta, written by a Hungarian.
items.gaffe: Calling Die Fledermaus or The Merry Widow an opera. Both are operettas, with spoken dialogue; the Staatsoper's New Year Fledermaus is the exception it makes once a year.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Operetta'
Richard Traubner, Operetta: A Theatrical History (2nd ed., 2003)

term: A short opera in one act, usually tragic, performed as half of a double bill.
An opera's overture played on its own as a concert piece.
A staged song recital with piano accompaniment.

items.definition: Light opera with spoken dialogue, dance rhythms and a comic or sentimental plot; in Vienna it runs from Strauss's Die Fledermaus (1874) to Lehár's The Merry Widow (1905) and its successors.

items.title: Der Vogelfänger bin ich ja (Papageno's aria)
items.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
facts: Papageno's entrance song in Act I of Die Zauberflöte, first heard at the Theater auf der Wieden on 30 September 1791, sung by Emanuel Schikaneder, who had written the libretto and owned the theatre.
A strophic song in G major, deliberately folk-like, the verses turning from birds to girls; Papageno's panpipes, five rising notes, punctuate it.
Papageno is a baritone in a suit of feathers who catches birds for the Queen of the Night's three ladies; his instruments are the panpipes and, later, a set of magic bells. The flute is Tamino's.
items.remark: Schikaneder wrote the words, owned the theatre and sang this himself on the first night, in feathers; it is a strophic song in G major with five rising panpipe notes between the lines, and it sounds like a street song on purpose.
items.gaffe: Handing Papageno the flute. The flute is Tamino's, the tenor's; Papageno, a baritone, has the panpipes and the magic bells, and what he wants is a wife, not wisdom.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Zauberflöte, Die'
Peter Branscombe, W. A. Mozart: Die Zauberflöte (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1991)

items.title: Die Entführung aus dem Serail (The Abduction from the Seraglio)
items.creator: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
facts: First performed at the Burgtheater on 16 July 1782, written for Joseph II's National Singspiel company; the libretto is by Gottlieb Stephanie the younger, reworked from Christoph Friedrich Bretzner's Belmont und Constanze.

Belmonte, with his servant Pedrillo, rescues Konstanze and her maid Blonde from the seraglio of Pasha Selim, a speaking part; Osmin, the overseer, is a bass whose rage aria goes down to a low D, and the Pasha lets them all go.

The 'Turkish' scoring, piccolo, triangle, cymbals and bass drum, opens the overture; Konstanze's 'Martern aller Arten' has a long concertante introduction for four solo instruments before she sings a note.

Mozart married Constanze Weber on 4 August 1782, under three weeks after the premiere. Niemetschek's biography of 1798 is the source for Joseph II's 'an enormous number of notes, dear Mozart' and for the reply that there were exactly as many as were needed.
items.remark: 'Too many notes' belongs here, if anywhere: Niemetschek's biography of 1798 has Joseph II say it of this piece and Mozart answer that there were exactly as many as were needed; the heroine is Konstanze, and Mozart married his own Constanze three weeks after the first night.
items.gaffe: Filing it with the Italian operas. It is a German Singspiel with spoken dialogue, written for Joseph II's National Singspiel company, and its Pasha never sings a note; the Italian Vienna operas came later, with Da Ponte.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Entführung aus dem Serail, Die'
Thomas Bauman, W. A. Mozart: Die Entführung aus dem Serail (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1987)
Franz Xaver Niemetschek, Leben des K.K. Kapellmeisters Wolfgang Gottlieb Mozart (1798)

items.title: Die lustige Witwe (The Merry Widow)
items.creator: Franz Lehár
facts: First performed at the Theater an der Wien on 30 December 1905, with Mizzi Günther as Hanna Glawari and Louis Treumann as Danilo; the libretto is by Victor Léon and Leo Stein, after Henri Meilhac's comedy L'Attaché d'ambassade (1861).

Hanna, a rich widow from Pontevedro, a Balkan state standing in for Montenegro, is in Paris; the embassy's Baron Zeta wants her millions kept at home by marrying her to Count Danilo, her old love, who refuses to court money.
The numbers: Hanna's 'Vilja-Lied', Danilo's 'Da geh' ich zu Maxim', and the Act III duet 'Lippen schweigen', the Merry Widow Waltz.
London had it at Daly's Theatre in June 1907 with Lily Elsie, New York that October; the 'Merry Widow hat' was a fashion, and the Silver Age of Viennese operetta is dated from it.
items.remark: Danilo will not court a woman with millions in case it looks like the money, so the two dance instead of talking until Act III, when 'Lippen schweigen' lets the violins say it; it opened at the Theater an der Wien on 30 December 1905 and was in London and New York within two years.
items.gaffe: Calling it Strauss, or Lehár Viennese by birth. He was a Hungarian bandmaster's son from Komárom, and the Widow belongs to the Silver Age of operetta, thirty years after Die Fledermaus.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Lustige Witwe, Die'
Richard Traubner, Operetta: A Theatrical History (2nd ed., 2003)

items.title: Salome
items.creator: Richard Strauss
facts: First performed at the Dresden Court Opera on 9 December 1905, in one act; Strauss set Hedwig Lachmann's German translation of Oscar Wilde's play, which Wilde had written in French in 1891, cutting the text himself.
Salome, Herod's stepdaughter, dances the Dance of the Seven Veils for the head of Jochanaan, John the Baptist, and kisses it when it comes; Herod has the soldiers crush her under their shields.

Vienna's censor refused it for the Court Opera despite Mahler; the Austrian premiere was in Graz on 16 May 1906 under Strauss, with Mahler, Puccini, Schoenberg and Berg in the house, and the Vienna Court Opera did not stage it until 1918.
The Metropolitan Opera gave it once, on 22 January 1907, and withdrew it under pressure from its board; the first Salome, Marie Wittich, declined to do the dance herself and a dancer stood in.
items.remark: The censor kept it off the Court Opera stage until 1918, so the Austrian premiere was Graz in May 1906 with Strauss conducting and Mahler, Puccini, Schoenberg and Berg in the audience; that is the performance to mention.
items.gaffe: Expecting waltzes or an interval. It is one act of about a hundred minutes, the dance is the Seven Veils and the first Salome would not dance it herself; the waltzes are Rosenkavalier, six years later.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Salome'
Derrick Puffett (ed.), Richard Strauss: Salome (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1989)
Michael Kennedy, Richard Strauss: Man, Musician, Enigma (1999)

items.title: Wozzeck
items.creator: Alban Berg
facts: Berg, born in Vienna in 1885 and Schoenberg's pupil, saw Georg Büchner's unfinished play at its Vienna premiere in May 1914; he composed the opera between 1914 and 1922, around his war service, and Erich Kleiber gave the premiere at the Berlin State Opera on 14 December 1925.

Three acts of five scenes each, every scene built as an instrumental form: the suite, passacaglia and rondo of Act I, the five-movement symphony of Act II, the inventions of Act III; the D minor interlude before the last scene is where the score turns tonal.

The soldier Wozzeck, shaved, lectured and fed on beans by the Captain and the Doctor, cuts Marie's throat by the pond and drowns looking for the knife; their child rides his hobby-horse in the last scene while the others run off to see the body.

The name is a misreading: Karl Emil Franzos, editing Büchner's manuscripts in 1879, read Woyzeck as Wozzeck, and Berg kept the spelling. The Vienna State Opera first gave it in March 1930 under Clemens Krauss.
items.remark: Berg saw Büchner's play in Vienna in May 1914 and needed eight years and a war to make it an opera, and the title keeps a misprint: Franzos, reading Büchner's hand in 1879, made Woyzeck into Wozzeck, and Berg never corrected it.
items.gaffe: Calling it twelve-tone. Wozzeck is atonal but not serial; Berg's row technique arrives with Lulu, and the shape of Wozzeck is old forms, a passacaglia, a symphony, a set of inventions, hidden under the drama.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Wozzeck'
Douglas Jarman, Alban Berg: Wozzeck (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1989)

items.title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
facts: Born in Salzburg on 27 January 1756; dismissed from the Archbishop of Salzburg's service in Vienna in June 1781 and stayed on as a freelance; died in Vienna on 5 December 1791, aged thirty-five, of a fever the death register calls 'hitziges Frieselfieber'.

The Vienna operas: Die Entführung aus dem Serail (1782) for Joseph II's National Singspiel, the three Da Ponte comedies Le nozze di Figaro (1786), Don Giovanni (Prague 1787, Vienna 1788) and Così fan tutte (1790), and Die Zauberflöte (1791) for Schikaneder's suburban theatre.
He signed himself Wolfgang Amadè; 'Amadeus' is the Latin form he used only in jest, and it stuck after his death.
Buried at St Marx cemetery in a common grave, which is what Joseph II's burial regulations of 1784 prescribed for most Viennese; the storm and the pauper's grave are later embroidery.
items.remark: He signed himself Amadè, not Amadeus, spent his last ten years in Vienna as a freelance after the Archbishop's man had kicked him out of the room, and was buried in a common grave because Joseph II's regulations said so, not because he was a pauper.
items.gaffe: Repeating the poisoning. The register says fever, the Salieri story was gossip within a month and a Pushkin play by 1830, and Salieri taught Mozart's own son; Amadeus is a play, not a biography.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Mozart, (Johann Chrysostom) Wolfgang Amadeus'
Maynard Solomon, Mozart: A Life (1995)
H. C. Robbins Landon, 1791: Mozart's Last Year (1988)

image.source: Barbara Krafft, posthumous portrait of Mozart, 1819, Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, Vienna, via Wikimedia Commons
image.license: Public domain (artist died 1825); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Christoph Willibald Gluck
facts: Born at Erasbach in the Upper Palatinate on 2 July 1714, a forester's son; worked in Milan, London and Prague before settling in Vienna, where he married a merchant's daughter in 1750 and died on 15 November 1787.

With the librettist Ranieri de' Calzabigi he made the Vienna reform operas, Orfeo ed Euridice (1762), Alceste (1767) and Paride ed Elena (1770); the printed dedication of Alceste (1769) is the manifesto: music to serve the poetry, no da capo repeats, no ornament for its own sake.

He had taught the Archduchess Maria Antonia her music in Vienna; as Marie Antoinette she backed him in Paris, where Iphigénie en Aulide (1774) set off the pamphlet war between his partisans and Niccolò Piccinni's.
A papal Knight of the Golden Spur from 1756, hence 'Ritter von Gluck'; the Paris operas run to Armide (1777) and Iphigénie en Tauride (1779), after which strokes ended his career.
items.remark: A Bavarian forester's son who taught Marie Antoinette her music in Vienna and followed her to Paris, where his Iphigénie en Aulide of 1774 started the Gluckist and Piccinnist quarrel; the reform manifesto is the preface to Alceste, printed in 1769.
items.gaffe: Shelving him with Handel as Baroque because he wrote an Orpheus. The point of Gluck is the break with Baroque opera: no da capo arias, no display for its own sake, the drama first; Berlioz worshipped him and Wagner revised his Iphigénie en Aulide for Dresden.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Gluck, Christoph Willibald Ritter von'
Patricia Howard, Gluck: An Eighteenth-Century Portrait in Letters and Documents (1995)
Bruce Alan Brown, Gluck and the French Theatre in Vienna (1991)

image.commons: File:Joseph Siffred Duplessis - Christoph Willibald Gluck - Google Art Project.jpg
image.source: Joseph Siffred Duplessis, Christoph Willibald Gluck, 1775, Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna, via Wikimedia Commons (Google Art Project scan)
image.license: Public domain (artist died 1802); verify the file's tag when fetching

items.title: Franz Lehár
facts: Born at Komárom in Hungary on 30 April 1870, the son of a military bandmaster; trained as a violinist at the Prague Conservatory and was himself an army bandmaster, lastly in Vienna, until 1902.

Die lustige Witwe (1905) made him; the operettas of the 1920s, Paganini (1925), Der Zarewitsch (1927), Friederike (1928) and Das Land des Lächelns (1929), were written around the tenor Richard Tauber, whose song in the last is 'Dein ist mein ganzes Herz'.
Giuditta, his last stage work, opened at the Vienna State Opera on 20 January 1934 with Tauber and Jarmila Novotná; he died at Bad Ischl on 24 October 1948, where his villa on the Traun is a museum.

Hitler's favourite operetta was The Merry Widow. Lehár stayed in Vienna after the Anschluss, his Jewish wife Sophie protected by a special status, while his librettist Fritz Löhner-Beda, who had written Das Land des Lächelns, was murdered at Auschwitz in December 1942.
items.remark: Every Lehár of the 1920s has a tenor part built for Richard Tauber, and 'Dein ist mein ganzes Herz' from Das Land des Lächelns is the one Tauber sang in every language he had; the composer was a Hungarian bandmaster's son who stayed in Vienna through the Nazi years.
items.gaffe: Counting him among the Strausses, or the Widow as Golden Age. He was born in Hungary in 1870, trained in Prague, and is the Silver Age of operetta, the generation after Die Fledermaus.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Lehár, Franz'
Richard Traubner, Operetta: A Theatrical History (2nd ed., 2003)
Bernard Grun, Gold and Silver: The Life and Times of Franz Lehár (1970)

items.title: Theater an der Wien
facts: Opened on 13 June 1801 by Emanuel Schikaneder, the librettist and first Papageno of Die Zauberflöte, to replace his Theater auf der Wieden; the Wien in the name is the river it stands on, and the Papagenotor on Millöckergasse, with Schikaneder as Papageno, survives from the original building.

Beethoven lodged in the building and used it: Fidelio opened there on 20 November 1805, the Eroica had its first public performance there on 7 April 1805, and the concert of 22 December 1808 introduced the Fifth and Sixth Symphonies.
The operetta house of the Golden and Silver Ages: Die Fledermaus (1874), Der Zigeunerbaron (1885) and Die lustige Witwe (1905) all opened here.

Closed after the Staatsoper company left in 1955, reopened in 1962, and from the 1980s a musicals house, where Cats ran for seven years from 1983; since 2006, the Mozart year, it has been an opera house again on the stagione system, one production at a time.
items.remark: The Wien in the name is the river, not the city: Schikaneder built it on the Wien in 1801, Beethoven lodged in it and gave Fidelio there, Fledermaus and The Merry Widow opened on its stage, and it spent the 1980s running Cats before going back to opera in 2006.
items.gaffe: Calling it a musicals house. It was one from the 1980s to 2006; since then it has been Vienna's third opera house, one production at a time, and it is the room where Fidelio, the Eroica and Die Fledermaus were first heard.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Vienna'
Lewis Lockwood, Beethoven: The Music and the Life (2003)
Theater an der Wien, 'History of the house'

items.title: Volksoper Wien
facts: Opened on 14 December 1898 on the Währinger Strasse as the Kaiser-Jubiläums-Stadttheater, a playhouse marking Franz Joseph's fifty years on the throne; it took up opera in 1903 and became the Volksoper.
It gave Vienna its first Tosca, in 1907, and its first Salome, in 1910, neither of which the Court Opera on the Ring had yet staged.
From 1945 to 1955, while the bombed State Opera was rebuilt, the Staatsoper company played here and at the Theater an der Wien.
Today it is a repertory house for operetta, opera sung in German, musicals and dance, out by the Gürtel rather than on the Ring.
items.remark: It began as a jubilee playhouse for Franz Joseph's fifty years in 1898 and only turned to opera in 1903, then gave Vienna its first Tosca in 1907 and its first Salome in 1910 while the Court Opera on the Ring had staged neither.
items.gaffe: Treating it as the Staatsoper's understudy. It is the house for operetta and opera in German, it housed the Staatsoper company itself from 1945 to 1955, and it is on the Gürtel, not the Ring.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Vienna'
Volksoper Wien, 'History of the Volksoper'

items.title: Opernball (the Vienna Opera Ball)
facts: The Court Opera held its first ball soirée in 1877; the first ball under the name Wiener Opernball was in 1935, and the modern series dates from 1956, the first carnival after the rebuilt house reopened.

The seats come out and a dance floor goes in level with the stage in the days before; dress is white tie for men and floor-length for women, and the debutantes' committee, in white with tiaras, opens with a polonaise before the call of 'Alles Walzer' clears the floor for everyone.
It was cancelled in 1991 during the Gulf War and in 2021 and 2022 for the pandemic; the demonstrations against it in the late 1980s and 1990s, the Opernballdemo, became a fixture of their own.
items.remark: The seats come out and a floor goes in level with the stage, so the debutantes open the ball on what is normally the set; it is white tie, on the Thursday before Ash Wednesday, and it was cancelled in 1991 for the Gulf War.
items.gaffe: Turning up in black tie, or calling it the Philharmonic Ball. Black tie is turned away at the door, the Philharmonic's ball is another night in the Musikverein, and the Opernball is the Staatsoper's own, once a year, on the Thursday before Ash Wednesday.
sources: Wiener Staatsoper, 'The Vienna Opera Ball: history'
Wien Geschichte Wiki, 'Opernball'

term: The gala performance that opens the Vienna State Opera's season each September, with the orchestra on stage and the audience in evening dress.
The Vienna Philharmonic's carnival ball in the Golden Hall of the Musikverein in January.
The New Year's Eve performance of Die Fledermaus at the State Opera, followed by dancing in the foyers.

items.definition: The ball held inside the Vienna State Opera on the Thursday before Ash Wednesday, the last great night of the Viennese carnival: the stalls are floored over level with the stage, dress is white tie and floor-length, and a committee of debutantes in white opens the dancing.

items.title: Regietheater
facts: The usual starting point is Patrice Chéreau's centenary Ring at Bayreuth in 1976, which set Wagner among the dams and frock coats of the industrial nineteenth century; it was booed in 1976 and given a long ovation in its last year, 1980.

Its roots are earlier: Wieland Wagner cleared the scenery off the Bayreuth stage from 1951, and Walter Felsenstein's Komische Oper in East Berlin made the director's reading the point of the evening from 1947.

Hans Neuenfels's Frankfurt Aida of 1981, with Aida as a cleaning woman, and Calixto Bieito's Entführung at the Berlin Komische Oper in 2004, set in a brothel, are the productions opponents cite; English critics say 'director's theatre' or, less kindly, 'Eurotrash'.
Vienna's Staatsoper has been the conservative pole: Otto Schenk's 1968 production of Der Rosenkavalier is still in the repertory, and the Theater an der Wien has taken the newer stagings since 2006.
items.remark: It is a German word for a German habit: Chéreau's Bayreuth Ring of 1976, booed on its first night and cheered off in 1980, is where the argument starts, and Otto Schenk's 1968 Rosenkavalier, still on at the Staatsoper, is the argument on the other side.
items.gaffe: Using it to mean modern dress. Updated costumes are the least of it; the word means the director's reading outranks the libretto, and a production can be in period and still be Regietheater if it rewrites what happens.
sources: Grove Music Online, 'Production'
Frederic Spotts, Bayreuth: A History of the Wagner Festival (1994)
Carolyn Abbate and Roger Parker, A History of Opera (2012)

term: A production that follows the composer's stage directions and reproduces the sets and costumes of the premiere.
The German repertory system, in which a house keeps a resident company and rotates dozens of works through a season.
The practice of performing opera in the language of the audience rather than the original.

items.definition: German for director's theatre: opera staging in which the director's concept, not the libretto's stated time and place, governs the production, relocating or reinterpreting the work and sometimes contradicting its text; used by admirers and, more often, by opponents.

items.title: Prompter (Souffleur, Souffleuse)
facts: The opera prompter's box is sunk into the stage at the front centre with its hood towards the audience; the prompter sees the conductor on a monitor or in a mirror and passes on words and, when needed, the beat.
In the spoken theatre the prompter sat at the side of the stage, which is why 'prompt side' and 'opposite prompt' are still British names for the two sides, prompt side usually being stage left.

A repertory house such as the Staatsoper, which changes its opera almost every night on little rehearsal, still depends on prompters; the Metropolitan Opera keeps a box too, and some houses have done away with theirs.
The word is from the French souffler, to breathe or whisper; the Italian suggeritore is the one who suggests.
items.remark: The hooded hump at the front of the stage is the prompter's box, and in a repertory house like the Staatsoper, which can change its opera every night on a morning's rehearsal, the Souffleuse is the one feeding every singer the next line a beat early.
items.gaffe: Assuming a singer who glances at the box has dried. The prompt is routine and a word ahead, and in a house running dozens of operas a season almost nobody sings without it; the one who has forgotten is the one who stops.
sources: The Oxford Companion to Music (ed. Alison Latham, 2002), 'Prompter'
John Warrack and Ewan West, The Oxford Dictionary of Opera (1992), 'Prompter'

term: The stage manager who calls the scene changes and lighting cues from the wings, 'on the book'.
The répétiteur who plays the piano at rehearsals and coaches the singers in their roles.
A paid group in the audience who lead the applause at agreed moments, the claque.

items.definition: The person in the hooded box at the front centre of the stage who, facing the singers and watching the conductor, gives them the first words of each phrase a moment before they sing them; the Souffleur or Souffleuse of a German house, the maestro suggeritore of an Italian one.

scenarios.setting: A bench in the Tribune of the Accademia, under the David. Your host has queued forty minutes for this.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "Extraordinary that they left him out in the rain for so long."

options.text: Nearly four centuries of it, 1504 to 1873, and outdoors was never the plan: he was carved for a buttress of the cathedral, and a committee with Leonardo and Botticelli on it argued over where he should go before he ended up in front of the town hall instead.
options.explanation: Agrees with the host, is specific, and adds two things they did not have: the block was meant for a cathedral buttress, and the placing was argued over by a committee that included Leonardo and Botticelli. The dates are right: outside the Palazzo della Signoria from 1504, indoors at the Accademia from 1873.

options.text: Donatello had a go at the block first and gave it up, which is why it lay about the workshop for so long.
options.explanation: Wrong sculptor. Agostino di Duccio roughed out the block in the 1460s and abandoned it; Michelangelo, aged twenty-six, took it on in 1501. Donatello's David is the bronze in the Bargello, some sixty years older, and shows him after the fight with Goliath's head at his feet.

options.text: I preferred the one in the piazza, to be honest. The light is better outside.
options.explanation: A gaffe: the David in the Piazza della Signoria is a copy of 1910. You have just told your host, after their forty-minute queue, that you like the replica better than the marble in front of you.

sources: Galleria dell'Accademia, Florence, catalogue entry 'David'
Charles Seymour, Michelangelo's David: A Search for Identity (1967)
Museo Nazionale del Bargello, Florence, catalogue entry 'David'

scenarios.setting: Dinner in a house in the Oltrarno. Your host spent the afternoon in the Brancacci Chapel at Santa Maria del Carmine.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "Masolino's Adam and Eve are so much prettier than Masaccio's, aren't they? I felt rather sorry for his pair."

options.text: That contrast is the whole point of the chapel: Masolino's two are still in the garden, Masaccio's are being thrown out of it, and he paints the grief as body weight, Eve howling and Adam hiding his face. Michelangelo came here to copy Masaccio as a boy and answered this pair with his own Expulsion on the Sistine ceiling; and until 1990 Masaccio's two wore fig leaves the grand dukes had ordered.
options.explanation: Takes the host's observation seriously and turns it into the reading the chapel invites: the Temptation and the Expulsion face each other across the entrance arch on purpose. The two facts the host probably lacked are that Michelangelo studied here as a young man (Vasari says so, and his drawing after the Tribute Money survives) before painting his own Expulsion on the Sistine ceiling, and the fig leaves, added under the Medici grand dukes and removed in the restoration completed in 1990.

options.text: Masolino was his father, of course, so he had the head start; the names give it away.
options.explanation: Wrong. They were not related. Masolino da Panicale and Masaccio, born Tommaso di ser Giovanni in 1401, were two painters who shared the chapel; both names are nicknames from Tommaso, not a surname. Masaccio died in Rome in 1428 aged twenty-six, and Filippino Lippi finished the chapel in the 1480s.

options.text: Half an hour queuing for two patches of wall. It is all in the Uffizi anyway, in better light.
options.explanation: A gaffe on two counts: it dismisses the afternoon your host has just enjoyed, and a fresco is part of the wall; nothing of the Brancacci Chapel is in the Uffizi. Vasari says the later Florentine painters went to that chapel to learn, which is a reasonable reason to go yourself.

sources: Grove Art Online, 'Masaccio'
Umberto Baldini and Ornella Casazza, The Brancacci Chapel Frescoes (1992)
Giorgio Vasari, Lives of the Artists, Life of Masaccio

scenarios.setting: A house party in the hills above Florence. After dinner someone points out that Galileo's villa at Arcetri is just over the ridge.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "And when they made him recant he got up off his knees and said 'eppur si muove'. Marvellous man."

options.text: It is a marvellous line, and it turns up in print for the first time in 1757, in London, in a book by Baretti, who was Dr Johnson's friend rather than Galileo's. What is documented is better in a way: he went on saying the earth moved, in private, under house arrest at Arcetri, and Milton walked up the hill to see him there in 1638.
options.explanation: Generous about the line, honest about its date, and it gives the host something they did not have: Giuseppe Baretti's The Italian Library (1757) is the earliest known printing, a hundred and twenty-four years after the trial, and Milton's visit to Arcetri in 1638 is attested in Areopagitica.

options.text: He did, though that was in 1616, the first time they had him in Rome.
options.explanation: Wrong year. In 1616 Galileo was warned not to hold or defend Copernicus, and there was no trial. The trial, the sentence of 22 June 1633 and the abjuration on his knees at Santa Maria sopra Minerva came seventeen years later. And in neither year did anyone hear him say it.

options.text: And then they burned him for it, which rather makes the point about the Church and science.
options.explanation: A gaffe: he was not burned. He was threatened with torture, abjured, and served his sentence under house arrest at his villa at Arcetri, where he wrote the Two New Sciences and died in 1642. Giordano Bruno was burned, in Rome in 1600. Lecturing the table on a fact you have wrong is the exposing part.

sources: Giuseppe Baretti, The Italian Library (London, 1757)
Maurice A. Finocchiaro, The Galileo Affair: A Documentary History (1989)
J. L. Heilbron, Galileo (2010)

scenarios.setting: Interval at the Teatro del Maggio, the Maggio Musicale's new house by the Cascine, at Monteverdi's L'Orfeo.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "The very first opera, and in the city where opera was born. Rather moving, I thought."

options.text: The first one anyone stages for pleasure, certainly, though Mantua gets the credit: the Gonzagas put it on in 1607, seven years after the Medici had Peri's Euridice sung at the Pitti for a wedding. Did you notice the trumpet toccata at the start? He used it again to open the Vespers of 1610.
options.explanation: Agrees where the host is right, corrects the geography without making a point of it, and adds a fact they did not have: the opening Toccata reappears at the start of the 1610 Vespers. L'Orfeo was first given at the Gonzaga court in Mantua on 24 February 1607; the first opera with a surviving score is Peri's Euridice, Florence, 1600.

options.text: Monteverdi wrote it for the Medici, didn't he, for one of the weddings at the Pitti.
options.explanation: Wrong court. L'Orfeo was written for the Accademia degli Invaghiti at the Gonzaga court in Mantua, on Alessandro Striggio's libretto. The Pitti wedding opera was Peri's Euridice, sung on 6 October 1600 for the marriage of Maria de' Medici to Henri IV.

options.text: Moving? Two hours of recitative. Nothing happens in opera until Mozart.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it dismisses the evening your host has just enjoyed, and it is wrong. L'Orfeo has choruses, dances, ritornellos and a printed list of the instruments it needs, which is rare for 1609; the recitative is the part the Florentines had just invented, not the whole of it.

sources: Grove Music Online, 'Orfeo'
John Whenham (ed.), Claudio Monteverdi: Orfeo (Cambridge Opera Handbooks, 1986)
Grove Music Online, 'Euridice'

scenarios.setting: Dinner in a palazzo on the Via Maggio. The sorbet has just been put down.
scenarios.prompt: Your hostess says: "Florentine, of course. Catherine de' Medici took ice cream to France with her, and the fork, and taught them to cook."

options.text: She would have enjoyed hearing it; she was fourteen when she left in 1533, and nobody at the French court remarked on her forks. What she did carry across was Italian dancing masters: the festivals she staged are where the ballet de cour begins, and the granddaughter she brought up married the Grand Duke here in 1589.
options.explanation: Kind to the hostess, and it swaps a myth for two better facts: the French ballet de cour began in the festivals of Catherine's court, and Christine of Lorraine, whom she raised, married Ferdinando I in 1589, the wedding the Florentine intermedi were written for. Food historians have found no contemporary evidence for the forks, the ices or the cooks.

options.text: Married off to Francis I at fourteen. Imagine.
options.explanation: Wrong husband. She married Henri, Francis I's second son, at Marseille on 28 October 1533, with her kinsman Clement VII presiding; he became Henri II in 1547 and kept Diane de Poitiers as his mistress throughout. Francis I was her father-in-law.

options.text: Somebody had to. The French had no cuisine to speak of until a Medici showed them.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it inflates a story nobody in 1533 told into a slight on a whole country, at somebody else's table. The Medici cook legend has no sixteenth-century source; say something about the ballet instead.

sources: R. J. Knecht, Catherine de' Medici (1998)
Barbara Ketcham Wheaton, Savoring the Past: The French Kitchen and Table from 1300 to 1789 (1983)
Nina Treadwell, Music and Wonder at the Medici Court: The 1589 Interludes for La pellegrina (2008)

scenarios.setting: A private concert in a palazzo near Santa Croce. The harpsichordist has just finished a set of variations on a tune your host knows.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "That was the Ballo del Granduca, wasn't it? From the first opera, I have always been told."

options.text: That is the tune, and it is nearly a decade older than opera: it closed the intermedi of 1589, the interludes between the acts of a comedy for Ferdinando de' Medici's wedding, and Cavalieri wrote it. Keyboard composers all over Europe wrote variations on it for a century, which is why we have just heard some; and Peri and Caccini both worked on those interludes before either of them wrote an Euridice.
options.explanation: Right, and generous: the host's tune is correctly named. Cavalieri's closing ballo 'O che nuovo miracolo' from the 1589 intermedi for La Pellegrina travelled as the Aria di Fiorenza or Ballo del Granduca and served as a theme for variations for a hundred years. The intermedi are a dress rehearsal for opera, not an opera: Peri sang Arion in the fifth, Caccini wrote for the fourth, and both had composed an Euridice by 1600.

options.text: From Euridice, surely; Peri wrote it for Maria de' Medici's wedding.
options.explanation: Wrong wedding. Euridice was sung at the Pitti on 6 October 1600 for Maria de' Medici's marriage to Henri IV; the Ballo del Granduca is Cavalieri's, from the intermedi of 1589 for Ferdinando I and Christine of Lorraine, eleven years earlier. Peri was in both, singing Arion in the fifth intermedio and Orfeo in his own opera.

options.text: No, no, that is the Camerata. They invented opera in Bardi's drawing room; Galileo's father was one of them, you know.
options.explanation: A gaffe: correcting your host with a famous misconception. The Camerata was a talking shop at Bardi's house about how the Greeks sang their tragedies; it staged nothing, and the first operas came from Jacopo Corsi's circle in the 1590s, after Bardi had left for Rome in 1592. Vincenzo Galilei was its theorist, which is the one true thing in the sentence, and it does not rescue the rest.

sources: Nina Treadwell, Music and Wonder at the Medici Court: The 1589 Interludes for La pellegrina (2008)
Grove Music Online, 'Intermedio'
Claude V. Palisca, The Florentine Camerata: Documentary Studies and Translations (1989)

scenarios.setting: Interval at a Christmas Messiah in the Albert Hall. Everyone stood for the Hallelujah chorus.
scenarios.prompt: The woman beside you says: "We all stand because George II did at the first performance, of course."

options.text: So the story goes, though it first appears in a letter of 1780, thirty-seven years after the London premiere, and nobody who was there mentions the king. I stand anyway, for the trumpets and drums.
options.explanation: The register to aim for: it agrees with her where she is right, that the custom is old, and adds the one thing she did not have. The story rests on a letter written in 1780; no contemporary account puts George II at Covent Garden in March 1743. Standing is a custom, not a record, and there is no harm in keeping it.

options.text: It was Dublin, in fact; the king stood at the premiere there in April 1742.
options.explanation: Wrong. Messiah was indeed first performed in Dublin, on 13 April 1742, but George II was not there. The standing story, such as it is, has the king in London, and even there it rests on a letter of 1780.

options.text: I never stand for it. It's a chorus from an opera, not the national anthem.
options.explanation: A gaffe twice over. Messiah is an oratorio, sung in concert with no staging and no characters, not an opera; and refusing a harmless custom in front of someone who has just kept it is not wit, it is rudeness. The chorus, incidentally, closes Part Two of three, not the work.

sources: Grove Music Online, 'Messiah'
Donald Burrows, Handel: Messiah (Cambridge Music Handbooks, 1991)

scenarios.setting: Interval at the Proms, Royal Albert Hall. The second half is the Enigma Variations.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "Nimrod always undoes me. He wrote it for a funeral, didn't he?"

options.text: It has become one, at the Cenotaph every November, but he wrote it about a living friend: August Jaeger, his editor at Novello, after an evening's talk about Beethoven's slow movements. Jäger is German for hunter, hence Nimrod.
options.explanation: Right, and generous: it grants your host's feeling and gives the fact behind it. Variation IX is a portrait of Jaeger, Elgar's editor at the publisher Novello; the title is a pun on his surname, Nimrod being the mighty hunter of Genesis, and Elgar said the opening was meant to recall the slow movement of Beethoven's Pathétique. The Cenotaph came later.

options.text: Yes, for Queen Victoria's funeral in 1901; that is why it is played every Remembrance Sunday.
options.explanation: Wrong. The Variations were first performed at St James's Hall on 19 June 1899, conducted by Hans Richter; Victoria died in January 1901, by which time Nimrod had been in the repertoire for a year and a half. It was written for no funeral, and the Remembrance Sunday custom is a later one.

options.text: Elgar is all bunting and empire, isn't he? One goes to the Proms for the Beethoven.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it dismisses the piece your host has just told you moves her, and it mistakes the man. The big tune in Pomp and Circumstance made Elgar the Land of Hope and Glory composer, but the words were A. C. Benson's, and Nimrod is a private portrait of a friend. Sneering at a programme you chose to attend is not a position.

sources: Grove Music Online, 'Elgar, Edward'
Julian Rushton, Elgar: Enigma Variations (Cambridge Music Handbooks, 1999)

scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "I had not expected Caesar to be sung by a woman. Is that a modern conceit?"

options.text: An old necessity rather than a new conceit: Handel wrote Caesar in 1724 for the castrato Senesino, so the choice now is a countertenor or a mezzo. If you ever hear a baritone Caesar, somebody has transposed it.
options.explanation: Right, and it answers the question actually asked. The title role was written for Senesino and Cleopatra for the soprano Francesca Cuzzoni; with the castrati gone, the part sits in a woman's or a countertenor's range. A countertenor is not a castrato: he is an intact man singing in a trained falsetto, which is why the sound is lighter.

options.text: Handel wrote it for a soprano, Cuzzoni, so it has always been a woman's role.
options.explanation: Wrong. Cuzzoni created Cleopatra, not Caesar. Caesar was Senesino, a castrato; the part goes to women or countertenors now because his kind of voice no longer exists, not because Handel wrote it for a woman.

options.text: It is absurd. Three hours and not a sign of Brutus. I came for Shakespeare.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it announces that you did not read the programme. Haym's libretto is Caesar in Egypt in 48 BC, with Pompey's severed head presented to him and Cleopatra in disguise; Brutus is four years and another author away. Complaining that the opera is not the play is the oldest way to expose yourself at Covent Garden.

sources: Grove Music Online, 'Giulio Cesare in Egitto'
Winton Dean and John Merrill Knapp, Handel's Operas, 1704–1726 (1987)

scenarios.setting: A bench in the National Gallery, in front of the Arnolfini Portrait.
scenarios.prompt: Your companion says: "It's their wedding, of course; you can see him taking her hand for the vows."

options.text: That was Panofsky's reading in 1934, and the argument has never stopped; what nobody disputes is the line over the mirror, 'Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434', the painter telling you he was here. Look in the mirror: two people are standing where we are sitting.
options.explanation: Right, and it keeps your companion's idea alive rather than squashing it. Panofsky argued in 1934 that the picture records a marriage, and art historians have argued about it since. The Latin above the mirror, 'Jan van Eyck was here', reads like a witness's signature, and the convex mirror reflects two figures in the doorway, one of whom may be the painter. The wedding is a theory; the signature is a fact.

options.text: Yes, and the mirror shows the priest who married them.
options.explanation: Wrong. The mirror reflects two figures in the doorway, and neither is identifiable as a priest; one may be Van Eyck himself. The inscription above says only that the painter was here. Whether a marriage is happening at all is what art historians have argued about since Panofsky.

options.text: I've seen the original in Bruges. This one is rather dull by comparison.
options.explanation: A gaffe: this is the original, and the only one. The National Gallery bought it in 1842 and it has hung in London since. Claiming to have seen a better version somewhere else, while sitting in front of the thing itself, is boasting that does not survive the catalogue.

sources: National Gallery, London, catalogue entry NG186
Erwin Panofsky, 'Jan van Eyck's Arnolfini Portrait', Burlington Magazine (1934)

scenarios.setting: A private view in Cork Street. The pictures are large and abstract, and someone has just muttered 'a pot of paint in the public's face'.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "That was Ruskin on Whistler, wasn't it? And Whistler sued and won a fortune."

options.text: He won, in 1878, and the jury gave him a farthing; the costs bankrupted him the next year, which makes it the most expensive farthing in English art. The picture was Nocturne in Black and Gold, a rocket falling over Cremorne Gardens.
options.explanation: Right: it agrees with your host, corrects the one detail gently, and adds the farthing. Whistler v. Ruskin was heard in November 1878; the jury found for Whistler with damages of one farthing and each side paid its own costs, and he was declared bankrupt in 1879. Ruskin's sentence, in Fors Clavigera in 1877, was about Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket, painted from the fireworks at Cremorne Gardens in Chelsea.

options.text: Ruskin won, in fact; the jury agreed the Nocturne was unfinished, and Whistler left for Venice in disgrace.
options.explanation: Wrong on the verdict. Whistler won; it was the derisory damages and the divided costs that ruined him. He did go to Venice in 1879, but on a commission from the Fine Art Society to make etchings, and he was back in Chelsea by the end of 1880.

options.text: Ruskin had a point. It's splashes. My daughter could do it, and she's nine.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it repeats the philistine's line at a private view where the artist may be standing behind you, and it puts you on the losing side of a case decided in 1878. Whistler's answer under cross-examination, that he asked two hundred guineas not for two days' work but for the knowledge of a lifetime, is the line to have ready instead.

sources: Linda Merrill, A Pot of Paint: Aesthetics on Trial in Whistler v. Ruskin (1992)
Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, 'Whistler, James Abbott McNeill'
James McNeill Whistler, The Gentle Art of Making Enemies (1890)

scenarios.setting: A house party in Hampshire; Sunday lunch. Your host's son has just got into Eton.
scenarios.prompt: Your host, raising a glass: "Well, as the Duke said, Waterloo was won on the playing fields of Eton."

options.text: The Duke would be surprised to hear it: the line first appears in French, in Montalembert, four years after he died, and the famous wording is not found before the 1880s. He was an Etonian himself, though, so the school may keep the toast.
options.explanation: Right, and kind: it lets the toast stand while marking the quotation as legend. Montalembert printed 'C'est ici qu'a été gagnée la bataille de Waterloo' in 1856, four years after Wellington's death in 1852; Creasy's Memoirs of Eminent Etonians (1876) already has him watching cricket on the playing-fields, but the exact wording 'won on the playing fields of Eton' is not found before the 1880s, and Sir William Fraser's Words on Wellington (1889) is the usual citation. No contemporary record has the Duke saying either.

options.text: He loved the place. Five years there, and captain of the cricket, before he went on to Sandhurst.
options.explanation: Wrong in every particular. Wellington was at Eton for three years, from 1781 to 1784, was taken away early because the family could not afford it, and was not fond of it; the cult of school-organised games at Eton is Victorian, well after his time. Sandhurst did not yet exist: he was finished at a riding academy at Angers in France.

options.text: Poor boy. It is a very expensive way of learning to be rude to waiters.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it sneers at your host's son, at your host's table, over your host's wine. Whatever you think of the school, the moment called for a raised glass and one graceful sentence; there is nothing clever in a snub, and the Duke, who disliked Eton himself, would not have thanked you for it.

sources: Oxford Dictionary of Quotations (8th ed., 2014), 'Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington'
Elizabeth Longford, Wellington: The Years of the Sword (1969)
Charles de Montalembert, De l'avenir politique de l'Angleterre (1856)

scenarios.setting: Dinner in the seventh arrondissement. The conversation has reached Versailles.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "Of course, Versailles was Louis XIV's way of keeping the nobles busy, wasn't it?"

options.text: Busy and broke. Making them live at court on his timetable was the point; the etiquette was the leash, and Saint-Simon spent forty years resenting it in his memoirs.
options.explanation: Specific, agrees where the host is right, and adds one thing they did not know (Saint-Simon's memoirs). This is the register to aim for.

options.text: It was Louis XV who built it, actually; Louis XIV preferred the Louvre.
options.explanation: Wrong. Louis XIII built the hunting lodge; Louis XIV turned it into the palace and moved the court there in 1682. Louis XV inherited it.

options.text: I have never understood why anyone bothers with Versailles. It is just a very big house.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it dismisses your host's subject and announces you have nothing to add. Philistinism is not the same as wit.

sources: Saint-Simon, Mémoires

scenarios.setting: Interval at the Musikverein. The second half is Beethoven's Fifth.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "Fate knocking at the door. He said so himself, didn't he?"

options.text: His secretary Schindler said he said so, in a biography published thirteen years after the funeral, and Schindler is the witness scholars handle with tongs; he was caught adding entries of his own to the conversation books. What is certain is the first night: 22 December 1808 at the Theater an der Wien, four hours in a freezing theatre with the Pastoral and the Fourth Piano Concerto on the same bill.
options.explanation: The register to aim for: it keeps your host's phrase, tells her where it comes from, and adds a date she did not have. 'So pocht das Schicksal an die Pforte' is Anton Schindler's, from his life of Beethoven of 1840; Beethoven died in 1827, and Schindler was later shown to have written entries into the conversation books after the fact, so nothing rests on his word alone. The premiere is documented: the marathon concert of 22 December 1808 at the Theater an der Wien, where Fidelio had opened three years earlier, also introduced the Sixth Symphony and the Fourth Piano Concerto, and Reichardt, who sat through it, complained of the cold.

options.text: He did, and this is the one he dedicated to Napoleon and then scratched out when Bonaparte crowned himself.
options.explanation: Wrong symphony. The Napoleon story belongs to the Third, the Eroica of 1804: by Ferdinand Ries's account Beethoven tore the title page in two on hearing that Bonaparte had made himself emperor, and a copyist's score with the name scratched out survives in the archive of the Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, in this building. The Fifth was dedicated to Prince Lobkowitz and Count Razumovsky, two of his Viennese patrons.

options.text: Da-da-da-dum. Everyone knows the first four notes and nobody listens to the rest. I usually make my excuses at the interval.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it dismisses the piece your host has brought you to hear and announces that you intend to leave her at it. The Fifth is the argument that follows the four notes, and the finale, where C minor turns into C major and Beethoven brings in trombones, piccolo and contrabassoon for the first time in one of his symphonies, is the part nobody should walk out on.

sources: Lewis Lockwood, Beethoven: The Music and the Life (2003)
Grove Music Online, 'Beethoven, Ludwig van'
Grove Music Online, 'Schindler, Anton Felix'
Franz Gerhard Wegeler and Ferdinand Ries, Biographische Notizen über Ludwig van Beethoven (1838)

scenarios.setting: New Year's Eve at the Staatsoper, Die Fledermaus. The interval after Orlofsky's party.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "I do enjoy their giving the Prince to a woman. Is that a modern liberty?"

options.text: The original casting, in fact: Orlofsky has been a mezzo in trousers since the first night at the Theater an der Wien in April 1874, in the Cherubino line. The part people forget is that the whole plot is French, a play by Meilhac and Halévy, who wrote Carmen for Bizet the year after.
options.explanation: Right, and it gives your host something to take home. Prince Orlofsky was written for a mezzo-soprano and has been a trouser role since the premiere on 5 April 1874, like Cherubino in Figaro and Octavian in Rosenkavalier. The libretto, by Carl Haffner and Richard Genée, derives from Le Réveillon (1872) by Henri Meilhac and Ludovic Halévy, whose Carmen followed in Paris in March 1875.

options.text: A modern habit. Strauss wrote Orlofsky for a tenor; the mezzo came in with the New Year tradition.
options.explanation: Wrong. Orlofsky was a mezzo from the start, and the Staatsoper's New Year's Eve Fledermaus is a custom of long standing, not a rewrite. The tenor in the piece is Alfred, the singing teacher who is arrested in Eisenstein's dressing gown; the Prince's bored couplets, 'Chacun à son goût', have always been sung by a woman.

options.text: And to think his son went on to write Der Rosenkavalier. Quite a family.
options.explanation: A gaffe, and a famous one: Richard Strauss was no relation. He was born in Munich in 1864, the son of Franz Strauss, principal horn of the Munich court orchestra, and Der Rosenkavalier opened in Dresden in January 1911. Johann Strauss the younger's father was the other Johann Strauss, of the Radetzky March; the family made waltzes, not Elektra.

sources: Grove Music Online, 'Fledermaus, Die'
Richard Traubner, Operetta: A Theatrical History (2nd ed., 2003)
Grove Music Online, 'Strauss, Richard'

scenarios.setting: A bench in the Bruegel room of the Kunsthistorisches Museum, in front of Hunters in the Snow.
scenarios.prompt: Your companion says: "This is the cycle of the months, isn't it? All twelve of them in one room."

options.text: Three of them, all painted in 1565 for an Antwerp merchant, Niclaes Jongelinck: this one, The Gloomy Day and The Return of the Herd. The haymaking is in Prague and The Harvesters got away to the Metropolitan in New York; there were probably six, and one is lost. He had dropped the h from his name by then; the sons put it back.
options.explanation: Right, and it turns your companion's guess into a map. The series of the seasons was painted in a single year for Jongelinck; five survive, three in this room, one in Prague and one in New York, and most scholars think there were six, each covering two months. Twelve is the number of Bruegel panels the museum owns, the largest holding anywhere, which is where the confusion comes from. Bruegel signed without the h from 1559; Pieter the Younger and Jan kept it.

options.text: All twelve, yes: the museum has the whole calendar, a panel for each month.
options.explanation: Wrong. The museum does own twelve Bruegel panels, but they are not a calendar: they include The Tower of Babel, The Peasant Wedding, Children's Games and The Fight Between Carnival and Lent, and only three of the seasons. The seasons series was probably six pictures; the museum has three, and the other survivors are in Prague and New York.

options.text: A Christmas card, really. I would trade the whole room for the one Vermeer down the corridor.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it sneers at the museum's greatest possession while sitting on the bench put there to look at it, and your companion came for Bruegel. The Vermeer is here, The Art of Painting, and worth the walk; but the Bruegels are here because the Habsburgs wanted them early, Antwerp having given the seasons to Archduke Ernst in 1594 and Rudolf II having gathered more for Prague, and nobody has assembled anything like them since.

sources: Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien, Gemäldegalerie, inv. GG 1838
Manfred Sellink, Bruegel: The Complete Paintings, Drawings and Prints (2007)

scenarios.setting: Dinner in Döbling. Your hostess has spent the afternoon at the Belvedere.
scenarios.prompt: Your hostess says: "We went for the Woman in Gold and could not find her anywhere. Is she on loan?"

options.text: Gone for good, I'm afraid: her niece Maria Altmann won her back in 2006 and she hangs at the Neue Galerie on Fifth Avenue. She is Adele Bloch-Bauer, painted in 1907 after Klimt had seen the mosaics at Ravenna, and the Belvedere hung her for decades as the Woman in Gold, which kept her name off the label. You had The Kiss, though, and the state bought that one off the wall before Klimt had finished it.
options.explanation: Right, and it turns a lost afternoon into a story. Adele Bloch-Bauer I was seized after the Anschluss and shown in the Belvedere under an anonymous title until an Austrian arbitration panel restituted it to Maria Altmann in 2006; Ronald Lauder bought it that year for the Neue Galerie in New York for a reported 135 million dollars. Klimt's gold owes something to the Byzantine mosaics he saw at Ravenna in 1903. The Kiss, shown unfinished at the Kunstschau of 1908 and bought by the state there, is still the Belvedere's.

options.text: She has moved to the Leopold, with the Schieles. The Belvedere only ever had The Kiss.
options.explanation: Wrong on both counts. The Leopold Museum is Rudolf Leopold's collection, strongest in Schiele, and has never had the portrait; and the Belvedere showed Adele Bloch-Bauer I from the war years until 2006, when it was restituted to her niece and sold to the Neue Galerie in New York. It has not been in Vienna since.

options.text: Nobody knows who she was, anyway. Klimt cared about the gold, not the girl; it is a poster, not a portrait.
options.explanation: A gaffe: everybody knows who she was, and the not-knowing was manufactured. She was Adele Bloch-Bauer, wife of the sugar industrialist Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer, painted by Klimt twice; the Belvedere's title 'Woman in Gold' was what kept a Jewish sitter's name off the wall for decades. Calling a restituted picture a poster, to a hostess who has just tried to see it, is the wrong kind of memorable.

sources: Neue Galerie New York, collection entry 'Adele Bloch-Bauer I'
Anne-Marie O'Connor, The Lady in Gold (2012)
Belvedere, Vienna, collection entry 'The Kiss (Lovers)'

scenarios.setting: Supper in the Josefstadt after a revival screening of Amadeus.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "Poor Salieri. Do you think he really did it?"

options.text: Seven weeks before he died Mozart fetched Salieri in his own carriage and took him to The Magic Flute, and wrote to Constanze that Salieri shouted bravo at every number; and Salieri went on to teach Beethoven, Schubert, Liszt and Mozart's younger son. The poison is Pushkin's, from 1830. Shaffer only borrowed it, and gave Salieri the best part.
options.explanation: Right, and it answers the question with evidence rather than a shrug. Mozart's letter of 14 October 1791 describes collecting Salieri and Caterina Cavalieri in his carriage, taking them to Die Zauberflöte and hearing Salieri call out bravo or bello at every number; Mozart died on 5 December, and the register gives an acute fever. Salieri, court Kapellmeister until 1824, taught Beethoven, Schubert, Liszt and Franz Xaver Mozart. Pushkin's Mozart and Salieri of 1830 put the poison in his hand; Shaffer's Amadeus of 1979 and Forman's film of 1984 made it permanent.

options.text: He confessed, though, on his deathbed in 1825, and the confession is in the Vienna death register.
options.explanation: Wrong in the particulars. The register entry that exists is Mozart's, and it says fever, 'hitziges Frieselfieber'. What Salieri is said to have done is accuse himself in 1823, old and in mental decline; he denied it to Moscheles on his word of honour, and the story survives only second-hand, in remarks visitors wrote into Beethoven's conversation books. He died on 7 May 1825 with no confession on record.

options.text: Obviously he did. Mediocrity always hates genius; that is the whole point of the film.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it takes a play for a biography and insults a composer who taught Beethoven, Schubert and Liszt, at a table where somebody may know that. Amadeus is Peter Shaffer's invention of 1979, built on Pushkin's little tragedy of 1830 and on gossip a Berlin paper printed within a month of Mozart's death; F. Murray Abraham won an Academy Award for Salieri, which is not the same as a conviction.

sources: Grove Music Online, 'Salieri, Antonio'
H. C. Robbins Landon, 1791: Mozart's Last Year (1988)
Emily Anderson (ed.), The Letters of Mozart and His Family (3rd ed., 1985), Mozart to Constanze, 14 October 1791

scenarios.setting: A house party in the Wachau. Before dinner your host opens a bottle of Fürst von Metternich.
scenarios.prompt: Your host says: "Fürst von Metternich. Did the old fox actually own a vineyard, or is that the marketing department?"

options.text: He did, and it was his fee: Francis I gave him Schloss Johannisberg on the Rhine in 1816, the year after the Final Act, for a Congress that in the Prince de Ligne's phrase did not walk but danced. He was a Rhinelander himself, born at Koblenz to a family the Revolution had turned out of its lands, so the Emperor was sending him home with a vineyard.
options.explanation: Right, and it gives your host a toast. Metternich hosted the Congress of Vienna from September 1814; its Final Act was signed on 9 June 1815, nine days before Waterloo, and in 1816 the Emperor rewarded him with Johannisberg in the Rheingau, which is why the name is on the bottle. He was born at Koblenz on 15 May 1773 and lost the family's Rhenish lands to the French; the Prince de Ligne's 'Le congrès ne marche pas, il danse' is the line to have ready.

options.text: Napoleon's present, in fact, for brokering the marriage to Marie Louise in 1810; he kept it through everything that followed.
options.explanation: Wrong donor. Metternich did arrange Napoleon's marriage to the Emperor's daughter Marie Louise in 1810, as Austria's new foreign minister, but Johannisberg came from Francis I in 1816 as the reward for the Congress, with Napoleon already on St Helena. The marriage was Metternich's policy; the vineyard was his fee, and it came from Vienna, not Paris, followed in 1821 by the chancellorship.

options.text: Sekt? I never touch it. If one cannot have Champagne one may as well drink water.
options.explanation: A gaffe: it snubs what your host has just opened, in his own house, before you have tasted it. A guest drinks what is poured and finds something to say about it, and this bottle offered a whole evening's conversation: a chancellor who held office for thirty-nine years, was paid for a congress in vines, and fell to the barricades of 13 March 1848. Thomas Lawrence painted him for the Waterloo Chamber at Windsor; you have just declined his wine.

sources: Alan Sked, Metternich and Austria: An Evaluation (2008)
Wolfram Siemann, Metternich: Strategist and Visionary (2019)
Adam Zamoyski, Rites of Peace: The Fall of Napoleon and the Congress of Vienna (2007)
